News.title: Donald Trump's wild week as he bans media from White House and brags over Greenland 'deal'
News.content:
Donald Trump's wild week as he bans media from White House and brags over Greenland 'deal'

Donald Trump is an old man backed into a corner, and he's grasping for anything he can control

View Image (Image: Pool/ABACA/Shutterstock)

Donald Trump has suffered a series of humiliations over the last few weeks. From the Supreme Court ruling his plan to screw up the midterms by making postal voting insanely complicated couldn't be implemented in time, to his hand-picked Fed chair voting through a rate increase...to another judge saying he can't write his name on the memorial to a dead president, it's been defeat after defeat.

‌



And despite offering the American people a $5,000 bribe each and urging them to pretend he's on the ballot, it looks increasingly like his Republican Party is going to lose both houses of Congress in November's election.

‌



And when you're an old man backed into a corner, being told left and right that you can't do the things you want to do, you grab onto pretty much anything you can control.

‌



And that's probably why Trump announced last night that three news outlets would be banned from the White House and made out a fairly benign treaty extension with Denmark was a major shift in power over Greenland.

Here's how Trump's week spiralled, and how he's now trying to claw his way back.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"Oh, the ban on the free press?"

Donald Trump last night announced he was throwing CNN, Politico and MS Now out of the White House, something he genuinely referred to as a "ban on the free press."

Why? Well, because he doesn't like the things they write.

‌



Claiming the outlets were "unfair" and "dishonest", Trump said it was a "very simple ban. I don't want them in my office, I don't want them here. I would say the ban will go as far as you can. If they could straighten themselves out I'd love it."

He went on to warn the New York Times and Washington Post they could be next.

Trump tried to ban now former CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House during his first term, taking his White House pass away from him.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

But the move was blocked by a federal court after Acosta argued it infringed on his rights under the first amendment (freedom of the press) and fifth amendment (due process).

Asked if he was trying to "intimidate" the press, Trump said: "No, no, no. I dislike dishonest press, like you, I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press."

‌



Asked how the move was constitutional, Trump said: "I don't think someone should be allowed to come in and write fake stories....It's sick. There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories. Now, if they want to write them that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my...into the people's house."

At the time of writing, reporters are starting to arrive at the White House to find their passes have been deactivated.

As it stands, CNN is still down to be the nominated pool outlet travelling with Trump on Monday, so we'll see.

‌



"We've got Greenland!"

Trump last night posted a message on Truth Social that seemed to suggest Denmark had kind of given Greenland to the US. He followed that up by posting a map of the country overlaid with the Stars and Stripes.

And it's certainly been taken that way by a decent chunk of MAGA - with Utah Senator Mike Lee tweeting: "We've got Greenland! This is what winning looks like."

But it ain't really so, though, Joe.

‌



Trump said on Friday that the agreement would give the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.”Denmark and the US already have a long-standing security agreement that has allowed the US to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal was different from that.

The deal is expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York, which Trump will attend from Monday.

"Sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift"

So you might remember earlier this year that Donald Trump's adult son, Don Jr, got married for the second time. It made a bit of news at the time, because the ceremony took place in the Bahamas and Trump...the father of the groom...did not go.

‌



His excuse was that he was a little busy with the Iran war. And, sure, maybe.

But we learned this week that while the wedding itself was a smallish affair in a chapel on a private island, there was a two-day after party on a different island, which was paid for by Umar Kremlev a Russian Oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin.

The island rents for about a hundred thousand dollars a night, and other costs covered by Kremlev are said to have included a fireworks display that cost another 70 grand.

‌



Jr's new wife Bettina, described Kremlev as a "dear friend" and said he "very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us after our wedding."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

She went on to say: "It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful"

‌



Jr's people said he and Kremlev are "personal friends" but don't have a business relationship.

And the happy couple added: "It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from.

"Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."

‌



So who is this guy? Well, Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association, which is funded by the Russian state-backed energy firm Gazprom.

The group has been suspended by the Olympics, in part, for failing to report its ties to Gazprom.

As recently as this year, Kremlev was part of a Russian delegation to China led by Putin himself. Putin has also given Kremlev the Order of Friendship, one of the Russian Federation's highest honours.

‌



Donald Trump senior said: "I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn't pay for Don and Bettina's wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day."

And last night in the Oval Office Trump said he had "heard" that Don Jr had reimbursed Kremlev for the cost of the festivities - which, assuming it's true (and we shouldn't assume that...) raises the question of...why? If it's all totally above board and fine, why pay it back?

Also, the Trump family is, famously, a billionaire family. Jr's personal net worth is in the region of $300 million.

‌



Why didn't he just pay for his own party? I suspect we'll find out one day. Maybe some time before the LA Olympics.

"I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Center"

Long term readers will recall that Donald Trump has an obsession with the Kennedy Centre.

For newcomers, a quick recap: The Kennedy Centre is - or was - America's most renowned performing arts venue and organisation. A bit like The Barbican, except it's also the official national monument for John F Kennedy - one of America's most beloved presidents. A President, we should note, whose disappointing adult nephew serves in Trump's cabinet. More of him in a moment.

‌



Trump set his sights on it from day one of his second Presidency, mounting a coup to stuff the board with his own cronies and installing himself as chairman. He set about reforming it in his own image, changing the programme in a way that prompted a huge backlash plunging ticket sales. He also, in the dead of night, added his own name above the door - so it was officially called the Donald J Trump and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Literally people woke up to find he'd slapped his name on a presidential memorial. Why is he so obsessed with taking over this hallowed institution? Well, nobody really knows. But throughout history dictators have seized control of the creative arts to suppress dissent and break up alternatives to state propaganda. To be clear, I'm not saying Trump is a dictator. But I am saying he's read a few pages from the big book of things that dictators do.

Anyway, the courts, unsurprisingly told him, nah, can't do that. See congress if you want to change the name. So the name had to come down. Fast forward to a month or so ago and Trump's handpicked board came up with another plan. According to them, the building is in drastic need of repair. Now, we only have their word and some CCTV footage of bits falling off the ceiling for that. And this is the trump administration, so we definitely shouldn't take that at face value. Remember the thing with the reflecting pool?

They said Trump was willing to close the centre for repairs, and he'd ensure the funding was there to renovate - IF the courts agree to put his name back up on the wall. In smaller letters this time, and underneath JFK's name rather than on top. And a federal judge blocked both the closure and the name change.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

On Tuesday, the board closed the building anyway, in defiance of the judge's ruling. The same day, there was a reportedly chaotic meeting of the centre's board, during which they voted for a third time to close the building. This was opposed by Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat ex officio board member, who is behind the lawsuit that is blocking the process in the courts.

After that, Trump issued a pretty ominous statement on Truth Social. If the courts ruled against his appeal, and refused to let him put his name on the wall, he said, "the reconstruction and the renovation of the Kennedy Center will not take place." The centre would close "immediately" - and there was no indication of when...or if.. it would reopen.

‌



And then came the photos. Trump landed at Andrews Air Force Base after a speech in North Carolina, and a photographer snapped him looking at a big poster board, on which is clearly written "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED". The picture isn't clear, but it appears to be a manipulated image of the centre.

Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the centre, which he claimed was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it.

“We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it," he said. "I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Center.”

‌



Later last night, supporters and patrons descended on the legendary building, forming a human chain around it in protest against Trump's apparent plans.

Remember what happened with the East Wing. Do not be surprised if you wake up one morning in the near future to see footage of bulldozers.

"You've got a friend in the White House"

Robert F Kennedy Jr told members of an anti-vaccine group he founded that they have a "steadfast friend at the White House".

‌



RFK, who is Donald Trump's health secretary, was speaking at a convention of Children's Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade.

His speech came after four people did of measles in Pennsylvania, in the worst outbreak of the disease in decades.

"Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago," he said.

‌



Kennedy, who is not a medical professional, raised a string of baseless questions about long-established vaccine safety.

He boasted about how the Trump administration, under his guidance, had limited the number of life-saving vaccines routinely given to children in the US - including scrapping regular shots for hepatitis A and B and meningococcal, the rare virus that causes meningitis.

President Trump has made repeated and unfounded claims that the vaccine scheme was "dangerous" and contributed to increased autism diagnoses.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

And Trump suggested falsely that the Measles, Mumps and Rubella (MMR) vaccine could be "quite lethal" if taken as combined injection, and called for it to be split in to three separate shots.

Some 3,294 cases of measles have been confirmed in the US so far in 2026, up from 2,289 in the whole of 2025. according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Nearly half of the 2026 cases (45%) were in children and young people aged 5-19, with 18% of the cases affecting the under 5s.

‌



Some 95% of the cases were in unvaccinated people, or people whose vaccination status was unknown. Just 3% had had both doses of MMR. Of the 2026 cases, 267 people were hospitalised, including 66 children under 5.

In 2024, the year before Trump returned to office, there were 285 cases, and in 2023 just 59. More cases of measles have been confirmed in the US so far this year than in the decade from 2014 to 2024.

RFK spoke alongside Andrew Wakefield, the disgraced British former doctor whose fabricated research first popularised the false claim that the MMR vaccine is linked to autism.

Article continues below

After being struck off in the UK, and ostracised by the medical community, Wakefield moved to the US, where he has since become a minor celebrity in the anti-vaccine world.

News.title: Major seaside hotel fire that evacuated guests during night treated as suspicious
News.content:
A fire at a seaside hotel where about 280 people were evacuated is believed to have been caused deliberately, police have said.

A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said.

Kent Police said that the fire was being treated as suspicious and is appealing for witnesses.

"Inquiries into the circumstances are under way," police said.

News.title: Davey says Lib Dems are 'firewall against Farage' as conference begins
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.

The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance.

On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state".

Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs.

Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak".

In an essay, external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"

She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".

Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that.

"If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives."

He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world.

"I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration."

Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government.

"One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said.

"Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well.

"We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform."

He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away".

Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union.

The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems.

"An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said.

"Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency.

"A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass."

Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink".

Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.

A fresh cohort of famous faces â including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips â also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

News.title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he is telling the truth about a phone call with Charles after Diana's death
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother said King Charles "went ballistic" during a phone call with him in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer spoke exclusively with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg about claims he has made in a new book, alleging the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly-worded response to the book claims, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Read more about Laura Kuenssberg's interview with Earl Spencer.

News.title: Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals
News.content:
At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."

He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.

Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.

The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".

Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.

Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.

Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.

The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.

Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".

There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.

That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".

Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997.

"This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.

Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby, who led the BBC's coverage of Diana's funeral, said it seemed "odd" Earl Spencer would release the book now.

"Why 30 years later for God's sake you should do it... you have to ask him," he said on Radio 4's Today programme, adding he wished the appetite for the "cycle of gossip" would decline and instead that focus would shift to what kind of monarchy the country needed.

News.title: When a cherished tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
News.content:
Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.

But this year, one tree was visibly suffering.

"Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.

The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.

A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?

The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym.

"Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die.

"How heartbreaking would that be?"

So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.

News.title: Analysis: Trump escalates media fight after week of setbacks
News.content:
The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.

First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".

These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.

His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions.

The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.

Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.

In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka â a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.

Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.

News.title: I found my partner at an Irish matchmaking festival - now I want others to do the same
News.content:
Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.

The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner".

But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.

So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.

Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
News.content:
One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".

The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.

In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK.

"In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."

He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.

Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.

Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."

Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.

Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.

Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".

Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, told the BBC: "Reforming parenting orders in this way risks being ineffective at best and counter-productive at worst.

"Criminalising parents is unlikely to help children who need support, and putting them behind bars would only put further strain on a failing prison system that is already bursting at the seams."

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum Â£1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all".

In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response".

The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14.

On Thursday, ministers met with local leaders and experts in Manchester to discuss how devolution could help reform youth justice.

Additional reporting by AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul & Shelley Phelps, political correspondent

News.title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
News.content:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
News.content:
Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief.

She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases.

"We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture.

"There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so.

"Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it."

Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve.

She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more.

"In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could."

For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said.

"The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say.

"People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'.

"It can mean even more coming from a stranger."

Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies.

"But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said.

Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do.

"So if anybody can find the way of looking at themselves and just thinking, this hurts right now because I'm decent, because I'm caring, because I have a heart. And I think that's a way of easing ourselves through it."

If you, or someone you know, have been affected by child bereavement, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
News.content:
Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them.

The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city.

"It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said.

Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates.

One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre.

"I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said.

"People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check.

"They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens."

News.title: Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice
News.content:
Reform UK's deputy leader has accused the party's former Senedd Member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd of lying to them about her political beliefs before she defected to Plaid Cymru.

Richard Tice was speaking after a chaotic week for his party in which its Welsh leader resigned after being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Helen Jenner, the party's deputy leader in Wales, is favourite to take over next week.

Tice insisted the events had not distracted the party from the issues it was tackling, saying there were good days and bad days in politics.

Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been "honest about her political beliefs" and had acknowledged her views had changed.

Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, made the dramatic political move to Plaid Cymru, claiming Reform UK was "far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions".

As well as saying she was now a supporter of Welsh independence, she also revealed she had voted to Remain in the EU referendum a decade ago.

Converse has apologized and pulled a sneaker ad after online backlash over imagery critics compared to the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.

The ad, part of Converse’s global campaign for its Chuck 70 X sneaker, featured K-pop star Karina of the group Aespa standing beneath a star-shaped spotlight while holding a pair of black high-top Converse sneakers. She wore a long white skirt, while the lighting made her silhouette look to many social media users like a KKK hood, with the dangling sneakers drawing comparisons to a lynching victim.

The Chuck 70 X was released globally on August 27, and the controversial image was posted to Converse’s social media accounts earlier this month. But the backlash intensified after social media users circulated an uncropped version of the , which they said made the resemblance to a pointed hood and hanging body more apparent.

Converse, which is owned by Nike, told The Independent in a statement: “We’re sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.”

Still, fans and public figures alike continued to share their thoughts on the ad.

open image in gallery Converse has apologized and pulled a sneaker ad after critics online said its imagery evoked the KKK and lynching ( Converse )

“No, you’re not crazy. Yes, the Converse ad is racist. Yes, it looks like a Klan outfit. Yes, it looks like a lynching. And no, ‘it’s just a shoe ad’ is not a defense,” one fan wrote on X.

Chicago-based photographer Stephanie Schwartz criticized the campaign on Threads, writing: “Shadow, light, and composition. Every photographer can tell you, whoever did this ad knew EXACTLY what they were doing.”

Actress Yvette Nicole Brown also reacted to the campaign on Threads, writing: “That’s a lynching, yes?”

The controversy also resurfaced a separate Converse campaign featuring footwear in a tree. The image, created for a collaboration with Copenhagen-based lifestyle brand Palmes, showed a person standing on a ladder with a pair of sneakers hanging from a tree branch. The image was reportedly released on September 14, Adweek reports.

Social media users shared the image alongside the Karina ad, saying the two campaigns together heightened concerns about the imagery.

One Threads user described the second image as doubling down on the symbolism, while another posted them side-by-side, writing: “There is NO REASON why WE should see an  & immediately think of Strange Fruit by Billie Holiday.”

Only one year ago, Mississippi fans hailed Lane Kiffin as the coach that helped them beat border-state rival LSU.

On Saturday, as the No. 8 Rebels prepared to host No. 7 LSU, Ole Miss fans were eager to mock and heckle Kiffin in myriad ways — and did so amid abundant security measures designed to ensure any expressions of betrayal, resentment or anger didn’t get out of hand as the lightning-rod coach returned to campus, this time with the Tigers.

The scene made Jessica Perkins, a 47-year-old Oxford-area dentist and Ole Miss graduate, a bit nervous.

She noted lightheartedly that “absolutely nothing good,” can happen when “the added animosity of the Kiffin situation” is layered upon longstanding rivals indulging in a full day of consumption of alcohol in oppressively hot weather — mostly sunny and in the mid 90s.

“Let's just play football and ignore the whole elephant in the room,” Perkins said. “We're the hospitality people. So, we're also praying that everybody stays safe, doesn't act stupid and we just show everybody a good time. Ole Miss is always going to win the party.”

LSU fans are regularly referred to as “corndogs” (because of the deep-fried aroma at their stadium) by fans at rival Southeastern Conference schools, and art posted at tailgate tents last year portrayed Kiffin riding one like a rodeo cowboy.

Predictably, Kiffin is now an object of sometimes creative derision in Oxford.

The famous, tree-lined, tailgating spot known as The Grove — where the Rebels walk on their way into Vaught-Hemingway Stadium — was teeming with people early in the morning. And when Kiffin's image appeared live on a big screen for an interview on ESPN, the first-year LSU coach was booed heartily.

Makeshift signs held aloft by members of the crowd behind the set referred to Kiffin as a traitor and portrayed him sticking corndogs up his nose and in his mouth. One stated, “This sign was listed as ‘doubtful,’” poking fun at Kiffin's apparent act of gamesmanship when he listed LSU quarterback Sam Leavitt as “doubtful” on Wednesday night before ultimately taking his name off the injury report by Friday night.

Matt Garrett, a 49-year-old Oxford resident and Ole Miss graduate, said a lot of the heckling was in good fun and that many in Mississippi were not “truly angry” at Kiffin because “he's done a lot for northern Mississippi and a lot for this program.”

Garrett said Ole Miss fans were just annoyed at the timing of his departure, right before the Rebels entered the College Football Playoff, and because of how Kiffin abruptly fled Oxford aboard a private jet sent to fetch him by LSU.

“How they kind of handled everything in the process was very unprofessional,” Garrett said. “There is going to be some anger, I'm sure, but hopefully with the Southern hospitality we have, we'll keep everything under control.”

Social media video late this week showed that Kiffin invited LSU fraternities and sororities to LSU's football facility to heckle the Tigers — an effort to provide a taste of what they would face on Saturday.

“We just try to do everything to simulate the game, simulate the day,” Kiffin said when asked about it during his morning TV appearance as boos and chants laced with vulgarities emanated from the crowd in The Grove. “There’s going to be a lot of emotion all through the stadium obviously that you’re feeling there right now.”

Mississippi state officials have said they were assembling the state’s largest law enforcement presence ever for a college football game this weekend in Oxford, a town of about 26,000 permanent residents, where authorities expected around 100,000 people to converge — many of them without tickets for 64,000-seat Vaught-Hemingway Stadium.

“Our priority is making sure everyone can enjoy the game and surrounding events safely,” said Sean Tindell, commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety. “This enhanced presence is about being prepared, staying proactive and working together.”

When Ole Miss played at Tennessee in 2021, bringing Kiffin back to another one of his previous coaching stops, play was halted for about 20 minutes after Volunteers fans upset about a fourth-down spot of the ball in the closing minutes of a close game pelted the field with objects. Kiffin said he was hit by golf balls and liquor bottles.

Ole Miss coach Pete Golding echoed the calls for restraint from Rebels fans.

“About Oxford, the first thing you talk about is the people there. Let’s not lose that over a game, over a person or anything else like that,” Golding said this week at his regular news conference. “There’s nothing wrong with being competitive, being in the moment, being really loud and being an unbelievable fan. At the end of the day, don’t lose what we’ve created.”

A Manchester teenager missing for eight days has been found “safe and well” by police.

Lillia, 13, disappeared after leaving her family home in Bolton on Friday 11 September, sparking a major search for the teenager.

Earlier on Saturday (19 September) Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers trawling CCTV in the hunt for Lillia have identified a further sighting of her at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on Monday 14 September.

open image in gallery 13-year-old Lillia missing since 11 September ( PA )

This followed a previous sighting earlier that morning, when the missing girl was seen boarding the number 36 bus from Salford before getting off in Manchester city centre.

In a statement released on Saturday evening, GMP thanked people for sharing its appeal and said: “We can confirm that she has been found safe and well in the city centre.

“She is currently with our officers, and her next-of-kin have been informed of this update. We will release more information in due course.”

The 13-year-old’s mother made a tearful appeal for her daughter to come home on Friday.

She said: "Lill, I love you so so much.

"My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe. We all you need back home safe and well."

open image in gallery Lillia at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on 14 September ( PA )

Police previously identified a sighting of Lillia at the Trafford Centre last Saturday (12 September), saying she caught a bus from there towards Altrincham.

She was seen at a McDonald's in Piccadilly Gardens the following day, before being pictured boarding a bus from Salford to Manchester last Monday morning.

Luke Littler edged his way into the last eight of World Series of Darts Finals with a narrow 10-9 win over Nathan Aspinall amid constant whistling from members in the crowd.

Littler came out on top in a nail-biting last-leg shootout to book a place in the quarter-finals with Jonny Clayton despite missing 22 darts at a double.

Earlier in the match, Aspinall alerted referee Charlie Costorphine to tell members of the crowd to stop whistling, but it continued.

The whistling, which was louder when Littler was at the oche, seemed to throw the ‘Nuke’ off his rhythm as he slipped from 3-1 up to 5-3 down.

Aspinall missed two darts at a double to make it 7-5 and Littler went on to take the next two legs to get back into the contest.

It looked like Littler would take the next leg but the game took another twist as the world champion’s double woes continued, missing two tries at double 15 which allowed Aspinall to level the contest once more at 7-7.

The crowd issues continued and Costorphine again had to remind spectators about their behaviour in the 17th leg just before Aspinall put himself 9-8 to the good and within one leg of becoming the first person to knock Littler out of a Premier event in 329 days.

However, Littler showed his class and reeled off the last two legs and pinned double 20 to book his spot in the final day

open image in gallery Jonny Clayton will be Littler’s next opponent in Amsterdam (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

After the game, he said: “We know what Nathan is like. He pushed me all the way and that’s what he’s done there yet again, and maybe if he had a better start in previous legs it would be a different game.

“I only played well in the last session. The first two sessions I didn’t feel confident.

“I know my doubling is never going to be 100 per cent perfect. I’ve just got to come back tomorrow and sharpen up.”

Clayton battled back from 6-4 down to beat Motomu Sakai 10-8 and reach the quarter-finals of the competition while Gerwyn Price averaged nearly 98 in a comfortable 10-5 victory over Canadian Jim Long.

Price will face James Wade, who beat Wessel Nijman 10-7, while former world champion Luke Humphries was dumped out of the competition by Dirk van Duijvenbode, losing 10-9, and he will face Gian van Veen.

Drivers in vehicles built to move low and slow cruised Saturday down San Francisco's Mission Street in celebration of one of the city’s most distinctive cultural traditions: lowriding.

Music played as hundreds of customized cars bounced, tilted and otherwise made their way along the annual King of the Streets event, part of National Hispanic Heritage Month. Spectators and participants of all ages celebrated the culture, which once was the target of police crackdowns and is now commemorated on U.S. Postal Service stamps.

“We finally got our stamp of approval,” said Roberto Hernandez, founder of the San Francisco Lowrider Council. In addition to this year’s rollout of stamps featuring five classic lowriders, California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently announced a specialized state lowrider license plate.

“We have a lot to celebrate this year,” Hernandez said.

Lowriding has deep roots in Mexican American and Chicano communities in the U.S. Southwest, with California widely credited as the birthplace of the modern lowrider movement. States including Texas and Arizona have their own long histories that contributed to the culture.

Hernandez calls lowriding an art form and each vehicle an art piece. Cars are transformed with lowered suspensions, elaborate paint, chrome, custom interiors and hydraulics capable of making the vehicles bounce and hop.

For many participants, it is also an expression of Mexican American identity, family and craftsmanship.

“It’s about driving low, being seen and going slow,” said Johnny Castro, who was participating Saturday, adding: “We go slow so people can see us, see our art that we put together here, because it does take time and money to put these cars together.”

The road to acceptance for lowriding has been long. Hernandez recalls a time when police issued citations, made arrests and shut down Mission Street. He ultimately sued the city and police department, arguing for the right to cruise. But the fight wasn't unique to San Francisco.

Beginning in the 1980s, other California cities adopted anti-cruising rules. Critics of those laws argued enforcement disproportionately affected Latino communities and stigmatized a cultural tradition.

In 2023, Newsom signed legislation removing California’s restrictions on cruising and stripping local governments of the ability to enact bans based on repeatedly driving through an area.

Lowriding has become a family affair for Castro.

“Rolling with my wife and my kids. We all have our own little rides, and it’s great,” he said.

News.title: Dani Dyer locked herself away for days after ‘devastating’ Strictly Come Dancing exit
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing contestant Dani Dyer said she was “heartbroken for days” after she was forced to leave last year’s series due to injury.

The former Love Island winner told presenter Emma Willis how she shut herself in her bedroom after being forced to withdraw from the 2025 series.

“I locked myself in my room, and my mum was like knocking on my door, and she was like, ‘that’s enough now, you’ve got to get out of bed’.

“I was like, ‘I’ve got nothing to get up for’, (and) mum, she was like, “you’ve got three children”, so yeah, when they asked me to come back, I was like, ‘yes, please’, I’m just so grateful.”

Dyer has now been reunited with professional dance partner Nikita Kuzmin.

News.title: Murder suspect who tried to surrender at police station was turned away by NYPD cop: report
News.content:

A murder suspect accused of beating a New York City mother to death and leaving her body with her 7-year-old daughter allegedly walked out of an NYPD station after trying to surrender, according to his attorney and the New York Post.

Tiliek Shamel Thompson, 41, went to the 33rd Precinct stationhouse in Washington Heights around 5 a.m. on September 11, accompanied by his two cousins, as police investigated the killing of Lovay Williams, 27. However, he was not successfully taken into custody until September 12, when he was charged with murder, assault, strangulation and acting in manner injurious to a child.

Williams was found dead inside her apartment on 156th Street on September 6, suffering trauma to her face and neck, according to the Post. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Her 7-year-old daughter was also inside the apartment but was found unharmed. Williams and Thompson were dating, relatives told the Post.

Days later, Thompson and his cousins went to the station because they understood police were looking for him, his attorney, Neville Onielle Dexter Mitchell, told the Post.

“His two cousins said, ‘You’re looking for him,’” Mitchell said, according to the Post.

open image in gallery An NYPD officer allegedly turned away a murder suspect who tried to surrender in the killing of 27-year-old mother Lovay Williams ( AFP/Getty )

The officer working the desk allegedly responded, “I just came back from vacation. Nobody’s here,” Mitchell said.

However, an NYPD spokeswoman disputed that account to the Post after reviewing audio and video from the encounter. She said the family did not tell the officer that police were looking for Thompson and that the officer misunderstood the group’s reason for coming to the station.

The officer reportedly believed the three were members of Williams’ family and relayed that information to a sergeant. The officer's reference to being on vacation was meant to explain that he had been away when Williams was killed, according to the NYPD spokeswoman.

The officer then gave one of Thompson’s cousins a phone number for homicide detectives and allowed the group to leave.

Thompson, who police sources reportedly identified as a person of interest in Williams’ killing, later returned to police and successfully surrendered. He was charged with murder.

The NYPD has acknowledged that the encounter was mishandled, according to the Post.

The Independent has contacted the NYPD for comment.

The alleged handling of Thompson’s attempted surrender has drawn criticism from current and former NYPD officers, who said officers should have detained him or contacted homicide detectives even if investigators were not immediately available.

“If he went there and said he was there to turn himself in, they should have investigated,” a senior police officer told the Post on the condition of anonymity.

“I’d say you should hold the guy and investigate further,” the officer added. “Even if detectives aren’t there, you can call them. I’m sure they’d love to take a homicide collar.”

open image in gallery The man went to the 33rd Precinct stationhouse in Washington Heights with his two cousins on September 11 as police investigated Williams’ killing, but he was not charged until the following day ( Google Maps )

Former NYPD Detective Michael Alcazar similarly said officers should have contacted detectives working the overnight shift, known as nightwatch.

“You got a homicide suspect turning himself in, so you detain him until the squad gets there,” he said. “I’m not surprised if they turned him away. We’re scraping the bottom of the barrel.”

The incident comes as the NYPD works to increase its ranks after years of recruitment challenges. The department hired 4,056 new officers in 2025, the largest number hired in a single year, according to the Post. The NYPD also lowered some hiring requirements, including reducing the number of college credits required from 60 to 24.

News.title: Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

News.title: Red Roses’ 39-match winning streak brought to end in Canada draw
News.content:
The record books will show that this meeting, a proper Test full of ebbs and flows, was neither. And, no matter the pre-match belief of England head coach John Mitchell, Canada are not on the same level of professionalism and funding as his side. Mitchell had brought back nine players, many of whom featured in last year’s World Cup final victory, after the thrashing of Australia last week with the expectation that the history of 2025 would repeat itself. Canada had other ideas.

“The plan on the field at the last scrum was to go for the win,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “And then the message came on from the sideline to kick it out. In that moment you have to trust your coach and your coaching staff, and we’ll have a discussion about it later. If we had given away a penalty off the next breakdown, we’d be sitting here going, ‘Why didn’t you kick it out?’”

England’s downfall came at the set-piece, where their line-out malfunctioned and their scrum never gained dominance, in a tale which was not too dissimilar to last week. The hosts came second in the physical battle, too, which was uncharacteristic of them; losing Hannah Botterman to a shoulder injury did not help, either. All told, Canada just looked as though they wanted it a little bit more and maybe this was the wake-up call the Red Roses needed: when you are at the top, and at the top by a margin, every team want to be the one to dethrone you.

News.content:
It was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”

News.title: Global fund utilises AI to tackle malaria, TB, and HIV amid aid cuts
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping to soften the blow from aid cuts, according to one of the world’s biggest development funds.

The Global Fund, which raises and invests billions of pounds to reduce the burden of HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria globally says new AI-driven products like portable pregnancy scanners are helping to mitigate the funding gap.

“[We] have adapted pretty quickly to the changes in the funding environment; it has undoubtedly had negative impacts on health outcomes [...], but in some ways, the resilience of life-saving services has been remarkable,” Peter Sands, the executive director of the Global Fund, told The Telegraph.

The Global Fund is managing a $6 billion (£4.4bn) shortfall for the period 2026 to 2028 and has been forced to make difficult decisions to continue their work, it confirmed this week.

The gap comes as Western governments shift money from foreign aid to defence. The UK reduced its contribution to the fund by 15 per cent last year to £850 million, down from £1 billion.

But Mr Sands said investments in tools to tackle infectious diseases – including those driven by AI – are starting to pay off.

“Innovation is absolutely part of the answer when money is short. One of the few ways you can get to make the money go further is to have a better tool, a better way of doing things,” Mr Sands said.

News.title: Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

News.title: Fiji declares national crisis as HIV epidemic escalates
News.content:
“The rollout has been slow and frustrating, and Fiji will pay for it in terms of lives lost,” said Prof Lisa Maher, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute in Sydney who is supporting Fiji’s response. “This is the only thing that will turn the epidemic around and stop people dying, and stop onward transmission of HIV to the general population.”

But the emergency declaration should provide political cover to introduce the needle and syringe programme, with a Cabinet subcommittee now created to remove barriers to action.

“The government is signalling that it is prepared to act in this particularly important and controversial area,” said Prof Maher. “It’s not coincidental that the draft bill [to legalise the distribution of needles and syringes for certain groups] now looks likely to go before parliament, after being blocked for 10 months… So it’s not just symbolic.”

Dr Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s HIV taskforce, added: “Since the government announced [the crisis], it has followed with some very rapid actions in progressing the needle and syringe programme. So that is being fast tracked through the necessary channels, and the government is determined to get that out in the next couple of weeks.

“We’ve gotten to the point where we really needed to take some really strong action,” he told The Telegraph. “This is the government realising that there have been challenges, and they need to step it up.”

It is hoped that the declaration will also turbocharge other elements of the response – for instance the scale-up of the post-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) scheme, which was introduced in May – as the virus gains a foothold in the broader population.

Although there has been a major focus on testing, treatment and education, UNAIDS still estimates that only 39 per cent of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in 2025 knew their positive status. Just 22 per cent were accessing antiretroviral treatment, and 117 people died in 2025, compared to 25 in 2021.

Former Chelsea boss Liam Rosenior found himself at the centre of controversy during Paris FC's clash with Strasbourg

Former Chelsea boss Liam Rosenior found himself at the centre of a melee following Paris FC's 2-1 win over Strasbourg in Ligue 1. The 42-year-old took charge of Strasbourg prior to his move to Stamford Bridge earlier this year.

‌



Rosenior spent just four months at the Blues before he was given his marching orders by BlueCo, who also have shares in the French club. His departure for Chelsea summed up why many of the Strasbourg supporters are unhappy with their ownership model.

‌



The former Strasbourg boss was reportedly verbally abused by supporters throughout the game, and went over to celebrate and gesture in front of them after the final whistle.

“In my opinion they need to look after the kid’s health and his care, but Manchester United can give him that, they’ve got a history of doing that. I don’t see the rush, I don’t see the panic.

Article continues below

“I don’t know what’s been said or promised behind the scenes but from the outside this stinks to me that someone is pushing, forcing and rushing it. And I don’t think it’s going to help the kid in any way, shape or form.

“As a say, I’m a big rival of Manchester United, but I’ve watched Manchester United from afar, there’s top coaches there, top people. I know Michael Carrick very well and, if this kid was ready, he’d be getting played.”

Sports.title: Wrexham troll Southampton over Spygate AGAIN after cheeky Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac jibe
Sports.content:
Wrexham troll Southampton over Spygate AGAIN after cheeky Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac jibe

Wrexham co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac starred in a video trolling Southampton over the Spygate scandal before the two teams met in the Championship on Saturday

View Image Southampton were beaten by Wrexham (Image: Matt Watson/Southampton FC via Getty Images)

Wrexham have trolled Southampton for the second time in three days after beating their Championship rivals 2-1. An 89th-minute own goal from Keven Schlotterbeck gave Wrexham all three points at the Racecourse Ground, ending a run of three games without a win for Phil Parkinson's men.

‌



It also marked a huge turnaround from five months ago when Southampton rocked up in Wales and won 5-1. Weeks later, it emerged that Southampton had been spying on their opponents' training sessions, admitting to getting intel on Middlesbrough, Ipswich Town and Oxford United - behaviour which saw them kicked out of the Championship play-off final.

‌



On Thursday, Wrexham published a video of their co-owners, Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac, poking fun at Spygate. Promoting shirt sponsor Firefox, Reynolds, who had emerged from behind a tree, began: "Today, for no particular reason, we want to talk about the importance of privacy." Mac added: "Specifically, how to prevent spies from seeing what you're doing."

‌



Reynolds went on to joke about searching for 'how to run a football club' before the pair emphasised the important to privacy is 'to people everywhere'. Wrapping up the video, Reynolds said: "Refreshing, huh? An organisation that actually respects your privacy."

‌



The clip ended with both co-owners looking at a smartphone screen, allegedly showing the Southampton pickleball team practicing. Now Wrexham have taken another swipe after their victory.

The club posted on X: "April 7 2026: Wrexham AFC 1-5 Southampton. May 7 2026: Southampton get caught spying on Middlesbrough. September 19 2026: Wrexham AFC 2-1 Southampton.

"Makes you think...," they added alongside a picture of Southampton legend Matt Le Tissier.

‌



The post accumulated more than 2,600 likes within an hour of it being shared. One user replied: "Admin needs to be arrested for murder. Ouch!"

Who'll finish higher - Wrexham or Southampton? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Another said: "Unreal s***housery." But one Wrexham fan took a different view. "Guys stop it now, the video was funny but don't do this s***!"

Wrexham weren't done there either, later sharing a video mocking a Southampton fan and Saints manager Tonda Eckert. During Saturday's game, home fans chanted: "You only win when you're spying."

For Parkinson, it was all about the result after a tricky period. "I think we all needed a lift today with a gritty Wrexham performance," he noted.

Article continues below

Wrexham are now level on points with Southampton (10) after eight league games going into the international break.

Millwall vs West Ham recap: Six arrests after spitting incident and red card in heated clash

It was Millwall who looked to have the best chance as Kyrell Lisbie went clear on goal but Kante popped up at the other end to haul him down and pick up a red card as a free kick was awarded. Neither side could secure the win as it ended honours even.
