World.title: Betel nuts are a top mind-affecting substance. Now there's evidence of ancient use
World.content:
Betel nuts are a top mind-affecting substance. Now there's evidence of ancient use

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

About 600 million people today chew on betel nuts —- the brownish green seeds of certain palm trees that are about the size of a walnut. Betel nut users say they get all kinds of benefits — relief from indigestion, fresh breath, an energy boost.

The medical community notes that long-term betel nut use can damage teeth, increase the risk of heart disease, and lead to oral cancer due to the chemicals within.

Still, many people in Asia and the Asian Pacific are addicted to chewing them. Betel nuts are considered the world's fourth most commonly used mind-affecting substances, after tobacco, alcohol and caffeine.

A new study, published in Science Advances , finds this love affair with betel nuts is nothing new. In fact, it's likely very, very old. By looking at ancient teeth, researchers uncovered what they think is an early stage in the practice, when hunter-gatherers had a habit of sucking on betel nuts, possibly for their painkilling effects.

"It's a chance archaeological discovery that reveals an initial stage in the development of this common drug used today," says Adam Brumm , a professor of archaeology at Griffith University in Australia who led the research, "We think it might have started with hunter-gatherers just sucking on the nuts, almost as though they were gobstoppers ."

Sponsor Message

Outside researchers find the evidence compelling though not conclusive — and further note that drug use has longstanding and deep roots among humanity: The instinct to experiment and expand our horizons with substances is part of human nature, says José Capriles , associate professor of anthropology at Penn State University, who has found drugs used by humans a thousand years ago in South America.

Puzzled by "strange grooves"

How did scientists uncover this ancient betel nut usage? The answer involves two puzzling sets of teeth, fake saliva — and some personal experimentation.

On an archaeological dig in Sulawesi, an island in modern-day Indonesia, Brumm and his colleagues excavated some very old human remains.

They belonged to a hunter-gatherer who lived as far back as 25,000 years. The remains posed a mystery. "There were really strange grooves in the teeth that we couldn't explain," Brumm says.

He emailed other archaeologists — "all of the world's leading experts in ancient dental wear" — soliciting their advice. "None of them could explain how these grooves could have formed," says Brumm.

About 20 miles to the east, they found a second set of teeth from a human who lived up to 8,000 years ago, with similar marks. "The grooves were so deep that they had actually exposed the pulp cavity, the nerve center, of several teeth," Brumm says, describing it as a pattern that likely took decades of repeated wear to form.

Sponsor Message

While hunter-gatherers from that time are known to have used their teeth as tools — holding, breaking, stretching things — none of those uses matched the grooves on these teeth. "We ruled out any type of food they might have been eating, we ruled out the possibility that they were processing plant fibers to make string in their mouth," says Brumm.

Brumm was stumped. Then he remembered another example of distinctive teeth wear, from the colonial period in Europe, America and Australia, when laborers habitually smoked tobacco from clay pipes. "They would have the pipe sticking out of their mouth, Popeye-style," Brumm explains, "Over a lifetime of this habit, they've got a perfectly round notch in their teeth that you can slot the clay pipe stem straight into."

Brumm and his colleagues thought the teeth grooves from Indonesia might originate in a similar habit, one grounded in cultural practices.

The case for the betel nut

In the Asia and Pacific region today, betel nuts are commonly chewed with other chemicals for their combined stimulant effects.

However, the wear patterns on the teeth were consistent with sucking — not chewing — hard, round abrasive objects over many years, Brumm says. He and his colleagues think they've uncovered an early developmental stage in the practice. "We think they were hooked on nut-sucking," Brumm says. Since sucking betel nuts is not common today, Brumm partnered with Professor Roger Papke , a neuropharmacological researcher at the University of Florida, to test whether the action could cause a drug effect ancient humans may have desired.

"We soaked whole betel nuts in artificial saliva, and then introduced the resultant extracts into frog egg cells engineered to produce human brain receptors," Brumm says. They found that the artificial saliva successfully extracted arecoline, an active chemical in the betel nut, and that the brain receptors turned on when they touched the saliva. "We've shown that if you just suck on the nut, there's a physiological reaction that can be released into your bloodstream and then into your brain, and that can alter human brain function," he says.

Sponsor Message

Then they sought to establish that these ancient people actually did it. In addition to matching the shape of betel nuts to the grooves in the teeth, they tested the dental tissues and found traces of arecoline — for which betel nuts are the only known natural source , Papke says.

Brumm also put himself in the mindset of ancient humans and tried sucking on betel nuts himself. "I had to give it a go," he says, "If you gently gnaw on the outside of it, it releases the betel juice. It has this extremely bitter and astringent taste that makes your whole mouth go numb."

He hypothesizes that the numbing, pain-relieving effect was what ancient hunter-gatherers were after. Brumm thinks the betel nut suckers eventually wore their teeth down to the nerve — which he says could have been very painful — leading to more nut-sucking to relieve the pain. "They were essentially caught in this cycle and they were basically addicted to this natural plant drug," Brumm says.

Human nature

Outside researchers say the paper makes a compelling case for ancient betel nut use. "There's evidence for the betel nut causing excessive tooth wear. When you add the chemical evidence, that's pretty much a smoking gun," says Peter Ungar, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the University of Arkansas who studies teeth and was not involved in this study.

"It fits with the bigger picture of our understanding of betel [nut] use and also the cultural dynamics of that time period," says Agustín Fuentes , professor of anthropology at Princeton University.

Others would like to see additional support for the theory. "I wish there was more, I must admit — there are two skeletons that they report," says Capriles at Penn State.

Capriles acknowledges that well-preserved ancient human remains are hard to find, especially in tropical areas where the heat and humidity breaks them down. Still, "more direct evidence would be the actual finding of the nuts, of the seeds, ideally in some form of cultural context," such as a hearth, house floor or burial site, he says.

Sponsor Message

And archaeologists not involved with the study are wary of making assumptions as to why ancient people were attracted to betel nuts. "We have to be very, very careful not to associate our particular assumptions of pain or patterns," says Fuentes, of Princeton. Regarding the researchers' theory that ancient peoples were addicted to betel nuts for their painkilling effects, "I think they're using a contemporary public health and dentistry approach to think about very complicated cultures of the past."

There might have been other social and cultural reasons for the teeth-damaging practice, Fuentes says. After all, people today eat hard candy, open bottles with their teeth, neglect to brush and floss. "All of these things are not directly good for your teeth, but they serve other social [purposes] in other kinds of contexts," he says.

Brumm, the lead researcher, acknowledges there are limitations to the work. "As always with archaeology, you're dealing with vast unknowns," he says, "But we've put a lot of thought into this, and we think this is what was going on."

World.title: Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm
World.content:
Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Last October, remnants of Typhoon Halong swept through western Alaska — causing widespread flooding and displacing over a thousand people in multiple far-flung villages off the state's road system.

In the coastal village of Quinhagak, the storm shook houses and damaged some buildings and infrastructure. And the day after it hit, Jenny Matthew and her husband rode four-wheelers along the torn-up beach, assessing the damage.

The wind and floodwaters had peeled the tundra up like discarded carpeting. And as Matthew scanned the debris, suddenly, something caught her eye.

"I said to my husband, 'Look, what's that?' We stopped. He got up and took it, and it was that bowl," Matthew remembered.

The bowl was wooden and smooth. It was carved by Quinhagak residents somewhere between 400 and 600 years ago and was one of thousands of cultural objects scattered along the coastline.

Sponsor Message

The storm had unearthed it from an archaeological dig site called Nunalleq that sits near the village. It's renowned as one of the best examples of Alaska Native Yup'ik culture before Western contact and serves as an important link to Quinhagak's past. Not only had the storm scattered many objects from the site, it also increased the risks for what was still in the ground by eroding more of the land buffer between the Bering Sea and where these artifacts are buried.

This past summer, a team of archaeologists came to the village for an emergency dig to recover as much as possible before the next big storm.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Precious objects slowly being excavated

Archaeologists have been working at this dig site since 2009, according to lead archaeologist Rick Knecht. He says that after thawing permafrost revealed significant numbers of these objects in the early 2000s, the village deliberated and decided to try to save these pieces of their culture.

They include hand-carved animals, grass rope, sewing needles, ornate wooden masks and pieces of kayaks.

According to the archaeologists, the frozen ground has helped preserve artifacts composed of organic material, which they say would have likely eroded under different conditions.

The team, Knecht says, is mostly made up of volunteers and has a shoestring budget with funding from the Pacific Northwest Archaeological Society and the Daughters of the American Revolution, among others.

The whole archaeological site is about the size of two Olympic-size pools, but the emergency dig area is smaller, about the size of a backyard pool. It's a hole that has been dug around the buried remnants of several sod houses that date back 400 to 500 years.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Digging against time

Charlotta Hillerdal, who has been part of this excavation for over 15 years, was home in Scotland when she heard about the storm damage.

Sponsor Message

"I was crying," Hillerdal said. "It was a horrible feeling."

Knecht said that since the dig began, they've watched the Bering Sea creep closer and closer to the site. Shorelines in this part of Alaska are now more vulnerable to erosion due, in part, to decreasing sea ice and permafrost thaw. Both are fueled by human-caused climate change.

Last October's storm closed the distance even more. Now, at some high tides, seawater can reach into the pit.

"It's every bit as tough as working in front of bulldozers," Knecht explained.

In October, the flooding was so extensive that the site was covered by feet of water. When it receded, it took many valuable objects with it. They're worried that could happen again.

Knecht said they hope to return to the site next summer, though they're still raising the money to do so through a GoFundMe campaign and Quinhagak Heritage Inc., the nonprofit that oversees the dig.

"I'll be damned if I'm going to leave this for the waves," Knecht said. "It's like you might as well take those pieces of artwork we're finding and skip it off into the Bering Sea."

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient … you get a boost"

At the Nunalleq Culture and Archaeology Center — a museum-style building and lab — these pieces of Quinhagak's past are available for their direct descendants to access, along with the public.

"We all as humans want to know who we are and where we come from, and having the Nunalleq there for us strengthens that," said Elizabeth Church, director of Quinhagak Heritage Inc., which manages the center as well as the dig.

Church said seeing the artifacts exploded onto the beach was traumatic. It underscored the community's desire to steward their ancestors' belongings.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

"They are interwoven into us as people, and we feel a great sense of responsibility to care for them well, and to take them into the future with us," Church said.

There's evidence of people adapting to environmental change and making technological progress.

"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient and so capable and so talented and so smart — you get a boost," Church said. "It's amazing."

Sponsor Message

She said that with fall storm season fast approaching, the scramble is urgent to recover what they can of this past.

World.title: Ever wonder how the Fed's interest rate actually works? We've got answers
World.content:
Ever wonder how the Fed's interest rate actually works? We've got answers

toggle caption LM Otero/AP

It may be the most important tool in the Federal Reserve's toolkit: the interest rate.

And on Wednesday, the Fed wielded it for the first time this year, raising rates by a quarter percentage point in a bid to slow down accelerating inflation. But what does it mean when the Fed raises — or lowers — rates? And how does that affect the economy and all of us?

Here's how to understand it all.

So what does the Fed actually do?

The Fed really has two main jobs. The first is to ensure that prices remain stable, which generally means inflation that is neither too hot, nor too cold.

Sponsor Message

The second job is to strive for an economy with maximum employment — meaning ensuring the labor market is growing at a healthy pace and people who want jobs can find them.

There are times when things are clicking in the economy and both of the two Fed mandates are at peace with each other. Inflation is just at the right temperature, meaning everyday prices are not rising too much, while the labor market is growing steadily, meaning people who want work can find them.

But more often than not, the Fed finds itself in a situation where it has to focus on one of the two — or worse: Both inflation and the labor market are flashing warning signs and policy makers have to confront the agonizing choice of which one to focus on first.

Loading...

So how does the Fed accomplish its goals?

The Fed has several tools at its disposal to try to influence the economy — but none is more important than the interest rate.

When inflation is running hot, the Fed typically springs into action by raising interest rates — just like it did this week.

Although the Fed doesn't directly control what firms charge for mortgages or credit cards, it's hoping that by raising its own interest rate, it can lead to a domino effect across the economy that can then push up many kinds of borrowing costs across the economy.

It's the equivalent of applying the brakes on the economy. The main goal is to try to cool down prices by trying to get people and businesses to think more carefully about their spending. People might think a little harder about whether to buy a home if mortgage rates are higher — or whether to take that business loan if banks are charging more.

Sponsor Message

On the flip side, when the Fed is concerned about the labor market and wants to push up economic activity, it cuts interest rates in the hopes that the opposite will happen. It's the equivalent of trying to press on the accelerator for the economy.

Take what happened during the Covid-19 pandemic— the Fed, then led by Jerome Powell, was concerned that the pandemic would lead to massive layoffs.

So Powell and the Fed slashed interest rates to near zero, hoping it would spur financial firms to charge less for loans or mortgages — and thus encourage more spending across the economy. It worked — until inflation began climbing and then the Fed had to do the opposite and start raising rates.

So why is the Fed raising interest rates now?

As Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday, "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."

Inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for five years, and the central bank is not confident it would cool off without higher interest rates.

Warsh also made the case that it's the right moment to act with the economy strong enough to absorb the impact of what is ultimately a modest interest rate hike.

Consumer spending has been growing even as higher prices continue to pinch many households. And the job market appears to be on solid footing to weather higher borrowing costs without triggering a surge in layoffs.

toggle caption Win McNamee/Getty Images North America

So what happens now in the economy — and our pocketbooks?

The Fed's rate hike is small enough that it shouldn't have a dramatic effect — but it does come as many borrowing costs are already rising, partly in anticipation of higher interest rates.

The average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage jumped to 6.95% this week, almost two-tenths of a percent higher than a week earlier, according to mortgage giant Freddie Mac data out on Thursday.

Sponsor Message

That's enough to increase the cost of a standard home loan by hundreds of dollars each month and further stall hopes of a recovery for the country's stagnant housing market.

"It's like that Godfather movie," said Kara Ng, senior economist at the real estate company Zillow. "Every time it tries to break out, something pulls it back in."

A higher interest rate also trickles down to the cost of carrying a balance on a credit card or a Buy Now Pay Later deal, though the moves are not as substantial as with mortgages.

Analysts at LendingTree, an online loan marketplace, estimate that for someone with $7,000 in credit card debt, the Fed's rate hike would cost just a few extra dollars each month.

But these higher borrowing costs come as Americans have already been struggling with the high cost of living. The Fed, though, is hoping that the added near-term pain to households will be worth it if it can eventually help bring down inflation.

So now what?

This depends on how the economy responds to the Fed's rate hike — and on forces beyond the central bank's control, like the war in the Middle East, which is pushing up energy costs such as gas prices.

Any improvement on the cost of living is not likely to happen quickly. In fact, the Fed's rate-setting committee signaled a plan to raise rates once more this year, before holding steady in 2027.

At the end of the day, there are no quick fixes to inflation — and it may be a while before households see any relief from high prices.

World.title: Russia holds parliamentary vote in areas it seized from Ukraine in the war
World.content:
Russia holds parliamentary vote in areas it seized from Ukraine in the war

toggle caption AP Photo/AP

Russia's parliamentary election for the first time includes residents of regions that Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine after the start of its full-scale invasion more than 4 1/2 years ago, part of Kremlin efforts to cement its gains.

Officials in Kyiv vigorously denounced the action as illegal, and a human rights activist described residents there as being coerced to participate in the election.

While the vote across Russia started Friday and lasts until Sunday to help boost turnout, balloting actually has been underway in the annexed parts of Ukraine and some areas on the Russian side of the border since the end of last month. Officials cited security reasons for the extended period.

Sponsor Message

Russian authorities say the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia territories, often referred to by Moscow officials as the "new regions," have over 3.5 million voters. They were annexed by Russia in September 2022, despite not fully being under Moscow's control. The move has not been recognized internationally.

At one polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box as an armed Russian soldier stood nearby and watched.

Putin stressed the importance of voting in the regions

In a speech Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin emphasized the importance of balloting in those regions for the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. Residents there will be voting for the Duma "for the first time since their reunification with Russia."

He noted that Russian soldiers involved in the fighting also will vote.

Voting also is taking place in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014.

The first wartime election to the State Duma is intended to secure the Kremlin's political dominance and showcase public support for the war.

"Your choice and resolve will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our fighters, that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland and that nobody can divide or intimidate us, undermine our statehood and political system," Putin said.

Sponsor Message

Ukraine urges other countries not to recognize the vote

Authorities in Kyiv called the voting in those territories illegal and urged foreign governments and international organizations not to recognize the election. They warned Ukrainians that taking part in organizing the vote could carry criminal liability.

A coalition of nine Ukrainian human rights groups called on residents of the Russia-held territories to stay away from the polls.

"We urge residents of the temporarily occupied territories, above all, to protect their lives and health and to look after their own safety," the coalition said in a statement. "Holding Russian elections in the temporarily occupied territories is an attempt to use the electoral process to legitimize the Russian occupation and the attempted annexation of Ukrainian territories."

European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said the voting in Russian-held regions represented "another blatant violation of international law. The European Union does not, and will never recognize either the holding of these, so-called elections, sham elections, in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results."

Activists describe coercion to vote

Violeta Artemchuk, coordinator of the Donbas SOS human rights group who was among those who signed the statement, said members of local election commissions were going house to house, escorted by Russian troops and security agents, to force people to vote.

Moscow-appointed authorities exert pressure on residents, threatening those who work in the public sector with dismissal if they fail to vote and making pensions and other social payments conditional on participating, Artemchuk said.

"For instance, if a person with a disability or a pensioner relies on social assistance and does not take part in the 'voting,' they could be added to a list of individuals deemed 'disloyal' to the so-called authorities and subsequently deprived of their benefits or humanitarian assistance," she said.

Volodymyr Fesenko, a political analyst with the Kyiv-based Penta Center, emphasized that "elections held at gunpoint are a farce."

Sponsor Message

"The very fact that voting takes place amid endless shelling and bombing reflects the Kremlin's attitude toward the people and the electoral process in the occupied territories," Fesenko told The Associated Press.

"It's nothing short of a mockery. Any electoral procedures conducted by the Russian occupation authorities have nothing to do with democracy," he said.

World.title: Why molasses has long been a sticky point in Canada-U.S. trade, well before Trump's import ban
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. ban on Canadian molasses imports has resurfaced allegations of sugar smuggling and an industry battle involving a company with a major refinery in Hamilton, Ont.

Spats over dairy, automobiles and booze have become ingrained in the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the U.S. during President Donald Trump's second term in office. But when the U.S. announced earlier this month that it would ban the import of molasses, it left some scratching their heads.

The ban is due to take effect Sept. 29 alongside bans on motorcycles, most alcoholic drinks and some dairy products.

It comes after months of American sugar producers lobbying their government to raise tariffs on foreign sugar products, saying they're being undercut by cheaper products from other countries.

They're also taking aim at Canadian refineries, who they claim are importing mixes of raw sugar, molasses and water but disguising them as pure molasses as a way to circumvent sugar tariffs and quotas.

'Closing the spigot'

Sugaright, a division of Connecticut-based refiner CSC Sugar, said stopping the flow of watered-down molasses from Canada was a main topic of conversation at the International Sweetener Symposium, a major industry event held in Vail, Colo., this summer.

"Canadian 'molasses' containing substantial sugar is being viewed as a potential sugar-program circumvention problem, and not only does the U.S. sugar industry want the flow to stop, but now the federal government is fully engaged to 'finish the job' of closing the spigot completely," reads an August blog post on Sugaright's website.

The issue appears to stem from a case in the 1990s, when Michigan-based Heartland By-Products mixed molasses with sugar and water at an Ontario facility to import the mixture tariff-free. The company would then refine it a second time in the U.S. to remove the molasses, sell the purified sugar, and ship the molasses back to Canada to reuse in its next batch.

The scheme was legal and approved by the U.S. government, but pressure from the sugar industry and a series of court cases and legislative restrictions forced the company to shut down operations in the 2000s.

Sugar companies' claims of disguised molasses still flowing unchecked from Canada appear to be contradicted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report from August, which states that molasses imports for sugar extraction are "on a rapid decline" and are currently projected to be "zero" for next year.

Company says it was targeted

Don Hill, chair of Sucro Can Sourcing, says the latest round of accusations is specifically aimed at his company, which is headquartered in Florida but has its biggest refinery in Hamilton.

"They just don't like the fact that we're legitimately shipping that molasses over to the U.S. And they've chosen to link what we do to what Heartland did 20 years ago, just to create that negative aura — just to cast aspersions and to make it seem all dodgy," Hill told CBC News.

He says his fast-growing company was shipping about 50,000 tonnes of refiners' molasses annually to the U.S., which makes up a fraction of one per cent of the U.S. market — but marks a significant increase from a decade ago, before Sucro entered the picture.

WATCH | Carney responds to import bans: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection approved Sucro's molasses imports under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule in 2020.

Hill, who is from Toronto but now lives in the U.K., says the sugar lobby has gone "berserk" trying to shut down his operation since then by pulling "every lever possible."

Congress gave the USDA funding as part of the 2024 American Relief Act to test the purity of molasses coming from Canada through Buffalo, N.Y., the route used by Sucro.

The resulting study found signs of "additives or blending," raising concerns about "potential circumvention of U.S. sugar tariff‑rate quotas." It was not officially published by the USDA, but appears to have been made public in an April 20 article on the website of brokerage platform Ag Bull Trading.

The industry has used this study in its arguments for shutting off molasses from Canada and raising tariffs on the product travelling through Buffalo.

Sucro issued a rebuttal to the study, which Hill says does not have "an ounce or shred of legitimate facts behind it." He called for its retraction, citing "glaring mathematical errors," and said he offered data and corrections to the USDA. He said he has not received any meaningful response.

In a statement emailed to CBC News, the USDA said, "This report was not formally published by USDA. There is nothing further to share on the contents."

Sucro stopped importing molasses to the U.S. after completing its latest $135-million refinery in Hamilton in April, Hill says, and has instead been focusing on the Canadian market.

"It just got to the point where the whole market, including the tariffs, including the sugar lobby, has just made everything so toxic and aggravating that there's just no point in even doing it," he said.

Sugar lobby backs ban

The American Sugar Alliance, the main trade association and lobby organization representing major U.S. sugar producers and refiners, emailed CBC News a statement applauding the molasses import ban.

"American sugar producers deeply appreciate President Donald Trump, the U.S. Trade Representative, and the Trump Administration's efforts to ensure that the products being imported into our country under our trade laws are actually the stated products," the statement said.

"The Trump Administration is committed to upholding our laws, restoring fair trade, and putting American farmers and workers first."

CBC News sent follow-up questions regarding Hill's accusations that the group targeted Sucro, but has not heard back.

WATCH | Toronto businesses feeling import ban: Trump hit Canada with new import bans. Here's how GTA businesses are being impacted | Duration closed caption 1:49 U.S. President Donald Trump is banning the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S. CBC Naama Weingarten spoke to GTA business owners about how they could be impacted.

David Singerman, an associate professor of history at the University of Virginia and author of Unrefined: How Capitalism Reinvented Sugar, says sugar refining has always been a low-margin, high-volume business.

He says this has inspired a long history of smuggling and tariff manipulation — and also of producers and refiners exerting political power to protect their profits.

Singerman says the lobby's influence gives sugar a "special status" in the American trade system, with a quota system backed up by a minimum price guarantee and high tariffs on foreign imports.

"Any time that there's a threat, or these growers perceive that someone is undercutting the system in some way, they get very nervous and they pick up the phone and call their friends in Washington. And this has been true for a long time," he said.

'Bit of a head scratcher'

Drew Fagan, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, says U.S. protectionism around its sugar industry is well known. He compared it to Canada's dairy industry, which Trump has frequently lambasted as being unfair to American businesses.

Fagan says there could be several issues at play. Molasses is used in the production of rum and other alcohols, for example, and is also used as feed for dairy cows, which could link it to the booze and dairy bans.

He also says it's not uncommon for lobby groups to use the political climate — in this case, a trade dispute with Canada — to push through long-sought changes.

"Special interests can have a big say if they know which buttons to push," Fagan said.

CBC News contacted the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative to ask for the reasoning behind the molasses import ban but has not heard back.

World.title: ‘Holy moly!’: Rare shark visit to Nova Scotia's Bedford Basin inspires shock and awe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s been a long time since swimming was encouraged in the Bedford Basin, but that didn’t stop one shark from making a rare and lengthy visit on Friday night.

"I have never seen a shark in the Bedford Basin before. That was a first," said Bedford resident John Calder.

Calder had nearly finished his commute home from work when he came across a crowd standing on the Shore Drive Bridge, which overlooks the basin where it meets the Sackville River.

“I got out of my car to see what was happening and lo and behold, there was two giant shark fins that were protruding from the water,” Calder said Saturday. “Right away, I said: 'Holy moly! That's a shark.'"

According to marine biologist and shark researcher Neil Hammerschlag, who reviewed multiple videos of the shark shared on social media, “it’s clearly a basking shark.”

“They pose no risk to humans, they eat little plankton, and they’re called basking sharks because they often spend time near the surface where they look like they’re basking in the sun,” said Hammerschlag, president of Atlantic Shark Expeditions.

The shark's habit of floating near the surface, combined with the fact that it is the second-largest fish in the world, made it easy to spot once it entered the basin.

However, finding one in such a busy waterway — surrounded by dozens of sailboats and densely populated shores — is highly unusual.

“I think this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see an animal this large so close to shore,” Hammerschlag said.

John Calder says he spotted the shark around 5 p.m. on Friday. (Submitted by John Calder)

Shark spent hours in basin

While Calder watched the shark for only 15 minutes before it swam away, he described it as a moment where time stood still.

“You go about your day, and then all of a sudden there’s a shark, and it’s like everything stops, nothing else is important and you’re just watching mother nature,” he said.

Around 7:30 p.m., Calder's wife, Lisa McCloskey, and his 14-year-old stepdaughter, Audrey Hill, spotted the shark near a dock at the Bedford Basin Yacht Club.

“It seemed kind of surreal,” McCloskey said. “We could almost see our house in the distance, and then we’re watching this massive shark come out of the water and it came near us and almost rolled over so we saw its whole body as well ... it was magical.”

Lisa McCloskey, pictured here with her 14-year-old daughter, Audrey Hill, along with Heather Sangster, Meghan Proude, Mana Wareham, Kathy McCarthy-Murphy and Ben and Lisa Trepanier, says there was a strong feeling of community among those who came down to the Bedford Basin Yacht Club to see the shark. (Submitted by Lisa McCloskey)

For nearly two hours, a growing crowd watched as the shark surfaced and submerged.

“There were probably like 30 or 40 of us, and people were hugging each other when they saw the shark,” McCloskey said. “It really felt like a community event. Everyone was chatting and it was really lovely.”

Hammerschlag said it remains unclear why the shark ventured into the basin. Basking sharks are far more common in open, plankton-rich waters like the Bay of Fundy.

The shark may have been unwell or disoriented, Hammerschlag said, but “unless it washes up on shore,” there's no way to know for sure.

“Either way, it’s a remarkable encounter, and this is a beautiful animal, completely harmless to people, and whoever had the opportunity to see it should consider themselves lucky.”

World.title: Greenland, Denmark say deal with U.S. will not cede sovereignty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after U.S. President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the U.S. to ‌develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting American adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of U.S. military presence in the self-governed ⁠Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland. P arliamentary action is still needed by the governments of Denmark and Greenland before it can be enforced.

"Next week could be a good week — for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Danish Foreign Affairs Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

"A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the [Danish] Kingdom's red lines," Rasmussen said.

But some residents in Greenland's capital, Nuuk, expressed skepticism about closer ties with Washington.

"The U.S. should not control Greenland. I think it's better if we have co-operation with NATO," said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65.

"Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland," Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk. "He should not expect our children and grandchildren to become Americans in the future."

Denmark and the U.S. already have a long-standing security agreement that allows the U.S. to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal would be different from that.

"I think it's obvious that we can expect more bases in Greenland. But it's important to say that if we look in the past, especially during the Cold War, the U.S. had immense military presence in Greenland," said Marc Jacobsen, an associate professor at the Royal Danish Defence College and the head of research at the Center for Arctic Security Studies.

WATCH | Trump says deal struck with Denmark over Greenland: Deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland: Trump | Duration 1:16 U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the United States and Denmark have struck a deal to bolster American military presence in Greenland. The announcement, which Trump made in a Truth Social post, comes after months of threats by the president to take the mineral-rich Danish territory by force.

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on his Truth Social platform late on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," he said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.

NATO welcomes agreement

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the U.S. and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of U.S. strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, in Denmark's capital.

If the Danish government cedes any formal power to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States," he said.

"I am pleased on Greenland's behalf that we are nearing the conclusion of an agreement — an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the continued development of this country," Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, said on Saturday in a post on Facebook.

"The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."

WATCH | Trump posts map showing U.S. flag covering North America, Greenland and Iceland: Does Iceland feel threatened by Trump's expansionist threats? | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 3:47 Iceland summoned the U.S. ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map showing the U.S. flag covering North America, Greenland and Iceland. Magnús Eyjólfsson, a journalist with national broadcaster RÚV, discusses how Icelanders are reacting to Trump’s expansionist rhetoric and why his recent threats to take over Greenland hit particularly close to home.

Trump's threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and co-operation in this vital region."

Steffen Nielsen, a 49-year-old sales worker living in Copenhagen, told Reuters: "I think that the U.S. is probably going to get what they could have had the whole time, if they just asked nicely."

"I don't like it," Kaj Jorgensen, an 80-year-old pensioner, also living in Copenhagen, said of the news. "I don't wish the United States to be present anywhere in the Danish Kingdom. I really don't trust Donald Trump."

World.title: Ed Sheeran to perform for 1st time since Macklemore dropped from tour, other acts withdrew
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ed Sheeran is set to take the stage in Philadelphia on Saturday night for the first time since facing backlash for rapper Macklemore's removal from his tour for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

All of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts and backing band have quit his tour after Macklemore was ousted earlier this week and Sheeran attributed Macklemore's removal solely to venues and promoters while defending his decision to remain apolitical.

Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support.

However, Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Sheeran's opening act, said Wednesday he is now donating $2 million US to "aid in the region" at the singer-songwriter's request.

As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday's show, and Sheeran's website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations plans to protest outside the show Saturday afternoon.

Police presence around Lincoln Financial Field increased in the lead-up to the expected protest. Dozens of vehicles and police officers patrolled the area and barricades were put up along the streets.

Police set up barricades and blocked roads near the entrance of the arena in Philadelphia Saturday afternoon, ahead of a planned protest. (Daniela Ramirez/CBC News)

One police officer CBC News spoke to said police presence around the stadium is typical for any sporting or entertainment event.

Macklemore was dropped from the U.S. leg of Sheeran's tour after chanting "Free Palestine" and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey.

WATCH | The scene in Philadelphia Saturday: Ed Sheeran to resume tour after Macklemore cut, other acts withdrew | Duration closed caption 3:43 Singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran is set to take the stage in Philadelphia on Saturday, his first show since all of his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage. Sheeran attributed Macklemore's removal solely to venues and promoters but has not commented publicly since losing the artists' support.

Sheeran said venues had threatened to pull his upcoming performances if Macklemore was not removed as his opening act because of "how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance."

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me," Sheeran said in his statement.

He added that while he tried to "build a bridge," the venues would not change their minds.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, was one of the people behind the call for Macklemore's removal, Sheeran confirmed.

Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel, said in a statement shared with CBC News Monday that his stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech," stating Macklemore spread divisiveness through "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas."

Macklemore had blamed his removal on Kraft in an Instagram post, claiming the billionaire said the rapper would not be allowed onstage and rallied other stadium owners to threaten to cancel scheduled concerts if he was not taken off the bill. The threats placed Sheeran, his friend, in a difficult position, Macklemore said.

Sheeran takes apolitical stance

Many of Sheeran's supporting acts said they were withdrawing from his tour to stand in solidarity with Palestinians .

In his statement, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," and called the suffering on "both sides" a "human tragedy."

But he defended his choice not to express his views on the conflict publicly.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," he wrote.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

WATCH | Supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour after Macklemore ousted: How Macklemore's 'Free Palestine' stance derailed Ed Sheeran's entire tour | Duration closed caption 2:12 Macklemore's ouster from Ed Sheeran's world tour over his support for Palestinians continued to snowball as other opening acts, and Sheeran's own backing band, quit in solidarity. Macklemore was dropped after calling for a 'Free Palestine' and referring to the war in Gaza as 'genocide' live on stage.

It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga.

Sheeran's other U.S. openers, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, also annouced they were leaving the tour.

Finneas, Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.

World.title: Canada's top general loses election to become head of key NATO Military Committee
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Despite a push from the federal government, Canada's chief of the defence staff has lost a vote to be the next chair of the NATO Military Committee, the alliance's top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders. Gen. Jennie Carignan and her German counterpart, Gen. Carsten Breuer, were vying for the position. Top military commanders from NATO's 32 members ultimately decided on Saturday to go with Breuer in a secret ballot election. The news was announced on social media by the current chair, Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who congratulated Breuer on his election. "Your operational judgement, your deep familiarity with this alliance and your leadership of the German Armed Forces will serve NATO well," Dragone said. A Canadian has not held this position in almost two decades — the last being retired general Ray Henault between 2005 and 2008. Had she won, Carignan would have been the first woman to lead the Military Committee in the 77-year history of the alliance. Statement on the election of a new chair of the NATO Military Committee: pic.twitter.com/8lMUTVhDQ5 —CDS_Canada_CEMD In a statement posted to social media, Carignan congratulated Breuer and said, "it was an honour to stand as a candidate and to engage with my fellow Allied Chiefs of Defence throughout this process." "There is important work ahead for our Alliance, and I know General Breuer will bring strong leadership to his new role. I deeply value the close relationship we have built and look forward to continuing to work together on our NATO initiatives," Carignan added. Speaking to reporters outside the Liberal caucus retreat in Ottawa on Saturday afternoon, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the country is proud of Carignan and her candidacy. He said the federal government doesn't know the breakdown of the votes. "The important thing is that Gen. Carignan will continue to serve with her colleagues — all 31 other chiefs of defence in the alliance. It's a very important contribution we're making," McGuinty said. "Gen. Carignan is doing a phenomenal job." Potential U.S. obstacles to Carignan appointment Experts who previously spoke to CBC News said a potential roadblock to Carignan winning would be U.S. President Donald Trump — particularly after Prime Minister Mark Carney formally unveiled his intent to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union. "Trump is not going to let a Canadian or a woman be the head of the military committee, if anybody around him has paid attention to it," said Steven Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University who's written extensively about NATO. Breuer is a 61-year-old army officer who earned the nickname "the chancellor's general" after then-German chancellor Olaf Scholz picked him to lead a crisis committee that helped manage the country's response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021 and 2022. He joined the Bundeswehr in an air defence unit in 1984, and later attended the U.S. general staff college in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., as well as German general staff training in Hamburg. German Chief of Defence Gen. Carsten Breuer gives a statement during a Lithuanian-German military exercise in Pabrade, Lithuania, in May 2024. (Mindaugas Kulbis/The Associate Press) In 2014, Breuer served with NATO's International Security Assistance Force in the Afghan capital Kabul. Dragone said on social media that Breuer will take office in July 2027.

World.title: If most Albertans don't want to leave Canada, where is the pro-Canada movement?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Over the last year, a steady drumbeat of polling has found again and again that most Albertans oppose separation — but based on fundraising and online chatter, you might not know that.

In a month, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the future of the province, and the separatists occupy an outsize share of the spotlight, having raised three times the money and dominating the online conversation by as much as eight to one.

The pro-Canada side, meanwhile, remains divided, thanks largely to election finance rules that prevent collaboration, and worries about complacency. More than one federalist organizer has said that the time for persuasion is over. After an emotional and hotly-contested few months, most Albertans have dug in their heels on a position, federalists say.

The challenge now? Getting people to actually vote.

“I think the federalist side in this referendum campaign has hit a point of real unease,” says Avnish Nanda, the spokesperson for Our Alberta Advantage, which launched a new campaign to get out the vote this week. Called 5x for Canada, it features a series of tongue-in-cheek videos designed to equip people to get their friends to cast a ballot. (Slogan: Votemaxxing for Canada.)

“The separatists are just everywhere,” Nanda said.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What questions do you have about Alberta's separatist movement and the upcoming referendum vote? Leave your question here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show.

Polling might cap support for independence at about a quarter of the province, but if a bigger proportion of separatists show up, the math gets dicey, he pointed out.

“Even if they don’t win outright, if the separatists get 30 per cent of the vote, I think Alberta is forever changed.”

Team Canada

Making the case for Canada is a patchwork of groups and individuals, including former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, who, along with volunteers, has spent over a year driving a maple leaf-emblazoned RV almost 40,000 kilometres around the province.

The Forever Canadian campaign's Unity Bus during a stop in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Aug. 13, 2026. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

There’s a team of academics and former politicians working as a “pop-up think-tank�” under the name Lead Not Leave , and Conservatives for Canada , the campaign launched by the federal party to target their own supporters. Polling suggests right-leaning voters are more likely to have separatist sympathies.

In perhaps the strangest case of odd bedfellows, rival ex-premiers Rachel Notley and Jason Kenney have joined forces for a Canadian Chamber of Commerce campaign in support of keeping Alberta in Canada. Kenney in particular has emerged as a vocal anti-separatist, who has argued that, historically, followers of the movement couldn’t “ get elected to dog catcher .”

Each group has functioned mostly individually.

“I see them rowing in the same direction,” Lukaszuk said of the other groups. “But in different canoes.”

Rules keep groups separate, leaders say

But unlike the generally cohesive Yes and No campaigns in Quebec, it was never realistic — or allowed — for pro-Canada groups to unite under the same banner, says Jared Wesley, a professor of political science at the University of Alberta and a member of Lead Not Leave.

During Quebec’s referendum, each side was required to more or less co-operate under a national committee. In comparison, Alberta’s rules prevent collaboration. Campaign finance rules say groups — third party advertisers, specifically — can’t work together lest they risk running afoul of spending limits.

“Any conversation among federalists that are a part of these various groups always starts off with, ‘To be clear, we’re not co-ordinating, right?’” Wesley says with a laugh. “I mean, to be frank, the law simply does not allow us to compare notes.”

The separatists are all going to vote. Every one of them will crawl over broken glass to vote. - Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi

That means groups can’t share resources, co-ordinate events or vet each other’s public communications, he said.

In some ways, the splintered nature of the movement is an advantage, he argued.

“I think the notion that everyone should be part of one team on either side of the debate is based on an old way of political communications,” he said.

The media environment right now is very divided, Wesley said, meaning people get their information from a dizzying array of news organizations, websites and social media posts, often based on their own interests and political leanings.

Because the federalist groups are similarly varied, they speak to different parts of the population, he added.

“Some of them are partisan; some aren’t. Some of them are moderate, some are progressive, some are conservative,” he said.

“The way that our public sphere is fractured suggests that’s not a bad strategy.”

Alberta's ad campaign

There are also questions about the role — or lack thereof — of the institutional voices more common in political campaigning. Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she does not want Alberta to separate, but also put the question about separatism on the ballot and has been criticized by both sides for the role she has played in the campaign so far.

This week the Alberta government launched a $4-million advertising campaign on the referendum questions, which urges viewers to “stand up for a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” but doesn’t otherwise argue the federal case.

In an emailed statement, Smith's press secretary, Sam Blackett, said the government will use "various channels" to communicate with Albertans about the referendum questions, including online, TV, radio and social media.

"The Premier also travels across Alberta every summer and will continue speaking directly with Albertans through town halls, public events, media interviews and more," he wrote.

The prime minister has been critical of the referendum — calling it a “dangerous bluff” back in May — and recently met with Forever Canadian campaigners, but hasn’t spearheaded a campaign.

In July, Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre appointed Alberta MP Dane Lloyd as the party’s point person on the referendum, writing at the time that Lloyd’s task was “not to scold Albertans” but to “hear” them.

But the party’s third-party advertiser, Conservatives for Canada, was only registered on Sept. 4 and has yet to raise any funds. This is the official entity that allows them to raise money and take a position on the referendum under election financing rules.

Alberta separatists gather at the Alberta Legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29, 2026, for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project. (Amanda Erickson/The Canadian Press)

In an email, a spokesperson said turnout will be key, so Lloyd had been focused on “doorknocking and roundtable discussions in addition to social media, media appearances and much more.”

The concern about turnout is being echoed across the political spectrum.

Speaking to media this week, Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said his party had been working on getting out the vote all summer, but he remained worried about motivation in the federal camp.

“The thing that worries me the most is I hear every single day, ‘Naheed, why are you so worked up about this? The separatists are never going to win,’” he said.

“The separatists are all going to vote. Every one of them will crawl over broken glass to vote."

And if the other side doesn’t also turn up, that could be a real difference, he added.

Boost in motivation

There are some signs the federalists might be beginning to stir. Vote motivation on the federalist side has had a “significant boost” in recent weeks, according to new polling data from Pollara Strategic Insights.

In order to gauge motivation, Pollara asked people whether they would wait an hour in line to vote, which, with an unprecedented 10 referendum questions on the ballot, may not be a theoretical question come October.

For the first time, their most recent numbers found those voting to stay in Canada were more eager to cast a ballot than their opponents, with 64 per cent saying they were “very motivated” to vote. What the separatists may lack in numbers they make up for in enthusiasm, and their motivation number has hovered around the 60 per cent mark all summer.

“I think that’s a notable swing,” said Dan Arnold, Pollara’s chief strategy officer.

“My sense is that the biggest reason that we’re seeing a growth in motivation among voters who want to stay in Canada is a reaction to what’s going on with Trump,” he added.

In other signs of life, Canadian singer and songwriter Jann Arden is set to headline a free unity concert in Calgary this weekend at The Confluence billed as “for everyone who calls Canada home.”

The event really snowballed in the last three weeks, says event producer Ian Menzies, with both artists and organizers volunteering their labour, the city issuing the permits and Forever Canadian chipping in funding.

“I think there’s a lot of pent up [energy],” he said. “People are feeling like they want to have a way to express their fealty to Canada and their desire for unity.”

World.title: After 20 years with no police force, safety tops voter concerns in this Quebec community
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Provincial election signs are up in Chief Steeve Mathias’s community of Long Point First Nation, but he says there’s been silence when it comes to the issue he wants addressed for his community: an independent police force.

The community of 600, located in Winneway, Que., 630 kilometres northwest of Montreal in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region, has been waiting to get their own police service reinstated for 20 years.

In the meantime, they’ve had to come up with their own solutions while relying on the closest available provincial police station in Ville-Marie, Que., 100 kilometres away — where Mathias says officers can take two to three hours to arrive in an emergency.

“We're trying to take all the different types of measures … through our own means that are very limited," Mathias said.

The long-term impact of the policing desert is contributing to an increase in violence and drugs, he says. He argues the problem wouldn’t be this serious if the community had a consistent police presence.

“We're getting a lot of pressure from our people. They say, ‘do something about the drug dealing … it's getting out of hand, completely out of control,’” he said.

Long Point First Nation plans to purchase a vehicle for security agents to patrol the community to try to provide a sense of security to elders, women and youth. (Ismaël Houdassine/Radio-Canada)

Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, Mathias is speaking out, noting he wants “to see a government that cares.”

“It’s a human right to have public security … and [it] seems like my community is not eligible,” he said.

‘I feel safer now with my door locked,’ says resident

The police force in Winneway was officially dismantled on March 31, 2006, when a tripartite agreement with the federal and provincial governments ended.

A number of issues led to it, including a failure to come to an agreement on matters such as a lack of resources, infrastructure, jurisdiction and the number of police officers, says Mathias.

The band council began incurring a deficit, he says — significant and untenable for a community of its size.

After the police force was dismantled, the provincial police took charge. Over the years, Mathias says they stopped patrolling regularly.

Now, the response time can be lengthy and is contributing to heightened fear.

“I never used to lock my door at night,” said resident Diane Polson. “I feel safer now with my door locked.”

Diane Polson says she feels safer in the community with her door locked. It wasn't always this way, she says. (Bianca Sickini-Joly/Radio-Canada)

A lifelong resident of Winneway and interim director of the child-care centre, Polson says the question of security and safety is top of mind for her.

Twenty years ago, Polson served as part of a negotiating team in an effort to keep and expand the small police force the community had in the early 2000s.

In 2022, the community signed a collaboration agreement with the province for a temporary police force made up of officers from neighbouring First Nations.

But Mathias notes one of its conditions stipulated that provincial police still needed to be present for interventions.

“The two First Nation police services cannot come to the community without … the Sûreté du Québec being present,” he said.

“People found that very ridiculous. You know, there was a situation happening in the community and then like our First Nation police, they couldn't intervene.”

The office of Quebec's minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit, Ian Lafrenière, said the situation involves complex challenges that predate its government.

He agreed that the area should have police coverage, but said the government would not negotiate publicly.

Training locals to protect community

For now, the community is mobilizing to find solutions. It's hired a private security firm to train about 15 to 18 locals to help keep residents safe.

With the plan to purchase a vehicle for security agents to patrol the community, Mathias says the community is trying to give a sense of security particularly to elders, women and youth.

Last winter — in response to growing concerns from residents over the presence of drugs and violence in town — the Long Point First Nation held a general assembly where a decision was made to mandate the council to take action. It allowed them to forbid certain individuals from coming into the community.

LISTEN | Chief Mathias calls on candidates to bring back police force: Quebec AM 11:20 Long Point First Nation calls on provincial candidates to bring back police force Members of the Long Point First Nation in Abitibi-Témiscamingue say they're living in fear because of a lack of law enforcement. The community has been fighting to get its own police force back for over 20 years now to no avail. Quebec AM guest host Gordon Lambie spoke with Chief Steeve Mathias to find out the latest.

As part of this resolution, an individual who lives outside the community was banned. Mathias says he's known in the community as a drug dealer.

But the chief notes, without resources to enforce such bans, there are concerns about violence escalating.

“I find that very shameful that the government are not taking these matters more seriously [as] they should,” he said.

“Take accountability… provide the means and the resources.”

World.title: 6 people injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at festival in Saint-Tite, Que.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec provincial police are investigating after six people were injured after they were struck by a vehicle on the site of the Festival Western de Saint-Tite early Saturday morning.

Police say a collision between a vehicle and pedestrians took place on Saint-Joseph Boulevard in Saint-Tite, about 200 kilometres northeast of Montreal.

Witnesses say police arrived on scene around 4:30 a.m.

The vehicle fled the scene, according to the Sûreté du Québec (SQ). It was later found in the Quebec City region around 5:30 a.m.

The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns. (Pierre Millot/Radio-Canada)

A man in his 20s was arrested by police and was being questioned by investigators.

The victims, two young women and four young men aged between 17 and 21, were transported to hospital with various injuries, none of which were life threatening, police confirmed later Saturday.

Alcohol is not thought to be involved in the incident, according to a spokesperson for the SQ.

Police said it is unclear if those injured were involved in an argument with the driver.

The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns.

Festival officials say Saturday's activities will go ahead as planned.

"An isolated incident beyond our control occurred early this morning on Saint-Joseph Boulevard. Our thoughts are with those involved and their families. We wish them a speedy recovery," the organizers said in a statement.

"The safety of our festival-goers, volunteers, and staff remains our top priority. The Festival is a festive event where everyone should feel safe. That's why every effort is being made to ensure this."

WATCH | Police investigation into incident at Quebec festival ongoing: 6 injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at Quebec festival | Duration closed caption 1:49 Six people were injured after a vehicle struck pedestrians at the Festival Western de Saint-Tite in Quebec early Saturday. Police later located the vehicle in the Quebec City region and arrested a man in his 20s.

Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene.

Quebec's Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière said that there was no reason to believe that the incident was related to terrorism. He said that there had been an argument among several individuals that escalated.

In an update Saturday afternoon, SQ spokesperson Marc Tessier said the driver of the vehicle was likely to be released later in the day with a promise to appear in court at a later date.

Tessier specified his release would also likely entail conditions.

Quebec leaders react

The early morning incident took place as three Quebec party leaders were expected to attend the festival. The Quebec Liberals (PLQ), Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) and the Parti Québécois (PQ) all had stops planned for Saturday.

PLQ leader Charles Milliard said he spoke with members of the festival’s organizing committee to offer them support following what he called “the tragic event.”

“My thoughts are especially with the victims and their families,” he wrote on X. “Despite the confusion and sadness that mark this day, I wish everyone a wonderful festival.”

Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene. (Pierre Millot/Radio-Canada)

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette posted her condolences to the victims on X.

“My thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected by the events that took place at the Western Festival in St-Tite. The ongoing investigation will determine the causes of this act,” Fréchette said.

PQ Leader Pierre St-Pierre Plamondon also offered his condolences.

“My thoughts are with the injured individuals, their loved ones, and all those who witnessed the distressing scene in Saint-Tite.,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on X.

" Thank you to the first responders who acted quickly. Quebecers should be able to enjoy places where they can gather and celebrate safely."
