World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Independence Day fireworks give way to trade deal hopes
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s Independence Day on Sept. 16 was the focal point this past week, even as less celebratory news circulated. Over the weekend, 21-year-old Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, attending the Autonomous University of Morelos (UAEM) in Cuernavaca, Morelos, was stabbed and killed in Cuautla — the fourth femicide of a UAEM student just this year. On Thursday, Morelos authorities announced the arrest of a suspect, Francisco Javier “N,” but the attack on Tacoronte and the emergency medical response were met with indignation both locally and in Spain.

Also on Sept. 12, Pemex admitted it had contained another oil spill off the coast of Campeche, which the Navy and the state oil company moved quickly to seal and clean up — a contrast to the government’s slower handling of a major spill in February. Meanwhile, the peso spent most of the week trading above 17 to the dollar, weakening toward its worst week since March as markets digested the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, narrowing the Mexico-U.S. rate differential.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Industrial activity posts best growth in years

Mexico’s industrial sector delivered its strongest annual performance in nearly three years in July, with industrial activity up 2.4% in seasonally adjusted terms, according to INEGI — triple June’s 0.8% reading and the best showing since November 2023.

Construction led the gains, climbing 6.7% annually, while mining rose 1.6% and manufacturing grew 1.3%. Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, a second straight month of sequential gains. Still, industrial activity is up just 0.4% for the first seven months of 2026, a modest rebound after a 1.3% contraction in 2025, with manufacturing down 0.7% year-to-date. Economists at Grupo Financiero Monex expect only “moderate” growth ahead, citing USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

Coahuila is Mexico’s safest state

For the first time, Coahuila topped INEGI’s national safety perception survey, the 2026 ENVIPE, with just 27.8% of residents calling the state unsafe due to crime — a 9.9-point improvement that pushed Baja California Sur out of the top spot.

Coahuila registered only 100 homicides in 2025, a turnaround from more than 1,100 killings in 2012, when cartels such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel dominated large swaths of the state. Analysts credited beefed-up federal forces and prevention programs. Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, in office since December 2023, credited “great teamwork.” Nationally, the picture is less rosy: 74% of adults still consider their state unsafe, and México state overtook Morelos this year as Mexico’s least safe state, with 90% of respondents reporting security concerns.

Mexico’s independence is celebrated at home and abroad

On Tuesday night, President Sheinbaum delivered her second Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony before a crowd the Mexico City government estimated at more than 300,000 in the Zócalo, marking 216 years since Miguel Hidalgo’s original Cry of Dolores.

Sheinbaum issued 21 arengas honoring independence heroes including Hidalgo, Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario and Vicente Guerrero, alongside Mexico’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and migrants abroad, several of whom were included in a national Grito for the first time.

Abroad, Iran marked the holiday by lighting Tehran’s Azadi Tower in green, white and red, the first time the landmark has been illuminated in tribute to Mexico — an occasion the Mexican ambassador to Iran called “a great gesture of friendship.” In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani served as grand marshal of Brooklyn’s Mexican Independence Day parade, days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance mocked a Mexican flag-carrying protester at a Dallas rally.

Antitrust regulators probe Liga MX

Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has opened an investigation into whether Liga MX operates as a monopoly, examining whether a small group is unfairly controlling “affiliation, organization and access” to professional soccer competitions in violation of federal competition law. The probe follows Liga MX’s 2020 decision — upheld through the 2026-27 season by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — to scrap promotion and relegation with the second-tier Liga Expansión and end payouts to lower-tier clubs, a move Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed. No defendants have been named; the probe can run up to 120 business days and be extended. If wrongdoing is found, Liga MX and its clubs could face fines of up to 10% of annual income.

CFE advances Project Oasis in Baja California Sur

The Federal Electricity Commission unveiled Project Oasis BCS, a solar, battery and green hydrogen initiative meant to bring reliable power to the isolated Mulegé region, which has no direct connection to the national grid and has historically relied on fossil fuels.

The project pairs a 72-megawatt photovoltaic plant with a battery system, electrolyzers to produce hydrogen and fuel cells to convert it back into electricity for use when sunlight is scarce. CFE projects the initiative will serve 40,000 households and cut emissions equivalent to taking more than 31,000 vehicles off the road annually. If completed, it would be CFE’s first-ever green hydrogen power generation project.

Democracy index shows modest gains

According to International IDEA’s annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, Mexico’s democracy score edged up slightly in 2025 — Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — rising to 1.778 out of 4 from 1.770 the year before. The country improved in rule of law and participation, held steady in rights and declined in representation, its best-ranked category at 83rd out of 173 nations. Mexico ranked in the top 100 in only one of the four measured categories. The report’s authors flagged rising political polarization and “us versus them” identity politics as threats across Latin America, while separately noting democratic backsliding tied to the Trump administration’s consolidation of executive power in the U.S.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump cartel pressure

Responding to a Trump “presidential determination” pressuring Mexico to take “additional action” against cartels and arrest complicit officials, Sheinbaum turned the spotlight on U.S. drug consumption, asking what Washington is doing to curb domestic drug demand, money laundering and the flow of American-made weapons into Mexico.

“We don’t need to be judged from the outside,” Sheinbaum said, insisting “we know what Mexico’s problems are and we act against them every day.” Trump’s determination, submitted to Congress on Tuesday, named Mexico among 23 countries as major drug producers or transit points and singled out Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — on leave amid U.S. accusations of cartel collusion but still free — as an official Washington wants arrested. The exchange came a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mexico isn’t doing enough against cartels, even as he acknowledged Mexican efforts had increased.

Record fuel bust in Guanajuato

Authorities announced on Thursday that they had seized 59 million liters of stolen fuel at a property in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato — the largest single-site fuel bust in Mexican history and roughly five times last year’s record seizure in Tamaulipas. The operation traces to a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, which led investigators to the storage facility, capable of holding up to 80 million liters. No arrests had been made as of Friday, and officials say specialized personnel will be needed to safely handle the seized hydrocarbons. Guanajuato’s security minister said the bust would help choke off a funding source for organized crime in a state that has seen four smaller fuel-theft busts this year.

Trade talks hover ahead of US midterms

The fourth round of formal USMCA-related trade talks between Mexico and the United States is tentatively set for next week, with officials on both sides eager to hammer out a deal before U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework deal would benefit both governments: Trump wants an economic win as he risks losing control of Congress, while Mexico is contending with investor unease and a cooling economy. The push follows the collapse last month of parallel U.S.-Canada trade talks, making the Mexico-U.S. track an effort at an interim bilateral deal.

According to José Medina Mora, president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus.

Pups in the news

Rollo, an adopted mixed-breed puppy, is the National Palace’s newest resident, officially tasked with supporting “the emotional well-being of everyone,” per government videos; his brother Theo still awaits adoption, and the palace’s resident cats, including Coco and Zeus, remain in place.

In Morelia, a dog named Maple dressed as a taco stand won the city’s inaugural Patriotic Pup Contest, beating roughly 40 costumed competitors, with runners-up dressed as an elote-and-pork-loin vendor and a pozole bowl nearly twice their size.

Looking ahead

Next week brings a busy convergence of bilateral trade and security missions as well as the potential for currency swings.

The fourth round of USMCA-focused trade talks in Washington, D.C., could yield either a resolution or more setbacks. According to reporting by Politico, a preparatory call between Trump and Sheinbaum on Wednesday may have placed more topics on the discussion table than just Section 232 tariffs. However, Sheinbaum said after the call that “we’re making progress on trade issues.”

Any signs of progress or friction on tariffs are poised to move the peso. Meanwhile, 139 U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division are scheduled to land in Chihuahua on Sept. 20 for 11 days of joint training exercises with Mexican forces at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento, the military’s largest training facility.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Junípero Serra: A complex character with a controversial legacy
World.content:
Standing in the plaza of Jalpan de Serra, a town in Querétaro’s remote, mountainous Sierra Gorda, I gazed up in awe at an enormous, intricately designed mission. Having lived in California for 30 years, I was familiar with the missions, designed by the Franciscan priest Junípero Serra, and for whom one of the busiest freeways in the Bay Area is named. But none of the California missions I’d visited were anywhere near as elaborate and baroque as this structure. In fact, I later learned that the style of the five Sierra Gorda missions is known as “mestizo baroque.”

Junípero Serra, a priest from the island of Mallorca, achieved his dream of becoming a missionary in the Americas at the age of 36, in 1749. After disembarking in Veracruz, he refused to ride horseback to Mexico City, instead journeying on foot the entire 270 miles, despite a severe leg injury. Five months later, he walked another 175 miles from Mexico City to the Sierra Gorda. He used the motto siempre adelante (always forward) to drive his missionary zeal.

In the Sierra Gorda, he evangelized the local population and used the sweat of the Pame, local Indigenous people, to build the five missions that, 250 years later, would become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There are several reasons for the dramatic difference in style between the two sets of missions, those in the interior of Mexico and the later ones on the Pacific coast, from Baja California to present-day San Francisco.

Location

The Sierra Gorda missions were close to rich colonial centers, like Mexico City, Querétaro and Guadalajara, which served as supply hubs, as well as to well-established trade routes and ample financial backing from New Spain.

On the other hand, the missions in Alta California (now the U.S. state of California) were built in remote, isolated outposts, thousands of miles from supply ports. Few overland routes existed, which forced Serra to rely on infrequent supply ships.

Skilled labor

In Mexico, the local Pame and other Indigenous artisans had been carving stone for centuries. After being converted, they blended Catholic iconography with Indigenous symbols, creating a hybrid of rich, intricate facades that look as if carved from stone filigree rather than masonry.

In contrast, unskilled workers in Alta California used local sun-dried adobe bricks, timber and river stones, resulting in a much simpler style.

The goal of the missions

In Mexico, the imposing mission architecture was designed to convey permanent control over wealthy interior mining and agricultural zones, whereas in Alta California the missions were built as a military strategy. International law at the time required actual physical settlement to hold a region. Placing missions next to military forts along the coast created a visible barrier against Russian fur traders moving south from Alaska and British explorers from the Pacific Northwest.

Leadership style differences

In addition to architecture, Serra’s way of governing also differed. While he used the same forced Catholic conversion and paternalism in both areas, his treatment of the locals differed. In the Sierra Gorda, he spent nine years learning the Pame language, translating catechisms, teaching European farming techniques and helping the Pames defend their agricultural plots from predatory Spanish soldiers and landowners. And he allowed the well-integrated Pames a high degree of freedom.

In California, however, Serra’s treatment of the Indigenous people was very mixed. On one hand, he wrote letters and reports condemning the violence, rape and mistreatment of native women by Spanish military officers, even walking hundreds of miles to Mexico City to meet directly with the viceroy to secure a “bill of rights” for Indigenous people.

But he was a harsh disciplinarian. Indigenous people were subjected to confinement in crowded, unsanitary conditions; forced labor; and corporal punishment if they tried to leave. Tragically, the isolated missions in Baja and Alta California also became vectors for European epidemic diseases, to which the local population had no immunity, leading to huge population decline, whereas the Pame had already developed relative immunity.

Reactions to Serra’s canonization

Pope Francis canonized Serra in 2015, during a visit to the United States. After such a complicated life, it’s no wonder that his canonization was greeted with very mixed reactions, especially in the U.S. Many traditional Hispanics cheered the decision, seeing it as a long-overdue acknowledgment by the Church of the role the Spanish-speaking missionaries played in bringing the faith to the Americas.

Others condemned the canonization, protesting at the archdioceses in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., and dubbing Serra the “saint of genocide.” They were also disappointed that Pope Francis canonized Serra when only a few months earlier he had apologized for the “grave sins” committed against Indigenous peoples during the conquest of the Americas.

Mexicans were ambivalent. Because most Mexicans are mestizo — a mix of Spanish Catholic and Indigenous — people wrestled with practicing a deep faith that they loved, yet with the painful awareness that it was introduced through brutal colonial subjugation.

Clearly, Junípero Serra was a complex character. On one hand, he went out of his way to defend Indigenous and women’s rights, yet at the same time betrayed a lack of respect for their human dignity and agency. I suspect he will always be viewed as a complicated historical figure with a controversial legacy.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: The story of Hotel Mocambo, Mexico’s original luxury beach resort
World.content:
When it comes to tourism in Mexico, one of the most popular options for international visitors is to spend a few nights at a majestic beach resort. From Cancún to Los Cabos, Mexico has established itself as a premier destination for world-class beach getaways, with Mexico’s Ministry of Tourism reporting that nearly half of Mexico’s visitors opt for ritzy coastal areas — where sprawling luxurious properties abound.

The shift toward Mexico’s coastline

The numbers show just how vital Mexico’s top-tier beaches are to its national tourism economy: Despite an overall lower number of visitors this year and a massive blow from U.S. airlines this summer, Cancún still leads the nation in international flight arrivals, accounting for 45% of Mexico’s airport activity as of June, with 4,844,588 reported flight arrivals.

Besides Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey, which are among the 10 most active airports in Mexico, every other visit is largely due to Mexico’s beaches. This year, Los Cabos, Puerto Vallarta, Tulum, Cozumel and Mazatlán have generated the most airport traffic, respectively, with roughly 66% of Mexico’s inbound flights touching down near those beaches.

And yet, Mexico’s identity as a destination for opulent beach resorts originated in a region that is nowadays overlooked, particularly by international visitors. But if you know where to look, a time-travel beach experience awaits along the Gulf Coast, with its own kind of grandeur and charm.

Hotel Mocambo: Mexico’s first grand luxury resort

It’s impossible to overstate the historical significance of Veracruz and its port city, where the Spanish colonization of continental Latin America began in 1519. Over centuries, many of the country’s earliest contributions can be traced back to its Gulf Coast origins, including coffee, jalapeños, vanilla and more.

Add to that list: Mexico’s first grand luxury beach resort.

In 1938, Hotel Mocambo — named after Playa Mocambo, the beach where the hotel was built, and which originally derived from an Afro-Portuguese word denoting the region’s legacy as a refuge for escaped African slaves — began construction, making it among the earliest (if not the first) major beachfront resort in all of Mexico.

A midcentury haven for Mexican stars and cinema

During its heyday, Hotel Mocambo became a national treasure, with famous Mexican actors, musicians and celebrities — including Agustín Lara, Chavela Vargas and Pedro Infante — becoming regulars throughout the midcentury.

In 1943, “María Eugenia,” starring the iconic Mexican actress María Félix (and featuring a cameo from popular Veracruz singer Toña la Negra, who also personally frequented the hotel in those days), was filmed at Mocambo, demarcating the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.

Mocambo began as a 15-room property with a palm tree-studded view of the coastline to be enjoyed from extensive outdoor terrazas, grand staircases, arched hallways and open-air patios. A large outdoor pool and nearby barroom with high ceilings and jacuzzis can be found on separate levels, with a staircase that connects everything and inevitably descends to the beach.

Spanish influence and architectural expansion

The hotel’s walkways are breezy and bedecked with a combination of maritime decorations and Moorish structural features designed by Jesús Martí Martín, an avant-garde architect who was exiled from Madrid, Spain, after the Spanish Civil War. Martín was commissioned by Gov. Miguel Alemán Valdés to lead the hotel’s design atop the highest coastal hill in Boca del Río — the city just south of the port of Veracruz, which sits on the Jamapa River along the Gulf of Mexico — around the time that other beach hotels were starting to sprout up in the Pacific states of Guerrero and Sonora.

Under the governorship of Alemán Valdés, who would go on to become Mexico’s president, Hotel Mocambo aimed to become the first grand-scale beach resort attraction in all of Mexico.

And for a time, it was.

Just two years after opening, the hotel’s first expansion was overseen by another Spanish architect, Enrique Segarra. At one point, the hotel grew to include 110 rooms, though today that number has dwindled to 70 (for context, Mexico’s grandest beach resorts can now exceed more than 2,000 rooms).

Though it is no longer the nexus of Mexican aristocracy that it once was, Mocambo remains an important historical fixture in Mexico’s development as an attractive beach resort destination.

Preserving the legacy of Mexico’s Golden Age

Before Mocambo and the subsequent rise of beach resorts all over Mexico, the country’s most opulent buildings and high-end tourist attractions were centered in Mexico’s cosmopolitan inland cities. Not until Mocambo in Veracruz — and the rise of Acapulco shortly after — did Mexico gain extreme popularity for its prime coastal real estate and beach resort culture.

Ironically, or perhaps symbolically, the once-tranquil escape of Mocambo is now surrounded by modern buildings, major avenues, parking lots and the nonstop bustle of Mexico’s largest port city on the Gulf Coast. One of the neighboring buildings is a recently built high-rise apartment that juxtaposes interestingly with the dilapidated glory of Hotel Mocambo. And the state’s largest and most glamorous mall is within a short walking distance, as modernity has crept up to overtake Mocambo’s place.

Although the paint is faded and signs of decay are apparent in its grand facades, the resort is still worthy of a visit — simply for the pleasure of reliving Mexico’s Golden Age origins of beachside luxury.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong About the Peso at 37’: An MND podcast
World.content:
Despite the recent weakening from the U.S. Fed interest rate increase, the Mexican peso has been on a tear. Just recently, it was at a multi-year high against the US dollar and below 17.

The peso’s strength has defied just about every single analyst and expert. Even our own MND Peso Index estimates that the peso is nearly 6% overvalued against the dollar.

Recently, I did some analysis and calculated that if the peso had performed since the year 2020 as it did over the previous 25 years, it would currently be at 37 pesos to the US dollar! I wrote about it here: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO.

So how can it be that it is currently trading at less than half of that rate? And can we expect it to devalue again anytime soon?

Check out the latest episode of “Confidently Wrong” as we talk through the latest peso strength and what might come next.

World.title: The ‘problem’ with Mexico’s 44% growth in exports: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A recent headline took just about everyone by surprise: Mexico’s export revenue in July of this year hit US $81 billion, up 44%. Think about that for a moment — an annualized run rate of nearly $1 trillion of export revenue for the country. Last year, exports hit a record $665 billion on 7.6% growth, up from $417 billion in 2020. So far this year through July, exports are up an impressive 27.7%. As a result, Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, far surpassing No. 2 Canada and No. 3 China. China had been the leader for years until Mexico overtook it in the years following the COVID pandemic.

One would think that a 44% growth in exports would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy … but is it really as good as it sounds? Let’s dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding:

1. Most of the growth has come from the category of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances, which increased by a massive 134% in July. For the first time in that month, Mexico’s exports in that category exceeded the category of auto and auto parts. That category had previously led Mexico’s export revenue figures for decades. I recently wrote about that development here: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO. Automotive exports have been roughly flat year-to-date, and oil exports are actually down. In other words, the vast majority of the export growth is not coming from a diverse set of industries but rather this one segment.

2. Import growth is also booming. Year-to-date, imports are up 25.6%, and in the month of July, imports exceeded exports. Mexico actually had a rare trade deficit in July as imports grew by 45.7%.

3. Mexico has begun to import a massive amount of products from Taiwan, growing by over 200% so far this year and hitting nearly US $40 billion in the first half of the year. For some perspective, Mexico only imported $14 billion from Taiwan in the same period last year. Mexican imports of Taiwanese products increased by only $2 billion in the first six months of 2025, compared to 2024.

4. The massive year-to-date import and export growth numbers are not resulting in an economy that is growing as much as would be expected or hoped. One would think that such a huge increase in exports would dramatically increase production capacity investment and domestic consumption. But neither is happening. Estimates vary, but Mexican GDP is generally only expected to grow in the 1.2%-1.5% range — only half of what is expected in the United States this year.

So what is going on here?

It’s important to look deeper into what is actually happening to these imports and exports, specifically analyzing two measures related to value added:

Domestic value added embodied in the exports (How much Mexican labor is going into the exports?) Mexican-origin content (How much Mexican product is going into the exports?)

What we see is that the rapidly growing electronics category is extremely low in both measures. Said differently, given the high value of the products, the actual amount of Mexican labor and Mexican-origin content going into them is minimal. It is estimated that less than 3% of the exported value of products in this category is Mexican added value — just 3 cents on the dollar! A cynic might say that Mexico is doing little more than receiving the product from Taiwan, adding a “Made in Mexico” sticker and then exporting it — and that cynic wouldn’t be too far from the current reality!

For some perspective, that is barely a tenth of the value that Mexico adds to products in the vehicle segment. Engineering, design, parts manufacturing and assembly in Mexico are all common in that industry. And here is where the real opportunity for Mexico comes in. If Mexico could capture more of the added value in the massive, fast-growing electronics category, it would be hugely impactful on employment in the country. So how can that happen?

Enter the USMCA negotiations. Mexico and the United States have had many rounds of discussions on the updated trade agreement, and despite clear disagreement in certain areas (I’m looking at you, Mexican tomatoes!), increased local content or value added requirements in areas like electronics seems to be an area of agreement and alignment. It is in both countries’ interests to shorten the supply chain and further “de-risk” from China and Taiwan. And it is in both countries’ interests to have more control of the production and supply of such a critical product line.

So will it happen? I am optimistic for a positive outcome given that both countries have similarly aligned interests. Stay tuned to MND as we bring you the developments in this critically strategic area.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Using US intelligence, Mexican Army downs drone and arrests its operator in Tijuana
World.content:
After receiving information from U.S. officials, the Mexican Army successfully deactivated a drone that crossed the border into Tijuana and arrested the operator in Mexican territory.

The Defense Ministry (Defensa) on Thursday provided details of the Monday operation, explaining that the drone was being used by a criminal group to monitor human trafficking routes.

En Tijuana, Baja California, como parte de la “Operación Águila Alta” y mediante el intercambio de información con autoridades de Estados Unidos, elementos de @Defensamx1 detectaron e inhibieron un dron utilizado por un grupo delictivo para vigilar rutas destinadas al tráfico… pic.twitter.com/xiRtDrlljY — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) September 18, 2026

The drone operator was apprehended and found to be in possession of a handgun, ammunition and the aircraft control system.

Defensa said the Tijuana operation resulted from information-sharing with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) after its representatives met with CBP agents in the border city.

On Friday, Defense Minister General Ricardo Trevilla confirmed that four drones have been disabled as a result of Operation High Eagle, a joint, binational anti-drone security operation being carried out in the Tijuana-San Diego border area, with each force operating within its own territory.

The current deployment featuring approximately 800 military personnel from both countries encompasses a 5-kilometer area. It relies on ground patrols and the use of anti-drone equipment capable of inhibiting these types of aircraft within a 3-kilometer radius.

Trevilla said representatives from both countries met on Tuesday to assess the results of Operation High Eagle, which was organized after U.S. officials said its agents had shot down more than 300 drones linked to organized crime in the past year.

Defensa said coordination with U.S. authorities aims to strengthen border security under principles of reciprocity, shared and differentiated responsibility, mutual trust and respect for the sovereignty and territories of both countries.



The second phase of the operation, which began on Sept. 7, is scheduled to end on Sept. 21.

On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump acknowledged Mexico’s security efforts but called for greater commitment.

“Mexico’s current investments in its security forces are insufficient to sustain and expand its campaigns against narcoterrorists, their finances and their criminal networks,” Trump said, adding that Mexico must do more to “expose corrupt public officials who have aided and abetted the cartels and betrayed their own country’s security and sovereignty.”

Also Wednesday, Trump sent a document to the U.S. Congress, blaming Mexico for the illicit substances entering the United States.

President Claudia Sheinbaum responded by saying she would like to see a report about what the U.S. government is doing to reduce drug use in its own country and combat drugs and weapons trafficking.

With reports from El País, LópezDóriga.com and El Mañana

World.title: Nairobi International Trade Fair: Kenya Show Opens 28 September
World.content:
KENYA · NAIROBI · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is Kenya’s largest annual trade and farm show, run by the Agricultural Society of Kenya, with roots in 1902.

— When and where Monday 28 September to Sunday 4 October 2026, Jamhuri Park Showground, off Ngong Road, Nairobi.

— What it costs Day tickets are listed at KSh350 (US$2.70) for adults and KSh300 (US$2.32) for children.

— Why it matters Over 500 exhibitors from more than 25 countries show where Kenya’s farming, trade and exports are heading.

— The catch The official opening day and guest are not yet announced, and officials are preparing for possible heavy rain.

The Nairobi International Trade Fair returns to Jamhuri Park for seven days, with more than 500 exhibitors from over 25 countries and cheap day tickets.

Nairobi’s city-centre skyline; the trade fair is held at Jamhuri Park off Ngong Road (Photo: Tall Black, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Nairobi International Trade Fair opens at Jamhuri Park Showground in Kenya’s capital on Monday 28 September 2026. It runs for seven days until Sunday 4 October, with more than 500 exhibitors expected.

What the fair is and who runs it

The Agricultural Society of Kenya (ASK) organises the fair through its Nairobi branch. Its roots go back to 1902, when the first Nairobi show was held at Jeevanjee Gardens.

The show became a formal trade fair in 2002, according to the society. ASK describes it as the largest trade fair in the East African region.

Agriculture is still at the centre, with livestock, crops and farm machinery on show. The fair now also covers finance, insurance, logistics, manufacturing, energy, education and technology.

ASK splits the grounds into three broad parts: livestock and crop demonstrations, local manufacturers and services, and international exhibition halls. Foreign companies are housed in those halls for the week.

Dates, theme and who is coming in 2026

This year’s fair runs from Monday 28 September to Sunday 4 October 2026. ASK has announced no change to the dates, and organisers said this week that preparations were 99 percent complete.

The 2026 theme is “Promoting Climate Smart Agriculture and Trade Initiatives for Sustainable Economic Growth.” It is the same theme ASK used in 2025.

More than 25 countries are expected, including Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Nigeria, France, India, China, Japan and Egypt. Organisers say this edition puts innovation and export opportunities at the centre.

The Kenya Export Promotion and Branding Agency is backing the fair through its Made in Kenya initiative. Its chief executive, Floice Mukabana, was chief guest at the exhibitors’ forum in late August.

That forum took place at Jamhuri Park on 26 August. It is where ASK announced the list of countries taking part.

What visitors can see

Exhibits are grouped into zones, including an Agri-Tech and Innovation Hub, a Livestock Pavilion and a farm block. A Culinary Delights and Family Entertainment Zone adds food, games and performances.

A Business Nexus and Technology Showcase will host product launches and meetings with institutional buyers. Organisers also plan training sessions on modern farming methods.

Judges will score entries in 63 classes using a new smartphone-based system. ASK says this makes judging paperless and more consistent.

Exhibitors can sell goods in a special shopping area or take orders on items on display. Anyone selling food or drinks needs a separate permit.

ASK has not yet said who will perform the official opening, or on which day. In 2025, President William Ruto was billed to open the fair.

Tickets, entry fees and discounts at the Nairobi International Trade Fair

Visitor day tickets for 2026 are listed at KSh350 (US$2.70) for adults and KSh300 (US$2.32) for children. Amounts here are converted at 19 September 2026 rates.

ASK has not posted a full 2026 price list on its own website. In earlier years, tickets were sold online and at the showground gates.

Organisers have announced a new family package for groups of three to nine people, plus special rates for schools. Branch chairperson Levi Mukhweso described discounts of 10 percent for one day and 12.5 percent for two to seven days.

Visitors who come on more than one day also get free parking, he said. Separately, ASK membership costs KSh2,000 (US$15.44) single, KSh3,000 (US$23.17) full or KSh8,500 (US$65.64) executive.

Membership includes badges and car stickers. Executive members and their guests also get parking inside the showground.

Getting there, security and weather

Jamhuri Park Showground lies off Ngong Road, about 10 kilometres from Nairobi’s city centre. ASK puts it roughly 15 kilometres from Wilson Airport and 30 kilometres from Jomo Kenyatta International Airport.

The showground has more than five gates, reached by public transport and private cars. Organisers expect large crowds, so it is sensible to allow extra travel time.

Police will set up a station at the showground and patrol with private security staff. Officers have warned about phone snatching and children getting separated from their parents.

Officials have also cleared drains ahead of possible heavy rain during the fair. Deputy County Commissioner Victor Kamonde urged residents to avoid flood-prone areas if storms hit.

Why it matters for foreigners in Kenya

For foreign residents, the fair is a rare chance to see much of Kenya’s economy in one place. Farmers, banks, regulators, manufacturers and small businesses all share the same grounds.

It also shows how Kenya wants to sell more abroad, beyond tea, coffee and flowers. Many exhibitors are small firms looking for buyers, partners and finance.

The fair also draws families and school groups from across Nairobi. For newcomers, it is a low-cost day out alongside Kenyans of every background.

ASK is upgrading the ageing showground under its 2025–2029 strategic plan. Works include a new arena and a borehole with the Kenya Defence Forces, and road repairs by the National Youth Service.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the Nairobi International Trade Fair 2026?

It runs from Monday 28 September to Sunday 4 October 2026. The venue is Jamhuri Park Showground, off Ngong Road, about 10 kilometres from central Nairobi.

How much does it cost to get in?

Day tickets are listed at KSh350 (US$2.70) for adults and KSh300 (US$2.32) for children. Organisers also offer a family package for three to nine people and special school rates.

Who will officially open the fair?

The Agricultural Society of Kenya has not yet announced the guest or the day of the official opening. In 2025, President William Ruto was billed to open the fair.

What should visitors prepare for?

Organisers expect large crowds, and police have warned about phone snatching and lost children. Officials are also preparing for possible heavy rain during show week.

World.title: Ruger in Accra: Ghana Club Show at MAD Club on Sunday 27 September 2026

Key Facts — What it is A late-night club show by Nigerian Afrobeats singer Ruger, hosted by MAD Club in Accra, Ghana.

— When and where Sunday 27 September 2026, 11:59 PM to 4:00 AM, MAD Club, Lagos Avenue, East Legon.

— What it costs One general ticket at GH₵300 (about US$26), sold on Ayatickets online or by USSD *365*88*39#.

— Why it matters Nigerian Afrobeats stars draw big crowds in Accra, and Ruger’s hits made him a regional club favourite.

— The catch It runs into Monday morning, no support acts are named, and the price has already risen from GH₵200 (about US$17).

Ruger in Accra is a one-night club show at MAD Club in East Legon, with general tickets now at GH₵300 (about US$26).

Ruger in Accra brings the Nigerian Afrobeats singer to MAD Club in Ghana’s capital on Sunday 27 September 2026. The show is listed to start at 11:59 PM and run until 4:00 AM on Monday.

What Ruger in Accra is

The event is billed as Ruger Live in Accra and is hosted by MAD Club itself. The organiser’s short promotion reads simply: Ghana get ready, Ruger takes over MAD Club live on 27 September.

This is a club night, not a concert-hall show. There is no seating plan and no published running order, so expect a DJ-led night with a headline appearance.

Ruger, whose real name is Michael Adebayo Olayinka, is a Nigerian singer who mixes Afrobeats with dancehall. He broke through in 2021 with Bounce and Dior.

He followed with Asiwaju in 2022, which topped the Nigerian Apple Music chart. In 2024 he released Romeo Must Die with fellow Nigerian singer Bnxn.

Why this show matters in Ghana

Accra and Lagos share one of Africa’s busiest music corridors. Nigerian artists play Ghanaian clubs often, and Ghanaian stars do the same in Nigeria.

For a foreigner, this is a useful window into how West African pop actually lives. Songs break online, but they are proven on club dance floors like this one.

A club date also puts fans much closer to the artist than an arena would. That intimacy is part of the appeal, and part of why tickets move quickly.

The organiser has not described this as part of a wider tour. It appears to be a single Accra date rather than one stop on a regional run.

Tickets and prices

Tickets are sold on Ayatickets, a Ghanaian ticketing platform. There is one ticket type, listed as General, at GH₵300 (about US$26) at 19 September 2026 rates of 11.55 cedis per dollar.

Earlier in September the same listing showed GH₵200 (about US$17). The price has since gone up, so the figure you saw elsewhere may be out of date.

You can pay by card or mobile money online, or dial the USSD code *365*88*39# from a Ghanaian phone. The USSD route works without a data connection.

No VIP or table packages appear on the ticket page. If you want a table, ask the club directly, since those are usually sold separately.

Getting to MAD Club

MAD Club sits on Lagos Avenue in East Legon, near the junction with Lome Street. East Legon is a residential and nightlife district in north-east Accra.

The club is known for its graffiti-covered front and a dance floor focused on Afrobeats, hip-hop and Ghanaian music. Venue guides list cocktails at around GH₵120–140 (about US$10–12).

Ride-hailing apps such as Uber and Bolt work well in East Legon. Book your ride home in advance or agree a pickup time, because demand spikes after 3:00 AM.

Traffic on a Sunday night is usually light. Even so, allow extra time if you are coming from Osu, Airport Residential or the city centre.

Timing and what to expect

The listed start time is 11:59 PM on Sunday, and the ticket page gives an end time of 4:00 AM on Monday 28 September. Ghana runs on GMT all year.

Headline sets at Accra club nights rarely begin at opening time. Plan on a long evening, and treat 11:59 PM as the doors, not the stage time.

The organiser has not published a line-up, support acts or a set time for Ruger. Check the club’s social media channels during the week for updates.

Bring identification, as Accra clubs often check age at the door. Dress codes are common at East Legon venues, so smart casual is the safer choice.

Expect the room to be loud, hot and crowded once the headliner arrives. Earplugs and a bottle of water before you go in are sensible, low-cost precautions.

Practical notes for expats

The biggest practical issue is the calendar. The show runs deep into Monday morning, so anyone with work or school that day should plan accordingly.

Buy early if you are set on going, since the price has already risen once. Keep your digital ticket or USSD confirmation handy at the door.

No cancellation or change notice had been posted by 19 September 2026. It is still worth checking the ticket page the day before, as club dates can move.

Carry some cash in cedis as a backup for drinks and tips. Card machines and mobile money are common, but networks can be slow on busy nights.

Keep valuables to a minimum and watch your phone on a packed dance floor. Go with friends if you can, and agree a meeting point in case you get separated.

MAD Club is on Lagos Avenue in East Legon, near the junction with Lome Street. Ride-hailing apps are the easiest way to get there and back late at night.

SOUTH AFRICA · DURBAN · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is A one-day township braai and music festival, now in its second edition, celebrating Durban’s shisanyama culture.

— When and where Saturday 26 September 2026, from 12pm to midnight, at Berea Rovers, 73 Jacko Jackson Drive, Durban.

— What it costs Tickets start from R180 (about US$11), sold online through the Howler ticketing platform.

— Why it matters It closes Heritage Month by putting township grill-house owners and local food businesses centre stage.

— The catch It is strictly over-18, cooler boxes and bottles are banned, and supporting acts remain unannounced.

The eThekwini Shisanyama Festival returns for a second edition on Saturday 26 September 2026 at Berea Rovers in Durban, with Kelvin Momo headlining.

The eThekwini Shisanyama Festival returns to Durban, South Africa, on Saturday 26 September 2026, with amapiano star Kelvin Momo as headliner. Gates open at 12pm at Berea Rovers, and tickets start from R180 (about US$11) at 19 September 2026 rates.

What the eThekwini Shisanyama Festival is

The festival brings shisanyama vendors from across KwaZulu-Natal to one site for an afternoon and evening of grilled meat and music. It is the second edition of an event that started in 2025.

The founder is Lunga Mkhize, who owns Metro Gents Shisanyama in Umlazi, one of Durban’s largest townships. He launched this year’s edition at a media event in Umhlanga on 30 July 2026.

Mkhize says the idea was inspired by the late Jabulani “Mjay” Zama, founder of Eyadini Lounge in Umlazi. Zama showed that a township grill house could become a business and a social landmark.

The stated aim is economic as much as cultural. Organisers say the festival should bring customers and income to small food businesses, and create short-term jobs around the event.

Why a shisanyama matters in Durban

A shisanyama is a butchery or grill spot where you choose raw meat, have it cooked on open coals and eat on site. The Zulu word roughly means “burn the meat”.

Side dishes usually include pap, a stiff maize porridge, and chakalaka, a spicy vegetable relish. Music, often amapiano, is part of the experience, and a visit can easily last all afternoon.

For many South Africans, these places are where friends meet on weekends. They also give work to butchers, cooks, DJs and car guards in township economies.

Who is playing

Kelvin Momo is one of the best-known names in amapiano, the South African house-music style that has spread worldwide since around 2019. He is known for a slower, soulful and jazz-influenced sound.

The organisers have named him as headliner but have not yet published a full line-up or set times. Local DJs and live performances are promised, alongside food and craft vendors.

Amapiano sets tend to build slowly through the evening, so the headliner is likely to play late. If he is your main reason to go, plan to stay into the night rather than leave at sunset.

Heritage Month context

September is Heritage Month in South Africa, and Heritage Day falls on Thursday 24 September. Many South Africans mark the day with a braai, which is why it is often called Braai Day.

The festival lands on the Saturday after the public holiday, so expect a busy long-weekend mood across Durban. Mkhize has framed the event as a way to celebrate food as something that brings communities together.

Durban itself is a natural home for the event. It is KwaZulu-Natal’s largest city, and its townships, from Umlazi to KwaMashu, have a long grill-house tradition.

Getting there and what to bring

Berea Rovers is a sports club on Jacko Jackson Drive, beside the Kings Park stadium precinct. It is a short drive north of the city centre, not within walking distance of most beachfront hotels.

Uber and Bolt both operate in Durban and are the simplest option, especially for the late finish. The ticket page says parking is available on site if you drive.

The venue rules are strict: no under-18s, and no bottles, cooler boxes, weapons, hubbly pipes, umbrellas or gazebos. Bring sun protection, because late-September afternoons in Durban are often warm and humid.

Tickets and money

Tickets are sold on Howler, a widely used South African ticketing platform. Entry starts from R180 (about US$11); the organiser has not published the full list of ticket tiers in detail.

Buy only through the official Howler page rather than from resellers on social media. Carry a bank card and some cash in rand, since smaller food stalls may prefer cash.

Food and drinks are paid for separately on the day, so budget beyond the entry price. Prices at shisanyama stalls are usually modest by international standards, and at many grill spots meat is sold by weight.

What it means for expats and visitors

For foreigners in Durban, a shisanyama is one of the easiest ways to meet locals and hear the city’s music outside the tourist strip. A festival gathers many vendors in one place, which helps if you do not know the townships yet.

The event runs until midnight, so plan your ride home in advance and keep your phone charged. Check the organiser’s social media in the final days for set times and any late changes.

If you enjoy it, ask vendors where their own grill houses are. Many run every weekend, and a return visit on an ordinary Saturday shows the everyday side of the culture.

When and where is the eThekwini Shisanyama Festival 2026?

It takes place on Saturday 26 September 2026 at Berea Rovers, 73 Jacko Jackson Drive, Durban. Gates open at 12pm and the event runs until midnight.

Tickets start from R180 (about US$11 at 19 September 2026 rates). They are sold online through Howler.

Guatemala vs El Salvador kicks off at 20:00 on Monday 28 September 2026 at El Trébol in Guatemala City. Guatemala’s football federation is selling just over 7,000 tickets, all of them online.

Guatemala vs El Salvador: date, time and venue

The match is on Monday 28 September 2026, with kickoff at 20:00 local time. That is also 20:00 in San Salvador and 22:00 in New York.

The venue is Estadio Manuel Felipe Carrera, which almost everyone in the city calls El Trébol. It sits in Zona 3, beside the busy road interchange that gives it its nickname.

Concacaf, the regional governing body, places the fixture in Group B of League A, its top tier. Guatemala’s national football federation, known as Fedefut, runs the home match and its ticketing.

Tickets, prices and the online-only rule

Fedefut opened sales on Tuesday 15 September 2026 through Ticketshow Guatemala at ticketshowgt.com. There is no box office, so every ticket has to be bought online.

At 19 September 2026 rates of 7.64 quetzales to the US dollar, General Norte costs Q280 (about US$37). Platea Sur and Preferencia each cost Q730 (about US$96).

The top price is Tribuna at Q1,330 (about US$174). Visiting Salvadoran fans are placed together in Preferencia Visita, which also costs Q730 (about US$96).

Buyers need a Ticketshow account, so first-time users should register before checking out. Fedefut has capped purchases at three tickets per person for each match.

Buy only through the official platform. Tickets offered by resellers or on social media may be fake, and Fedefut has not announced any official resale service.

Why only about 7,000 seats are on sale

El Trébol is an old and fairly small ground, so Fedefut is releasing just over 7,000 tickets per match. Local media give the split as 2,850 in Platea Sur, 2,500 in General Norte, 1,412 in Preferencia and 490 in Tribuna.

With so few seats for a rivalry match, late buyers risk finding their preferred section sold out. Anyone planning to go should check availability soon rather than waiting until match week.

Some local fans have openly questioned the prices, which are steep by Guatemalan standards. They point to the team’s early exit from 2026 World Cup qualifying and to tight household budgets.

What is at stake in Group B

The 2026–27 Nations League now starts with two six-team groups played in a Swiss-style format. Guatemala’s Group B also includes Honduras, Jamaica, Suriname, Martinique and El Salvador.

Guatemala open away to Jamaica in Kingston on Friday 25 September, three days before hosting El Salvador. They visit Suriname on Friday 2 October, then host Suriname at El Trébol on Monday 5 October.

El Salvador start at home to Martinique on 25 September, so both sides may arrive with points to protect. The top two in each group reach the November quarterfinals, where Mexico, the United States, Canada and Panama join.

The finals are set for SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles in March 2027. The competition also serves as the qualifier for the 2027 Gold Cup, so dropped points carry a real cost.

A rivalry between close neighbours

Guatemala and El Salvador share a border, a language and a long football history. Their meetings draw strong interest on both sides of the frontier, and home crowds take them personally.

Guatemala are coached by Mexican manager Luis Fernando Tena, who is rebuilding the side after the failed World Cup campaign. A home win over El Salvador would be the clearest early sign of progress for his team.

Practical tips for expats and visitors

Plan to arrive well before kickoff, as the roads around El Trébol are among the busiest in the city. A Monday evening match means stadium traffic will overlap with people heading home from work.

Ride-hailing apps and registered taxis are the simplest options for most visitors. Arrange your ride home before the match, since leaving the area late at night can be slow.

Carry identification, keep phones and wallets out of sight, and bring only what you need. Stadiums in the region often restrict bags, belts and bottles, so travel light.

If you have no ticket, many bars and restaurants across Guatemala City will show the match. Expect those places to be busy and loud, especially around kickoff.

What has not been confirmed

Fedefut has not published gate opening times or a list of banned items for El Trébol. Check Ticketshow and Fedefut’s social media channels in the days before the match.

The federation has not said whether a service charge is added to the listed prices at checkout. No change or postponement had been announced as of 19 September 2026.

The match is on Monday 28 September 2026 at 20:00 local time. It will be played at Estadio Manuel Felipe Carrera, known as El Trébol, in Guatemala City.

How much do tickets cost?

Prices run from Q280 (about US$37) in General Norte to Q1,330 (about US$174) in Tribuna. Platea Sur, Preferencia and the visiting section, Preferencia Visita, each cost Q730 (about US$96).

Tickets are sold only online through Ticketshow Guatemala at ticketshowgt.com. There is no box office, and each person may buy up to three tickets for the match.

World.title: Oktoberfest Panama 2026: Sixth Edition at Mi Pueblito on 16–17 October
World.content:
PANAMA · PANAMA CITY · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is Panama’s largest German-style beer festival, now in its sixth edition, with craft beer, Bavarian food and live music.

— When and where Friday 16 and Saturday 17 October 2026, from 5 p.m., at Mi Pueblito, Panama City.

— What it costs Day tickets from US$20 on TicketPlus, including an official glass and half a litre of beer.

— Why it matters It brings Munich’s autumn beer tradition to a park built to celebrate Panama’s own village cultures.

— The catch October is peak rainy season, Mi Pueblito is open-air, and closing time has not been announced.

Oktoberfest Panama holds its sixth edition at Mi Pueblito in Panama City on Friday 16 and Saturday 17 October 2026, with day tickets from US$20.

Mi Pueblito, the municipal heritage village at the foot of Ancón Hill in Panama City (Photo: Dozenist, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Oktoberfest Panama returns to Mi Pueblito in Panama City on Friday 16 and Saturday 17 October 2026, its sixth edition. Gates open at 5 p.m. each day, and TicketPlus lists day tickets from US$20.

What Oktoberfest Panama offers this year

The official TicketPlus listing calls the event the biggest Bavarian beer festival in Panama. It promises craft and seasonal beers, Bavarian food, live music, contests and prizes across both evenings.

Doors open at 5 p.m. on both days, so Friday suits people coming straight from work. Saturday usually draws the bigger crowd at weekend festivals, so Friday may be calmer.

The organisers have announced this as the sixth edition and promise it will be bigger than ever. They have not yet published a line-up of bands or DJs, or a list of participating breweries.

Every ticket includes an official souvenir glass and half a litre of beer to start. Buyers choose between a glass Das Boot and a ceramic Beer Stein when they book.

Guests are encouraged to dress in Oktoberfest style. Lederhosen and dirndls are welcome, though a light shirt will suit the evening heat better than wool.

Tickets, prices and the Fast Pass

Tickets are sold separately for each day through TicketPlus, whose online shop runs on the Entratix platform. Both Friday and Saturday are listed from US$20.

Each day needs its own ticket. Anyone planning to attend both evenings should budget at least US$40 before food, extra beer and any Fast Pass.

Prices in Panama are quoted in US dollars, which circulate as everyday money alongside the balboa, fixed at one to one. Visitors from the United States will not need to change money.

A Fast Pass is offered at the end of checkout. It gives priority lines at the entrance, the beer stations and the food areas, but its price is only shown during purchase.

Food and extra beer are paid for inside. The organisers have not said whether a day ticket can be upgraded at the door, so buying online in advance is the safer option.

Mi Pueblito: a Panamanian stage for a German party

Mi Pueblito is a tourist centre run by the Municipality of Panama on Avenida de los Mártires, beside the Pan-American Highway. It was created in the early 1990s to show the settlements of the country’s main cultures.

The site has three plazas. The Afro-Antillean square has colourful early-20th-century houses and a sea view.

The interior square has cobbled streets, tiled roofs and the Museo de la Pollera, devoted to Panama’s national dress. It is where most visitors picture the classic Panamanian country town.

A third plaza recreates Indigenous life from the Guna Yala, Emberá-Wounaan and Ngäbe-Buglé territories. During Oktoberfest, long tables and beer stations fill all three plazas.

Last year’s edition, on 10 and 11 October 2025, drew both tourists and locals, according to the Panamanian magazine Living Panamá. It said Panamanian craft brewers played a leading role.

How the festival grew

The current series began earlier this decade. In 2022 it was held at La Fábrica on the Amador Causeway, with tickets rising from US$20 in August to US$30 at the door.

The 2022 ticket already included an official mug and half a litre of beer. The formula has stayed much the same ever since.

It has since settled at Mi Pueblito, and the price of entry has barely moved in four years. That makes it one of the cheaper large-scale nights out on the city’s autumn calendar.

The timing is no accident. Munich’s 191st Oktoberfest opened today, 19 September, and runs until Sunday 4 October on the Theresienwiese.

The Munich festival began in 1810 with a royal wedding and now draws around six million visitors. Panama’s version comes two weeks after it ends, closing a month of beer festivals worldwide.

Practical tips for expats and visitors

October is usually one of the wettest months in Panama City, and afternoon storms are common. Pack a light rain jacket, as most of Mi Pueblito is open to the sky.

Taxis and ride-hailing apps are the easiest way to get there and back. Parking is limited, and nobody should drive after a half-litre welcome beer and a few refills.

For newcomers, it is an easy social evening. Long shared tables make it simple to start a conversation with Panamanians and other foreigners.

Bring photo ID, because the legal drinking age in Panama is 18. The organisers have not said whether under-18s may enter with adults.

The festival has not published a closing time or a detailed schedule for 2026. Check the TicketPlus page or the organisers’ social media channels in the week before the event.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Oktoberfest Panama 2026?

It runs on Friday 16 and Saturday 17 October 2026. Doors open at 5 p.m. on both days.

Where is Mi Pueblito?

Mi Pueblito is a municipal tourist centre on Avenida de los Mártires in Panama City, beside the Pan-American Highway. Most visitors arrive by taxi or ride-hailing app, as parking is limited.

How much are Oktoberfest Panama tickets?

TicketPlus lists day tickets from US$20 for each day. Each ticket includes an official glass and half a litre of beer, and a Fast Pass for shorter queues is offered at checkout.

Do I need to speak Spanish to enjoy it?

No, the event is built around beer, food and music rather than speeches. Ticket pages are in Spanish, but browser translation handles them well, and many staff in Panama City speak some English.

MOROCCO · TANGIER · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is Tanjazz, Tangier’s jazz festival since September 2000, holds its 23rd edition this weekend.

— When and where 18–20 September 2026; paid nights at the Palais des Institutions Italiennes, free concerts around Tangier.

— What it costs Day passes were sold at MAD 600 (US$63); the organiser now says the edition is sold out.

— Why it matters Local media call it a comeback after a year’s pause, mixing jazz, flamenco, swing and Cuban music.

— The catch The official programme no longer lists Dee Dee Bridgewater, and under-18s cannot enter the Palais concerts.

Tanjazz Tangier 2026 reaches its second night with Diego El Cigala and Buena Vista All Stars, then closes on Sunday with free concerts in the city.

The Grand Socco in Tangier, where Tanjazz stages free concerts on Saturday and Sunday (Photo: Aleksandr Zykov, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Tanjazz Tangier 2026, the 23rd edition of the city’s jazz festival in Morocco, is on its second day today, Saturday 19 September. Diego El Cigala and Buena Vista All Stars headline tonight’s ticketed concerts, and free city shows close the festival on Sunday.

How the festival is laid out

Tanjazz runs on two tracks. The paid part takes place on Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September at the Palais des Institutions Italiennes, in the Marshan district.

Locals also know the building as Palais Moulay Hafid. It is the festival’s main venue and the only one that needs a ticket.

Inside the palace grounds there are two stages. The Patio stage hosts swing, soul and funk sets plus the jam session, while the Jardin (Garden) stage carries the headliners.

The second track is Tanjazz en ville, a free programme at public squares and hotels across the city. It runs on all three days, with Sunday 20 September given over to it entirely.

The festival’s own site also mentions food stalls, a designers’ market and dance classes at the palace. The Palais des Arts et de la Culture appears in its general description, but not in the 2026 programme.

Saturday night at the Palais

Tonight opens at 20:00 on the Patio stage with The Swing Shouters, with a dance class led by Rabat City Swing. Spanish flamenco singer Diego El Cigala follows at 21:00 on the Jardin stage.

Swiss boogie-woogie pianist Ladyva plays the Patio at 22:00. Buena Vista All Stars, built around members of the Buena Vista Social Club circle, take the Jardin stage at 23:00.

French band Les Frères Smith start on the Patio at midnight. A jam session at 01:30 closes the night, so expect to be out late.

Earlier today, The Haggis Horns were scheduled to give a masterclass at 12:00. The British brass band played the Patio stage on Friday night.

Free concerts today and tomorrow

You do not need a ticket for the city programme. Today at 12:00, The Groovy Four play the Hilton Tangier City Center hotel.

At 18:00 today, American trumpeter and singer Ronald Baker performs on Place du Grand Socco. At the same time, The Haggis Horns play Hôtel Rembrandt.

Sunday 20 September is the closing day and is entirely free. Ladyva plays Place du Grand Socco at 18:00, while The Swing Shouters perform at Hôtel Chellah at the same hour.

On Friday, Remork & Karkaba opened the city programme with a street parade from Bab Kasbah. The festival has not published any further free events for Sunday.

What changed from the first announcements

Early announcements named American singer Dee Dee Bridgewater for Friday night on the Jardin stage. The programme now on the festival’s website no longer includes her.

Instead, Friday’s Jardin stage featured Rodrigo y Gabriela at 21:00 and Fehd Benchemsi & The Lalla at 23:00. A Moroccan press report on the first night lists the same acts, and does not mention Bridgewater.

The organiser has not published a statement explaining the change. The Mexican guitar duo Rodrigo y Gabriela were playing in Morocco for the first time, according to that report.

Tickets and entry rules

The festival’s ticket page says all tickets for the 23rd edition have been sold and the box office is closed. Its hotline, 07 77 77 77 59, answers from 09:00 to 19:00.

Tickets were sold through Webook, the official partner. A one-day pass cost MAD 600 (US$63) and an early-bird two-day pass MAD 1,000 (US$106), at 19 September 2026 rates.

Moroccan media reported later-phase prices of MAD 700 (US$74) for a day and MAD 1,200 (US$127) for both nights. Resale offers outside official channels carry an obvious risk.

The Webook listing still showed a Saturday day pass on 19 September. Check it directly before heading to the palace, because the organiser describes the event as sold out.

Access to all concerts at the Palais des Institutions Italiennes is strictly prohibited for minors. Families with children should stick to the free city concerts.

What Tanjazz Tangier 2026 means for expats and visitors

Tanjazz has run since September 2000 and draws a local, national and international audience. It is held under the High Patronage of King Mohammed VI, according to Moroccan press coverage.

For foreigners living in Tangier, Sunday’s free shows are the simplest way in. Place du Grand Socco sits at the edge of the medina and is easy to reach on foot.

If you hold a Saturday ticket, plan for a long evening. Seven sets and a jam session run from 20:00 until well after 01:30.

Taxis are the easiest way up to the Marshan after the concerts. Agree on the fare or check the meter before you set off.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Tanjazz Tangier 2026?

The festival runs from Friday 18 to Sunday 20 September 2026 in Tangier, Morocco. Paid concerts take place on Friday and Saturday, and Sunday is free.

Where are the Tanjazz concerts held?

Ticketed concerts are at the Palais des Institutions Italiennes, on the Patio and Jardin stages. Free Tanjazz en ville concerts take place at Place du Grand Socco and several hotels.

Can I still buy Tanjazz tickets?

The festival’s ticket page says the 23rd edition is sold out and the box office is closed. The free city concerts on Saturday and Sunday need no ticket.

Is Dee Dee Bridgewater playing Tanjazz 2026?

She was named in early announcements, but the current official programme does not list her. The organiser has not published an explanation for the change.

World.title: This Is Michael Panama City: Jennifer Batten Joins MJ Show on 3 October
World.content:
PANAMA · PANAMA CITY · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is A touring Michael Jackson tribute, sung live by Lenny Jay, making its first stop in Panama.

— When and where Saturday, 3 October 2026, 8 pm, Teatro Anayansi, Atlapa Convention Centre, Avenida Israel, Panama City.

— What it costs Tickets start at US$45 on TicketPlus Panama, the official seller; zone prices appear at checkout.

— Why it matters Batten played guitar on Jackson’s Bad, Dangerous and HIStory tours — a rare direct link to the original shows.

— The catch Batten is a guest, not the lead, and door times and running order are unpublished.

This Is Michael Panama City brings the touring Michael Jackson tribute to Teatro Anayansi for one night — with Jackson’s former tour guitarist Jennifer Batten on stage.

This Is Michael Panama City takes place on Saturday, 3 October 2026, at Teatro Anayansi in the Atlapa Convention Centre, Panama. The official ticket page lists an 8 pm start, tickets from US$45 and a special appearance by guitarist Jennifer Batten.

What This Is Michael Panama City offers

This Is Michael is a tribute production that recreates Michael Jackson’s concerts with a live band, singers and dancers. Its ticket page describes the show as 100% live.

The promoters promise more than 10 performers on stage, more than 20 songs and more than 10 costume changes. They also claim over 500,000 tickets sold in more than 25 cities and 15 countries.

Those figures come from the production’s own marketing, so treat them as a guide. They do show that this is a large touring show rather than a local cover band.

The ticket page presents the Panama date as the show’s first visit to the country. That makes it a one-off chance for now, with no second Panama date announced.

Who is on stage

The Jackson role is sung and danced by Lenny Jay. According to the production, he spent several seasons in a European musical about Jackson before joining this show.

The headline guest is Jennifer Batten, the American guitarist who played in Jackson’s touring band. She was on the Bad, Dangerous and HIStory world tours between 1987 and 1997.

Bassist Don Boyette, who also played on Jackson’s tours, is billed as a second special guest. Both names appear on the official TicketPlus page for the Panama night.

Batten’s own website lists the Panama City show among her dates with This Is Michael. Her listing places it between Guayaquil on 1 October and Saltillo, Mexico, on 7 October.

Why Batten’s name matters

Tribute shows are common across Latin America, and most rely only on a lookalike singer. A musician from Jackson’s own band changes the character of the night.

Batten was the guitarist fans saw on stage during Jackson’s biggest tours. She also played with him at the 1993 Super Bowl halftime show.

She later toured and recorded with Jeff Beck from 1999 to 2001. For fans who grew up with Jackson’s concerts, hearing her play those parts again is the main draw.

She is billed as a special appearance, though. The seller has not said how many songs she will play, so do not expect her on stage all night.

Tickets and prices

Tickets are sold online through TicketPlus Panama, which the page lists as the official seller. Prices start at US$45 before any service charges added at checkout.

Higher zones cost more, and exact prices show only once you pick seats on the map. Sales opened in mid-May, so the best seats may already be gone.

TicketPlus also runs an official fan-to-fan resale market inside its site. Use that rather than social-media sellers if the section you want has sold out.

Panama uses the US dollar alongside the balboa, so prices are the same for visitors from the United States. Card payment online is the simplest option.

Getting to Teatro Anayansi

Teatro Anayansi sits inside the Atlapa Convention Centre on Avenida Israel, near the Cinta Costera and the San Francisco district. Most people arrive by taxi or ride-hailing app.

Saturday evening traffic along the coastal roads can be slow. Plan to arrive at least 45 minutes before the 8 pm start, and allow longer if it rains.

The seller has not published a door time or an end time. Batten’s own calendar gives 9 pm, so check the ticket and email from TicketPlus for the final time.

Atlapa has on-site parking, though it fills up on busy nights. If you drive, allow extra time for leaving after the show as well, when taxis are in high demand.

What to know before you go

You do not need Spanish to enjoy the evening, as the songs are all in English. Announcements and signage at the venue will mostly be in Spanish.

The show is on a tight Latin American tour, with Costa Rica and Guatemala in late September and Mexico and Peru after Panama. Line-ups can change on such schedules.

Check the TicketPlus page and your email a day or two before the show. Any change to guests or timing would normally be announced there first.

For residents, it is an easy Saturday night out with a familiar soundtrack. For visitors passing through Panama in early October, it fits neatly into a short weekend stay in the city.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is This Is Michael Panama City?

The show is on Saturday, 3 October 2026, at Teatro Anayansi in the Atlapa Convention Centre, Panama City. The official ticket page lists an 8 pm start.

Is Jennifer Batten really playing in Panama?

Yes. The official TicketPlus page lists her as a special guest, and her own website includes the Panama City date. She is a guest appearance rather than the lead, so she will not play every song.

How much are tickets and where do I buy them?

Tickets start at US$45 on TicketPlus Panama, the official seller. Higher zones cost more, and service charges are added at checkout.

Who plays Michael Jackson in the show?

The lead role is performed by Lenny Jay, who previously worked in a European musical about Jackson. Bassist Don Boyette, from Jackson’s touring band, also appears as a guest.

World.title: Apocalyptica Panama City Debut: Plays Metallica Vol. 2 on 6 October
World.content:
PANAMA · PANAMA CITY · EXPATS

Key Facts — What it is Finnish band Apocalyptica playing Metallica songs on cellos, on their Plays Metallica Vol. 2 tour.

— When and where Tuesday, 6 October 2026, 7:00 pm, Teatro Ateneo, Ciudad del Saber, Clayton, Panama City.

— What it costs US$80 (Gold), US$100 (Platinum) or US$120 (VIP) through Ticketplus; service fees may be added.

— Why it matters It is the band’s first-ever Panama show, a rare metal date in a small concert market.

— The catch It is a Tuesday night in Clayton, so plan the ride home before you leave.

Apocalyptica Panama City show: the Finnish cellists bring Plays Metallica Vol. 2 to Teatro Ateneo on Tuesday, 6 October 2026, their first concert in the country.

Apocalyptica on stage at Rockhal, Luxembourg, in 2024 (Photo: WanderingTrad, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
