World.title: La Fiscalía investiga abusos y vejaciones en los centros de menores de Ceuta
World.content:
A las ocho de la noche del miércoles, el campo de fútbol del barrio ceutí de El Príncipe enciende las luces para iluminar a los que aún apuran el partido. También a un pequeño círculo de chicas que habla junto a las gradas, apretadas, muy serias. De pronto, una joven rebasa la verja de entrada corriendo en dirección a ellas, llega llorando, tropezándose. Las otras salen a su encuentro y chillan: “¿Cómo te has escapado?”, se abrazan, se le unen en el llanto. Ella se ha fugado de uno de los centros de menores que la ciudad autónoma ha habilitado en Ceuta para alojar a los menores no acompañados que cruzaron a finales de julio. Tiene 17 años y es la cuarta chica en este campo en escaparse, la séptima en total. Antes de la medianoche se unirá Nadia, la octava. Sus nombres han sido cambiados para proteger su identidad.

Todas estas migrantes, de origen marroquí, fueron alojadas en los centros de menores a inicios de septiembre tras más de un mes viviendo en los campos informales levantados con la solidaridad de los vecinos, como este de El Príncipe o el de Sidi Embarek, aún en funcionamiento. Se las reubicó en dos instalaciones gestionadas por dos entidades distintas (Samu y Engloba), ubicadas una al lado de la otra, dentro del polígono de las Naves de El Tarajal. Según han relatado en una denuncia a la Policía, a los pocos días comenzaron a sufrir malos tratos por parte del personal a su cargo, insultos, vejaciones y falta de atención médica. También castigos físicos y amenazas constantes con expulsarlas a Marruecos. Contactadas por este periódico, ninguna de las dos empresas ha querido hacer declaraciones.

Un grupo de menores, tras escaparse del centro de menores y refugiarse en la barriada de El Príncipe. Mònica Torres

“Nos llaman putas constantemente, nos golpean, nos castigan si pedimos usar el móvil o una almohada”, cuenta Fatima, acelerada. Ella escapó el martes junto a otras dos compañeras, y se atropella al tratar de resumir lo sucedido. Tiene un moratón en el muslo, que, asegura, es producto de una paliza por parte del personal del centro. El resto también tiene magulladuras y heridas de diverso tipo, que han fotografiado e incorporado al atestado policial. “Nos hemos escapado nosotras, pero hay muchas más que siguen dentro y no lo han conseguido. Lo hacemos también por ellas. Cuando tenemos algún problema de salud, no nos llevan al médico, y nos insultan para que nos aguantemos. Hay una chica que aún está dentro y ni siquiera cuando vomitó sangre la asistieron”, cuenta. Según su relato, a esa menor en concreto las vejaciones y los insultos se los profieren por su orientación sexual.

Uno de los episodios de mayor gravedad que refieren sucedió el pasado 10 de septiembre, durante la noche. Dos hombres con uniforme de seguridad entraron en el recinto donde dormían las jóvenes, las despertaron y pronunciaron insultos de índole sexual y amenazas explícitas de violación. “Yo ese día no trabajaba, esa noche no estuve, pero las chicas me lo contaron. Traté de enterarme de quiénes eran y lo comuniqué”, cuenta una de las auxiliares del centro. Asegura que en su presencia no se han producido esos episodios de abuso, aunque está al tanto de lo que relatan. “Yo trato de tranquilizarlas cuando quieren escaparse, les explico que en la calle no van a estar mejor”, explica. La auxiliar refiere que son frecuentes las peleas entre las jóvenes, y que en su presencia hay castigos, pero no de índole física.

Una de las menores que se ha escapado del centro de menores tras denunciar los abusos. Mònica Torres

Fue precisamente en una de esas peleas este martes cuando un grupo de cuatro menores aprovechó que el personal de seguridad se desplazó a la planta de arriba para intervenir, y escaparon. Salieron tras ellas, pero se dispersaron en el polígono. En su huida, Karima, de 16 años, se cruzó con una voluntaria de Médicos del Mundo, que mantiene su unidad móvil en el recinto para asistir a las decenas de migrantes que viven en asentamientos informales de la zona. “Apareció con una crisis de ansiedad, con magulladuras y una contusión en la espalda”, explica la sanitaria. Le realizaron un informe psicológico y otro de las lesiones, y ambos fueron incorporados a las denuncias. Según detallan fuentes de la organización, estaban al tanto de episodios de este tipo en los centros de menores habilitados, pero hasta esta semana no habían tenido una constatación porque no les está permitido el acceso. Apuntan a un problema de falta de formación del personal de estos centros y a una ausencia de atención sanitaria integral para las menores, muchas de ellas en situación de gran vulnerabilidad.

Investigación en curso

El jueves, la Fiscalía de menores de Ceuta recibió un informe con la denuncia policial, los informes médicos y psicológicos. Se tomó declaración a las jóvenes, y esa misma mañana el área de menores de la ciudad, que ostenta su tutela, intervino. Se identificó a los dos hombres de seguridad del episodio del 10 de septiembre y se los relevó de sus cargos, estableciéndose que fueran sustituidos por mujeres, ahora y en adelante. También se identificó a una de las educadoras a las que las menores acusan de golpearlas de manera reiterada.

Paralelamente, se buscó una nueva ubicación para las denunciantes y pasaron la noche en otra instalación habilitada para menores no acompañados. “Nosotros no podemos volver a acogerlas, no podemos estar otra vez como al inicio”, cuenta Ahmed Enfed-Dal, presidente de vecinos de El Príncipe. Hasta su campo llegó el grupo que se escapó el miércoles, aprovechando una salida del centro programada para que las chicas salieran al exterior. “Volvieron aquí contando lo que había pasado y a mí se me rompe el corazón, pero no podemos volver a montar aquí el campamento, porque eso no es solución. Nosotros no tenemos la tutela, se tienen que encargar ellos”, explica.

A pesar de eso, Hafida Mustafa, otra de las vecinas que levantó el campamento improvisado en agosto, busca soluciones. Al menos para esa noche. Ella acogerá en su casa a una de las chicas, y trata de reubicar a las demás hasta que a la mañana siguiente tengan que ir a declarar. “Mira cómo viene esta, tiene una infección en el pie”, dice, señalando una herida en el empeine de Nadia. “Ni cuando estaban aquí y dormían en el suelo estaban en estas condiciones”, critica. Las que huyeron del centro el jueves, como Fátima y Nadia, llegan sin sus teléfonos móviles ni ninguna de sus pertenencias. Se fugaron con lo puesto y regresaron al lugar anterior, que las refugió durante casi un mes al inicio de la crisis. “Pero eso no se puede volver a repetir, esto tiene que parar”, insiste Hafida, en vano. Un día después, en el campo aparecieron tres menores más, también del mismo centro.

Cuatro de las menores migrantes denunciantes, retratadas en la barriada de El Príncipe. Mònica Torres

Zineb también se fue, pero no regresó a El Príncipe: cruzó la frontera, otra vez. “No podía con más humillaciones, entre nosotras hay quienes llevan hiyab y quienes no, pero igualmente te insultan, te golpean. No pude más, volví a Marruecos, aunque no estoy contenta aquí con esta situación en la que estoy ahora, en la calle, pero no tengo qué hacer”, escribe desde allí. El sábado 12 de septiembre fue al puesto fronterizo y retornó voluntariamente. “Yo no tenía que volver a Marruecos, yo tenía que salir adelante y hacer mi futuro allí, porque tengo un hermanito pequeño allí al que tengo que apoyar y cuidar”, explica. Según sus compañeras de centro, es una de las cuatro que ha retornado voluntariamente, una opción que, según confiesan, cada vez ponderan más. Mientras tanto, la investigación sigue en curso.

World.title: Carlos Villar (Protos): “Bad Bunny salía en un vídeo cocinando en su casa con nuestro vino. Le escribí, pero no me contestó”
World.content:
El director general del grupo bodeguero tiene un método particular para sus vacaciones: cada mes y medio se toma cinco días de desconexión

Pertenece a la cuarta generación de una familia bodeguera. Carlos Villar (Valladolid, 54 años) estudió Ingeniería Técnica Agrícola y comenzó su carrera como director de Exportación en Bodegas Santa Eulalia. Posteriormente asumió la dirección general del Grupo Frutos Villar, con presencia en Ribera del Duero. En 2004 recibió la llamada de Bodegas Protos para incorporarse como director de Exportación. Durante cuatro años recorrió el mundo impulsando la internacionalización de la compañía, que pasó de exportar a 25 países a estar presente en 85 mercados.

En 2008 abandonó la empresa y el sector del vino para ponerse al frente de la Dirección de Comercio Exterior de la Cámara de Comercio de Valladolid. Apenas un año después recibió la llamada que marcaría su carrera: Protos le ofrecía la dirección general del grupo bodeguero, integrado por 270 accionistas. Desde entonces, la compañía ha registrado una etapa de fuerte crecimiento. El pasado ejercicio facturó 54,1 millones de euros y obtuvo 16 millones de beneficio. “El 40% del ebitda (beneficio bruto de explotación) lo reinvertimos y lo destinamos también a remunerar a toda la cadena de valor. Pagamos un 30% más de media que en la zona. Somos líderes en Ribera del Duero”, asegura, aunque no detalla el número de botellas vendidas. Villar también fue presidente de la Cámara de Comercio de Valladolid entre 2014 y 2016. Elige el restaurante Sacha, en Madrid, para mantener esta conversación.

Pregunta. ¿Notó el cambio de trabajar en una empresa familiar a hacerlo por cuenta ajena?

Respuesta. Tuve que aprender mucho, sobre todo porque cuando llegué a Protos me incorporé a una compañía que hasta entonces apenas había vendido fuera y tuve que empezar a desarrollar la exportación. A cualquier hora del día y de la noche. Era lo normal. Triplicamos las ventas, pero no porque yo fuera mejor, sino porque ya venía haciéndolo en una empresa familiar. Es muy sano trabajar fuera de la familia. No tomo decisiones que no tomaría para mí mismo. Fue más fácil que en la empresa familiar, porque estaba claro qué era la bodega y qué quería ser. Había una marca, y eso era lo que marcaba la diferencia. El desafío siempre es decir que no a cosas que pudieran perjudicarla.

P. ¿Qué rasgos cree que son los más importantes dentro de una compañía?

R. La honestidad y la lealtad. Parece que son lo mismo, pero no es así. Van juntas hasta que se separan. La lealtad es más importante.

P. ¿Viaja mucho?

R. Ahora menos que cuando era director de Exportación. Viajo, pero como apoyo. Lo que sí me encanta es viajar por placer. Soy motero y me gusta hacer viajes aventureros.

P. ¿Recuerda alguno en especial?

R. Mauritania, antes de que empezaran los secuestros. Me encanta la alegría de su gente. He recorrido Nepal en moto y el próximo viaje será a Nicaragua. Mi gran afición son las motos. Tengo cuatro: una de campo, una de trial, una scrambler y ahora me acabo de comprar otra de campo para enseñar a mis hijos.

P. ¿Le preocupa el descenso del consumo de vino entre los jóvenes?

R. Afortunadamente, los que tenemos marca estamos creciendo en ventas, pero nos preocupa el descenso del consumo. Si la crisis dura mucho, nos tocará. Las marcas, cuando llegan momentos difíciles, vendemos más que en épocas de bonanza.

P. ¿Y eso cómo es?

R. Durante la crisis de 2008 a 2014, los restaurantes dejaban solo los vinos líderes de cada zona, porque sabían que se vendían. La gente prefería lo que conocía.

P. Hay una corriente que desaconseja tomar vino. ¿Usted bebe vino?

R. Es de lo que más bebo. Mi vida es muy intensa y el mejor vino es el que me tomo cuando me relajo al llegar a casa. El mejor es el que te tomas en soledad.

P. ¿Cómo se mantiene en forma?

R. A las 6.30 de la mañana voy al gimnasio. Es el mejor momento. Antes salía a correr, pero ahora hago bicicleta y senderismo de montaña con mi mujer. Me encanta el deporte; me sirve para desconectar. Soy muy aeróbico. Sin saberlo, hago ayuno intermitente. Solo tomo un café cortado con sacarina por las mañanas, y mi mujer me aconsejó que le quitara la leche. De esta manera, hago el ayuno.

P. ¿Desconecta en vacaciones?

R. Mis vacaciones son atípicas: cada mes y medio me gusta tener cinco días de desconexión. Si me cojo muchas vacaciones seguidas, noto que tengo que estar pendiente de todo y no desconecto. De esta manera, durante esos cinco días no pienso en nada más que en descansar.

P. Por trabajo, tendrá que visitar muchos restaurantes.

R. Suelen llevarme, más que elegirlos yo, sobre todo a sitios donde tengo el vino y donde debo tenerlo. Al menos tres días laborables a la semana como en restaurantes.

P. ¿Alguno que le haya sorprendido?

R. Soy poco de parafernalias y más de producto. En Madrid me gusta ir a sitios de toda la vida: Zalacaín, Sacha, Rubaiyat o El Qüenco de Pepa. En Valladolid, me gusta la autenticidad de La Parrilla de San Lorenzo. También frecuento Trigo y Suite 22, que es de un cocinero que iba para ingeniero informático.

P. ¿Se mete en la cocina?

R. Nada. Hice una primera cosa mal y no volví a cocinar nada más. Eso sí, soy muy agradecido.

P. ¿Con los vinos es exigente?

R. Sé distinguir bien y soy exigente si el vino lo pago yo. España es un país de buenos vinos, y quien hace malos vinos es porque quiere. Soy exigente en cuanto a esas modas raras de premiar los defectos de un vino. No creo en eso. En el vino está tu identidad y no hay que variar nada para seguir modas. Creo que hay que valorar la elegancia, la finura y no perder esa identidad. No creo que las modas se beban, aunque sé que a los prescriptores les gusta hablar de cosas nuevas. Pero considero importante valorar a los restaurantes y a las bodegas por su trayectoria, por el paso del tiempo, y no solo por las modas.

P. Si le invitan a comer en una casa, ¿siempre lleva vino?

R. Sí, casi siempre. Suelo regalar alguna botella rara o desconocida para mí y para quien la recibe.

P. ¿Qué otras aficiones tiene?

R. Intento cultivar la familia y los amigos. Me pongo recordatorios para llamar a mis hermanos y a mis amigos, para ver qué tal están. Creo que es importante cuidar mucho estas relaciones.

P. ¿Qué le gusta leer?

R. Leo para dormir y elijo cosas sencillas. Acabo de leer La paciente silenciosa. Un tercio de lo que leo es para ser más listo, para aprender de diferentes disciplinas, algo que va en contra de las lecturas pensadas para conciliar el sueño. Duermo entre seis y siete horas y el 80% del tiempo duermo bien. Me voy a dormir a las 22.45 y leo durante unos 40 minutos.

P. ¿Es disciplinado?

R. Mucho. Mis amigos lo dicen y creo que me ha ido bien valorando la disciplina. En ese sentido, soy muy parecido a mi padre, siempre recto y estricto. Además, soy muy puntual. En una ocasión perdí un avión y llegué tarde a una cita con un alemán que no me atendió. Perdí una posible venta. La puntualidad es respeto. Soy de los que creen en dar ejemplo. Soy muy estricto conmigo mismo y menos con los demás.

P. ¿Escucha música?

R. Mucho, sobre todo rock. Antes iba a conciertos, pero ahora no porque me agobia que haya tanta gente. Los últimos a los que fui fueron los de AC/DC y Loquillo. Con Bad Bunny tengo una anécdota muy buena.

P. Cuente, cuente...

R. Hay un vídeo en las redes sociales en el que aparece cocinando en su casa de Puerto Rico con una botella de Protos. Fue en mayo de 2020. Le escribí, pero no contestó. En Puerto Rico nuestra marca es muy importante.

P. ¿Se ve trabajando el resto de su carrera en la misma compañía?

R. Sí, cuando termine mi carrera profesional, me gustaría hacerlo en Protos. Es una empresa que me ha dado la oportunidad de hacer cosas increíbles. Además, es una gran compañía española en la que nadie es propietario único de ella. Hemos invertido más de 50 millones de euros para hacerla crecer y ese sigue siendo nuestro objetivo. Tomamos decisiones pensando en el largo plazo, y eso redunda en beneficio de la empresa.

Puede consultar el resto de entrevistas de esta sección aquí.

World.title: 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa
World.content:
Esta localidad onubense se define por su luz y por su condición fronteriza con Portugal. Hay que visitar su parte alta y la baja, a pie del río Guadiana, y aprovechar el viaje para ir al cercano paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina

Ayamonte es una localidad onubense que se define por su condición fronteriza. Su localización geográfica, en la desembocadura del Guadiana, es un punto estratégico en el que estuvieron fenicios, romanos, musulmanes y cristianos y en el que confluyen el mencionado río, el océano Atlántico, marismas, esteros, dunas y dos culturas: la local y la vecina portuguesa. En la orilla de enfrente, se encuentran los pueblos lusos de Vila Real de Santo António y Castro Marim. Las costumbres de unos y otros se filtran en ambas orillas de manera natural. Son humedades enriquecedoras, como ese fado del cantante Carlos Cano titulado María la portuguesa, que narra el trágico incidente de contrabando y amoríos que le costó la vida a un ayamontino en los años ochenta.

Esa posición geográfica aúna valor estratégico y estético. Localización que hizo que Ayamonte, desde el siglo XVI, tuviera un vínculo especial con la navegación, el comercio marítimo y la pesca del atún y de la sardina, actividades que hicieron que la localidad se desarrollara económica y socialmente. En el siglo XIX, tras el tsunami provocado por el terremoto de Lisboa de 1755 y que tanto afectó a Ayamonte, fue el turno de la industria conservera y salazonera. En 1991, se inauguró el Puente Internacional del Guadiana, lo que supuso un gran hito en la relación con Portugal, en la movilidad y en la economía.

Más información Cinco ciudades en España para comer muy bien más allá de Madrid y Barcelona

A su patrimonio histórico y arquitectónico se ha sumado el de la luz. El proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset ha situado a Ayamonte entre los lugares del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde —los estudios científicos del proyecto lo han identificado como el lugar donde se produce el último atardecer de la España peninsular entre los meses de octubre y febrero—. Un espectáculo natural que suma otro motivo más por el que merece la pena el periplo hasta aquí. Por carretera se llega desde las ciudades de Huelva, Sevilla y Faro, en Portugal, donde se encuentra el aeropuerto más próximo a Ayamonte y principal puerta de entrada de muchos de los turistas extranjeros que se ven paseando por las calles y las plazas del Rosario, de La Laguna y de La Ribera. En estos escenarios tiene lugar en el mes de agosto Un paseo por el Arte, evento que tiene el fin de mostrar en la calle las obras pictóricas, escultóricas y fotográficas de cientos de artistas locales o con alguna vinculación con la ciudad.

La plaza de la Laguna, en Ayamonte. Vibrant Pictures (Alamy / cordon Press)

10.00 Una habitación con vistas

Si la de Virginia Woolf era una habitación propia, las del Parador Nacional de Ayamonte (1) lo son con vistas; al Guadiana, al Puente Internacional que lo cruza y a la ciudad. Aquí antes hubo un castillo de origen romano, reedificado por los musulmanes después y finalmente ocupado por los cristianos.

Desde lo alto de la colina se divisa el río, Portugal y Ayamonte, que está a sus pies. El pueblo tiene una zona plana, a orillas del Guadiana, y otra alta, donde está el parador. Aia, en árabe, significa zona elevada. Cuando llegaron los cristianos, se encontraron un pueblo que se llamaba Aia y ellos le añadieron el sufijo “monte”. La parte más baja del pueblo se encuentra a unos tres metros sobre el nivel del mar, en las zonas cercanas al estuario; la parte más elevada es la del parador, a 63 metros de altura.

11.00 Antes y después del terremoto

A mediados del siglo XIII, Ayamonte pasó de manos portuguesas a las castellanas. A partir de ese momento, creció al amparo de la familia Guzmán y se vertebró en torno a dos partes: La Villa, la parte alta, donde se concentraban los edificios administrativos y religiosos, y La Ribera, la parte baja, donde se concentraba la vida marítima y comercial.

La Villa está llena de calles estrechas, miradores, fachadas tradicionales, balcones floridos y pequeños rincones con encanto. En este barrio se encuentran templos como El Salvador (2), San Francisco (3) y San Sebastián (4), además de antiguos palacios y casas señoriales. Uno de los edificios más emblemáticos es el antiguo Palacio de los Marqueses (5), junto al “Patio de la Jabonería”.

La iglesia de El Salvador, en la localidad onubense. Felipe Rodriguez (Alamy / cordon Press)

En La Ribera están las casas blancas, el paseo fluvial y el ambiente que evoca su origen marinero. Destacan el Centro Cultural Casa Grande Manuel Rivero “El Pintado” (6), el Ayuntamiento (7), las plazas de la Laguna y de La Ribera, conventos como el de las Hermanas de Santa Clara (8) y la capilla de San Antonio (9) las iglesias de La Merced (10) y Las Angustias (11). La Casa Grande es la única casa que se conserva anterior al terremoto de Lisboa de 1775. Seísmo que derivó en un tsunami que afectó gravemente a Ayamonte y otras localidades de Huelva, como Isla Cristina. Destruyó muchos edificios y hubo que reconstruir gran parte de su casco urbano. Las fachadas que hoy se ven datan de aquella época.

La plaza de La Laguna —aquí antes había una— es el corazón histórico y social de la ciudad. En ella hay una la réplica de La pesca del atún en Ayamonte, obra de Joaquín Sorolla integrada en la colección Visión de España que la Hispanic Society de Nueva York encargó al pintor. La plaza de La Ribera la diseñó el arquitecto José Granados, inspirada en las obras de Aníbal González, arquitecto sevillano que hizo la plaza de España. En la misma hay cerámica y ladrillo mudéjar forjado en las farolas, los bancos...

14.00 Geografía en el plato

Puesto de mercado y marisco en el mercado central de Ayamonte. Marcos del Mazo (Alamy / cordon Press)

La gastronomía, como el turismo y la pesca, son algunos de los sectores que forman parte de la economía azul, esa que se nutre de los recursos marinos de manera responsable, generando un crecimiento económico y empleo al tiempo que preserva la salud de los ecosistemas acuáticos de la zona. El abanico de delicias que se pueden degustar incluye la gamba blanca de Huelva, el choco, el atún, la sardina, la caballa, el arroz marinero y la mojama, el jamón del mar.

Estas delicias se preparan desde hace 60 años en el Restaurante Casa Luciano (12). El negocio hoy lo lleva el hijo del marinero que lo abrió, Luciano Ramos. El menú depende de lo que se coja en el día. En la carta, unos días hay y otros no, morro de atún, gambas a la plancha, cazón seco con tomate, cocido de garbanzos con rape, etcétera. Mucha de esa materia prima viene de Isla Cristina, donde se encuentra la principal lonja de Andalucía y la segunda más importante de España, después de la de Vigo. Cerca de la misma se puede comer en el Bar Marinero (13) y en Doña Lola (14), a orillas de la ría Carreras.

17.00 Parajes naturales

“Un lugar con tanta riqueza ecológica, como Ayamonte y sus alrededores, tiene un gran potencial como destino de viaje responsable”, sentencia Margarita Arjona, directora de Healing Planet, consultora de turismo sostenible. Alrededor de Ayamonte hay dunas y las marismas del Guadiana y el paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina, bañado por la ría Carreras, donde se encuentran Las Salinas del Alemán (15). Es una explotación artesanal, entre esteros y caños, que tuvo como primer propietario a un espía germano que envió el gobierno nazi en 1939 a la zona, Hans Burghard (o Juanito el alemán, para los lugareños), y que en la década de los ochenta se puso al frente de las mismas Manuel Gómez, al que le siguieron su hija (Manuela) y sus nietas (Estefanía y Sabina).

El paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina. Sonia Bonet (Alamy / cordon Press)

Además de esta sal por aquí hay salicornia o espárrago de mar, una planta que nace en las marismas y que el proyecto Marshfood produce de manera pionera. Cocineros como Ángel León, Martín Berasategui y Quique Dacosta la han usado.

18.30 La luz como fuente de orgullo

Si en Ayamonte el Guadiana es frontera, la luz es un orgullo. El pasado mes de enero esta localidad acogió una jornada divulgativa en el marco del proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset que sitúa al municipio onubense entre los enclaves del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde. Es decir, es uno de los mejores escenarios europeos para ver el atardecer. Algo que se puede ver en tierra firme o a bordo de una embarcación, ya sea la que hace una travesía por el Guadiana o la que lo cruza con destino la orilla portuguesa.

El Puente Internacional del Guadiana, que conecta Ayamonete con la localidad de Castromarín, en el distrito de Faro (Portugal), al atardecer. juampiter (GETTY IMAGES)

20.30 Una cena de sabores allende los mares

Después de la navegación, se puede cenar en el LPA The culinary bar (16), un restaurante inesperado en Ayamonte. Su cocina fusiona la tradición con la creatividad con posos de los viajes realizados por su cocinero italiano, Fabio Zerbo. El risotto de boletus con trufa, un curri tikka masala con pan naan casero o un arroz de corvina y maracuyá son algunos de los platos de esta casa que se ha convertido en un patrimonio más de la ciudad.

World.title: Arrests after far-right protesters attack police in The Hague
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Police have made 24 arrests in The Hague after an anti-immigration march in The Hague organised by a far-right group turned violent.

Several hundred people gathered at the site near Centraal Station at around 11am after a group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”) announced the event, exactly a year after a similar demonstration descended into a full-blown riot.

Protesters wearing balaclavas, scarves and masks to cover their faces gave Nazi salutes and carried banners with racist slogans such as “remigratie” (remig “blanke mannen vooraan” (“white men first”).

Acting mayor Richard de Mos ordered riot police to clear the Malieveld after demonstrators attacked police and ignored earlier orders to remove face coverings.

The rioters threw smoke bombs and fireworks and ripped traffic poles out of the ground, at least one of which was hurled at police. Police beat back the crowd towards Centraal Station using dogs, pepper spray and batons, managing to restore order by 3.30pm.

However, the violence was less extreme than a year ago, when 1,000 rioters set fire to police cars, blockaded the A12 motorway and smashed windows at the offices of political party D66.

“Atrocious”

Justice minister David van Weel called the scenes “atrocious” in a post on social media site X, while De Mos said the violence directed at police “crossed a line”.

“Hitler salutes, anti-Semitic chants, violence against police and fireworks thrown at riot squad officers,” Van Weel said. “It’s important that these people are dealt with severely.”

“That is why we cancelled the march and only allowed a demonstration on the Malieveld,” De Mos said. “When the violence continued, it was necessary to put an end to it.”

World.title: Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht
World.content:
One of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, Maastricht lies in the southern part of the country, close to both the Belgian and German borders. It is no wonder that the founding treaty of the European Union was signed there, nor that the Belgian (and French) influence has created a food mecca.

No one can quite agree on its exact origins. Celts lived in the area at least as far back as the 5th century BC, and the Romans showed up about 600 years later to build a bridge over the Meuse River that now runs through the centre of the city. Maastricht played a vital role in the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, and its location made it quite coveted between the 16th and 18th centuries. Many of those fortifications are still standing.

It was the first Dutch city to be liberated by the Allies during World War II. Half-century later, the city hosted a series of councils that led to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which paved the way toward the establishment of the European Union and the euro.

Maastricht is now home for 125,000 people, including many of the students studying at nearby Maastricht University.

Five things to do

Enjoy the city’s long and storied past with a historic walk.

Start at the Vrijthof, the main square where Dutch conductor André Rieu holds his summer concert series and which turns into a Christmas market in the winter.

Vrijthof is home to the majestic Basilica of Saint Servatius, where Maastricht’s patron saint Servatius is said to have died in 384 AD. A stone church was built over his grave in the 6th century which has been gradually expanded to the looming structure you see today.

You can loop past Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Sterre der Zee), a popular pilgrimage site, and see the famous wooden statue of Mary that dates to the 15th century.

Walk under the Helpoort (Hell’s Gate), the oldest city gate in the whole of the Netherlands, and then stroll through the Stadspark. On a nice day, you can join the many students who spread out a blanket and enjoy a few beers in the sun.

The part is also home to a number of sculptures and art installations. You can walk along the city walls and even see a statue of the fourth musketeer d’Artagnan. The leader of King Louis XIV’s elite corps of gentlemen, died in battle in 1673 during the French siege of Maastricht and archaeologists recently announced they may have discovered his skeletal remains under the floorboards of a nearby church.

If you want to go deeper into history, go underground

You can tour the caves of Mount Saint Peter, a collection of limestone quarries which date back to the 13th century. During World War II, they were used to safeguard arms and valuables from the Germans, including The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn which was removed from its frame and rolled into a cylinder.

You can also walk through the casemates (kazematten), defensive corridors that run under the city. These structures are unique in the Netherlands, as the groundwater level is too high in other parts of the country.

Visit a bookstore

The 700-year-old Dominicanenkerk has quite the history. Along with serving as a house of worship, the church has been used as a warehouse, an archive, a printing house, and even a place to store bikes. Napoleon used it to store equipment and military personnel while invading the region in the 1790s.

It was converted into one of Europe’s most unique bookstores following a restoration project in the mid 2000s. If that’s not enough, you can also check out De Tribune, which was named the best literary bookstore in the Netherlands in 2024.

Shop til you drop

Maastricht is known for its shopping and the city is filled with boutiques, art galleries, vintage shops and more. The Rechtstraat is just one of many lovely shopping streets. On Wednesday and Fridays, the city holds a market with Friday wares more orientated towards clothing. On Saturday, hundreds of vendors turn out for the antiques market.

Go to the other extreme

Just outside Maastricht, you can find the highest point in the Netherlands. At a little over 322 metres tall, the Vaalserberg might merely be considered an average hill in other countries, but for the Netherlands, that’s a mountain.

It’s also home to Drielandenpunt, a three country-point where the borders of Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands meet. Its lookout towers offer great views of the surrounding region.

Where to eat

Limburgse vlaai is the local delicacy and a must have on any trip to Maastricht. It’s not quite a pie and it’s not quite a pastry, but it’s definitely delicious. De Bisschopsmolen currently has no less than nine on the menu at their bakery and cafe. If you’d like to try your hand at making your own, they also host vlaai workshops.

The Onze Lieve Vrouweplein has a collection of outdoor cafes where you can enjoy a coffee or a beer.

If you want a fancy meal, look to L’Auberge. This lovely restaurant sits in the former stables of Château Neercanne. For an even fancier meal, the companion Restaurant Château Neercanne. For a real treat, you can stay at the hotel.

Cycle outside of the city and have lunch at Grand-Café Buitengoed Slavante. The country estate has a great breakfast menu and you can also take a walk on the grounds.

Another great lunch option in the city is the hip, Marres Kitchen. It’s in the same building as the museum Marres, House for Contemporary Culture so enjoy some art at the same time.

Where to stay

For a boutique experience, try Townhouse Hotel Maastricht. It also offers apartments if you’d like to eat your vlaai at home. Kruisherenhotel is the only five star hotel in the region. It’s housed in a 15th century monastery along the Kommelplein and each one of its 60 guest rooms features unique art and decor. The the Easy Hotel is a clean and cheap choice.

How to get there

The train stops practically in the middle of the city and you can walk in along a beautifully landscaped boulevard. It’s about three hours from Amsterdam. The drive is a bit shorter, at 2.5 hours, depending on the traffic.

Anything else

Keep in mind that Maastricht is south of the river and therefore deep into Carnival territory. Andre Rieu’s summer concerts are extremely popular and thus make it impossible to find hotels and parking.

World.title: Man targeted in village shooting arrested over cocaine shipment
World.content:
The man whose farmhouse was besieged by dozens of gunmen in a suspected drugs feud has been arrested in Germany, Dutch media report.

German police said a 28-year-old man was detained in a car park in Soest, 150km beyond the Dutch border in North Rhine-Westphalia, on suspicion of trying to smuggle nearly four tonnes of cocaine through the French port of Dunkirk.

NOS quoted sources saying the suspect was Jan G., who is believed to have been the target of a group of heavily armed men who killed a security guard and injured two police officers in a shoot-out in Overasselt, Gelderland, three weeks ago.

Police traced G. in the wake of the shooting, as well as another man who was arrested in Dordrecht a week ago in connection with the drugs shipment.

French customs officers said the cocaine, with an estimated value of €225 mln, was concealed among plastic waste in a container from Ghana.

The Telegraaf reported that the shipment belonged to Jos Leijdekkers, known as “Bolle Jos”, the Dutch drugs baron at the top of Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives. The cross-border police force has issued a €200,000 reward for information leading to his capture.

G.’s house was closed on the orders of local mayor Joerie Minses, who also ordered the man to stay out of the village for three months in an attempt to restore order.

Some 33 men of varying nationalities, including Dutch, French, Algerian and Belgian, were arrested in the wake of the shooting on September 1. Six were from the Amsterdam area. Some were caught while hiding in fields or trying to flee the area by car or train.

Judges ordered all but one of the suspects to be detained in custody for the next three months while investigations continue.

World.title: Indian restaurant owners arrested in human trafficking inquiry
World.content:
Two owners of a chain of Indian restaurants in the Netherlands have been arrested as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking.

Europol and the Dutch labour inspectorate carried out a probe into allegations that a rule making it easier for Asian restaurants to hire specialist chefs from outside the EU was being widely abused.

The restaurant owners are said to have hired staff from India as chefs but employed them in non-specialist roles such as cleaning, washing up or waiting tables.

Labour inspectors also found the employees were working between 60 and 80 hours a week, rather than the 38 that was allowed under the terms of their work permit, and were being underpaid or not paid at all for the extra hours.

The two suspects owned eight restaurants that were part of a nationwide chain with branches in Utrecht, Amsterdam, The Hague, Hilversum and Hoofddorp.

Europol said around 70 staff had been hired on false premises, contributing around €4 million of unpaid labour. The investigation also covered allegations of similar abuses in Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg and Switzerland.

The owners arranged their workers’ housing and allegedly fined them if they left before the end of their contract, which deterred the victims from contacting authorities.

“There are also indications that their families in their home countries were put under pressure and threatened with violence by the suspects in order to make the victims work harder and prevent them complaining to the managers of the restaurant chain,” the inspectors wrote.

The Dutch government introduced a simplified work permit system for Asian chefs in 2019 to address a labour shortage, but scrapped it three years later after inspectors found evidence that it was being abused by employers.

Inspectors visited 50 restaurants in 2021 and 2022 in a mix of randomised checks and others targeting high-risk establishments, which found 60% of the high-risk restaurants and 45% that were selected at random breached the rules at least once.

World.title: Muslims launch hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques
World.content:
Muslim liaison organisation CMO has set up a national hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques amid concern that many incidents are going unreported.

Police have admitted that discrimination is underreported in the Netherlands, while community leaders hope the hotline will encourage victims to come forward.

Muhsin Köktas, chair of the CMO, said he believed the online portal, which will go live on September 20, “will lower the threshold for our community to report incidents here”.

Last year 414 cases of discrimination against Muslims were reported to police, 20 of which came from mosques, but Köktas said many crimes were not reported “because often nothing happens or if someone reports an incident, they don’t know what happens with it afterwards”.

A police spokesman said the force was aware of the low reporting rate, but urged victims to come forward.

“In broad terms discrimination is rarely reported, including discrimination against Muslims or incidents at mosques,” the spokesman said.

“[The hotline] can help people who experience discrimination to give their account, but we encourage these people to come to us as well. We can only take action, get a picture of problems in society and respond to them if we know what is going on.”

New Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernández has recalled Joey Veerman to the squad for the opening Nations League match against Germany next week.

The Borussia Dortmund midfielder, who has won 17 international caps, was left out of the squad for this summer’s World Cup in North America after falling out with Xavi’s predecessor Ronald Koeman.

The Spanish coach’s first squad is a mixture of youth and experience, with some senior players retained while others have made way for the Eredivisie’s young stars. Three members of the 26-man squad play their football in the Netherlands, while half are with clubs in the English Premier League.

Captain Virgil van Dijk is expected to win his 97th cap in Amsterdam next Thursday, ending speculation that the 35-year-old was considering retiring from international football.

Tijjani Reijnders and Crysencio Summerville have also kept their places despite moving to Saudi Arabia in the summer, in a departure from Koeman’s policy of not picking players from the Saudi league.

But there is no place for the Netherlands’ all-time leading scorer, Memphis Depay, who has struggled with injuries this year.

Twente’s veteran striker Wout Weghorst has also been left out, while Feyenoord’s in-form striker Gjivai Zechiël and PSV winger Ruben van Bommel, son of World Cup finalist Mark, are also in line to win their first caps.

After playing Germany in the Amsterdam Arena, Oranje will travel to Belgrade to take on Serbia on Sunday in their second match.

World.title: Dutch housing update: money for new homes, rising interest rates
World.content:
There was some good news for home buyers in this week’s budget with the announcement of a massive financial package to boost new residential development. There are also signs that house price rises are slowing down, although interest rates are shooting up and the issue of foundations continues to be confusing. This and more in the latest housing news round-up.

Budget briefing

There was not much in the way of direct measures impacting on the Dutch housing market in this week’s budget. For example, the government did not announce any new changes to the current mortgage interest deduction set up, although there will be a slight rise in income tax rate in the first and second tax bands, which will have a minimal impact on your rebate.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan did come up with a string of measures she hopes will boost supply in the rental sector and new construction, and is pressing ahead with plans to cut the property transfer tax for holiday homes and investment properties from 8% to 7%.

Most relevant for would-be home buyers? “Plenty of investment in large scale developments of new homes, so if you are looking for a new-build property, you could be lucky – although the changes will take time to filter through,” says Matthijs van der Heijden, a mortgage advisor with Expat Mortgages, which has been helping internationals buy a home for over 20 years.

The government is also putting a further €100 million into a special fund to help first-time buyers get a foot on the housing ladder.

Interest rate increases

Over the past 18 months interest rates have been pretty stable but have been trending upwards since the second quarter of the year, and are currently rising sharply as geopolitical uncertainties continue.

“We are not yet seeing these higher rates have an impact on house prices,” says Matthijs, “but there does seem to be a little bit of room for negotiation. And some buyers are able to have a second viewing of a property before they decide whether to put in a bid.

“So there is more opportunity for people who don’t want to rush into a purchase. And we have noticed that some estate agents are helping their clients to negotiate on or just under the asking price.”

The higher interest rates are also making it more important to have some savings if you are planning to buy, just to keep your costs as low as you can. “If you have €50,000 that you can put down towards the cost of your house, that means €50,000 you won’t have to borrow at well over 4% interest,” Matthijs points out.

Ask your mortgage-related questions

Expat Mortgages will be at the IamExpat Fair in Eindhoven on October 3, so come along and meet the team in person, or 

Seminars, whether online or in person, are a great way of getting direct answers to your questions and sharing your experiences with others. “We also try to focus on the more specific situations – people who have not even moved here yet, and entrepreneurs who may not have been active in the Netherlands for more than a year, when most banks want three years,” says Matthijs.

“We’ve also seen an increase in the number of PhD students wanting to buy, and banks are becoming a little bit more lenient. They used to say ‘no permanent contract, no mortgage,’ but that is changing as well.”

More homes on the market?

Despite there being room for negotiation in some parts of the market, the shortage of cheaper homes to buy is continuing, and single people or single-income families wanting to buy a home are still facing an uphill struggle. Demand continues to be very high for properties at the lower end of the market.

“Things have been very slow over the summer, but now more people are getting out there and looking,” says Matthijs. “And you can still expect to have to overbid if you are looking at cheaper properties. Much depends on what areas you are looking in as well.”

The fundamentals of foundations

Since April, banks have been taking more account of a property’s foundations when deciding whether or not to back a mortgage application. As yet, says Matthijs, there is no overall consensus about what to do if a property’s foundations are in need of urgent, or not-so-urgent, action. “It is primarily the bigger banks which have been the frontrunners on this,” says Matthijs. “It is very early days.”

“However, you can assume if the report shows there is €100,000 worth of repairs which need to be done before the house is properly stable, the banks are going to wonder how this is going to be paid. This could be done, for example, by increasing your mortgage loan – although many people are nowadays stretched to capacity because of the high house prices – or through having the savings in your bank account. One way or another, your bank will want to know if you can pay for the work.”

Are you thinking about buying a home in the Netherlands? Make an appointment to talk directly to a mortgage advisor and find out how much you can borrow.

Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. World.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. World.title: Russia planning “accidental” strikes on eastern NATO states, warns Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems. The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymyr Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly. “Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk. “The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw launches patrols to crack down on improperly parked electric scooters
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. E-scooters, which are currently unregulated in Poland, have been blamed for hundreds of accidents annually, with half of victims being pedestrians hit by riders https://t.co/TcrfPQocfr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 3, 2021 Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. The police have launched a campaign on the legal requirements for using e-scooters, including a warning that riding or parking them on pavements can be illegal. In 2022, accidents involving e-scooters in Poland resulted in 421 injuries and three deaths https://t.co/dMOBiNUBNG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish right-wing opposition MPs call for Independence Day march in Ukrainian city of Lviv
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
