World.title: Asian Games open in Nagoya with glitzy ceremony after troubled buildup
World.content:
PHILIPPINE DELEGATION. Filipino athletes get ready to compete at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Organizers hope the Asian Games opening ceremony will help resolve a rocky buildup filled with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport

NAGOYA, Japan – The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya on Saturday, September 19, with a glittering ceremony of dance and fireworks following a buildup marred by operational gaffes and logistical problems.

Five years after the Tokyo Olympics played out at empty venues due to COVID-19 restrictions, Japan welcomed fans to the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium for a curtain-raiser that was initially subdued before bursting into a festival of colour and sound.

Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open after watching the parade of 45 nations and regions at a dignitaries’ table along with International Olympic Committee boss Kirsty Coventry.

Naruhito’s visit with royal family members was accompanied by a heavy security operation. Organizers had said up to 10,000 police would be deployed for the ceremony.

“While the world is too often divided by conflict, they (the Asiad athletes) remind us that sport remains a powerful force for peace, understanding and friendship among nations,” Olympic Council of Asia President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani said in a speech.

Complaints from athletes and officials

Japan’s father-and-son duo of Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi, both former Asian Games champions in hammer throw, jointly lit the cauldron after climbing a set of stairs at the end of the torch relay.

Organizers will hope the ceremony can draw a line under a rocky buildup laden with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport.

Japan’s reputation for precision and efficiency has been under scrutiny as the nation welcomes more than 11,000 athletes competing for 369 gold medals in a whopping 43-sport program.

Instead of building a dedicated Games village, organizers have housed the athletes and officials in a mix of hotel rooms, temporary wooden containers and a cruise ship docked in the bay as a cost-cutting measure.

Several national team delegations, including hosts Japan, have found the arrangements below par, complaining of mix-ups and double-bookings, while South Korea said the containers at Garden Pier were too cramped for their basketballers.

India’s powerful cricket board took matters into their own hands, arranging for the men’s star-studded cricket team to stay in a separate hotel due to a tight allocation of beds from organizers.

Delegations have also lamented long waits for the athletes registering on arrival and have found buses turning up late or sending their athletes to the wrong venues.

The Olympic Council of Asia, which runs the quadrennial Games, acknowledged the problems on Saturday but played them down as teething difficulties.

Directed by Yukihiko Tsutsumi, the opening ceremony made a low-key start, with classical music and dance on a heart-shaped stage before the parade of nations which featured a delegation from reclusive North Korea.

The spectacle ramped up later though, with dancers in boiler suits marking Nagoya’s manufacturing tradition and a fireworks display closing the night.

The ceremony’s theme was “Harmonic Heart Beat” — intended to communicate Asian solidarity at an event often riven by geopolitical tension and historic grudges.

However, hopes for a peaceful Games have already been undermined by several incidents.

Taiwan’s delegation temporarily refused to participate in their welcoming ceremony on Friday after sports minister and former Olympic champion Lee Yang was blocked from attending it.

The South Korean men’s hockey team were upset when North Korea’s national anthem was played at the stadium before a match instead of their own.

While competitions for basketball, soccer and other sports have already started, the first gold medal will be won on Sunday, likely in the triathlon.

A high-class swimming competition kicks off in Tokyo on Sunday, with the programme featuring China’s 100 metres freestyle world-record holder Pan Zhanle and 13-year-old sensation Yu Zidi.

Apart from traditional Olympic sports, the Games will stage regional favourites kabaddi and sepak takraw along with quirky, modern events.

Esports will award medals again after making its debut at Hangzhou, while teqball, a mix of table tennis and soccer, and “virtual taekwondo” will make their first appearance at the Games. – Rappler.com

World.title: Greenland, Denmark say US deal will not cede sovereignty
World.content:
DENMARK. Denmark's Minister of Defense Jeppe Bruus, along with Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Mute B. Egede, visits the NATO military exercise Arctic Shield 2026 in Narsarsuaq, Greenland, on Wednesday, September 9, 2026

Denmark and Greenland assure sovereignty in US military deal, aiming to enhance Arctic security while respecting self-determination amidst Trump's controversial claims.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark – Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington “permanent control” over the Arctic island’s security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the US to ‌develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of US military presence in the self-governed ⁠Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump’s threats to seize control of Greenland.

“Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom’s red lines,” he said.

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”

The deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington’s express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

“I am pleased on Greenland’s behalf that we are nearing the conclusion of an agreement — an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the continued development of this country,” Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said on Saturday in a post on Facebook.

“The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he added.

Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region.” – Rappler.com

World.title: James Reid is finally home, and he’s right where he wants to be
World.content:
James had spent much of his career feeling undeserving of all the recognition he was getting. But all along, there was really no need to strive to be anything more — and he would make that groundbreaking realization by fully diving into the music.

Sometime in 2010, a young, wide-eyed James Reid would exit the Pinoy Big Brother (PBB) house with more fame than he knew what to do with.

Within the walls of PBB, contestants would typically go months with no outside contact, but almost every move they made and every word they uttered was made known to everyone watching. And so, when the then-17-year-old Filipino-Australian emerged as the season’s Big Winner, hordes of people had come to celebrate him, much to his surprise.

Having just arrived in the Philippines, James hadn’t fully grasped what he had gotten himself into. He was timid, mostly spoke in English, and would, more often than not, merely flash a toothy grin in conversation with other housemates.

Still, he was immediately put on this pedestal and thrust under a spotlight he had no idea how to navigate. Fans would constantly assure him that there were plenty of reasons to love him, but the then-rising star didn’t feel worthy of any of that at all — even after topbilling film after film and giving life to songs (case in point: “Randomantic”) that have long found a permanent place in Filipino pop culture.

“I’ve just had such a backwards career where I already started with, at least in the Philippines, almost the maximum amount of fame without having done much to feel like I had deserved it or proven myself,” James told Rappler. “I just felt like a fraud in this whole industry. I’m not talking poorly of PBB or anything, but that’s the reality of the situation we get put in.”

Now 33, James is a completely different person. After taking a break from showbiz for six years to focus on other creative endeavors, he now carries himself with a greater sense of self-assurance, and no longer finds himself desperately searching for the feeling that he had earned the right to be where he stands now.

All along, there was really no need to strive to be anything more — and he would make that groundbreaking realization by fully diving into the music.

On learning to love and be loved

Make no mistake, though. James’ relationship with music hadn’t been perfect from the get-go either. It had gone through a noteworthy arc of its own, where he had felt restricted from displaying vulnerability and the liberty to write what he truly wanted.

“Definitely with past projects, I love the songs that I’ve made before, and I think there’s still a place for it in my life. But I can hear where I’m holding back. I can hear where I don’t want to go all the way or say too much or express myself too much because I know that one day it’s not going to be just in the studio, it’s going to be everywhere else,” James confessed.

This blatant display of openness used to scare the singer-actor. The creative process, he had once mentioned, is all him, but the minute it gets put on streaming platforms for the rest of the world to hear, the work no longer becomes his alone. It had taken a lot for James to get comfortable with that. But his genuine love for his craft had proven to be greater than any apprehensions he ever had. Now, he just sits back, lets his creativity flow, and just allows genuine inspiration to take over until it all builds up into something he can say he poured his whole soul into.

James Reid

“I think that became so much of the point of all of it that I accepted it. So I didn’t really care about it anymore. And maybe that’s what made me feel more comfortable and more safe to just write whatever the hell I want to write about,” he shared.

This is something the “Pahinga” hitmaker truly makes evident in his latest creation, Honey I’m Home, a 10-track album that also happens to be his most personal body of work to date.

Most of it had been conceived at a songwriting camp in February 2025. It wasn’t anything glamorous, really — just James, some producers, writers, and artists making music in an open outdoor space uninterrupted, with nothing but a fan spinning above them.

“I just wanted to try something different where the creative process was not cut by people needing to go home because I feel like sometimes, you get into a groove, but then I get busy and I have to do some other thing. And then my mind and my heart is just not in the same place as it was that day. It’s difficult to bring things back,” he explained.

People came and went, but James remained there for two whole weeks, churning out the messiest of ideas until he finally began to strike gold.

At that point in time, it had only been a few months since James dropped his six-track EP jgh, which speaks of home in the physical sense. It was more of a compilation of random love songs he had put together after having just returned from traveling and being in the US, and overall feeling more grounded being back in the Philippines.

But in Honey, I’m Home, James speaks of love in an entirely new way. It’s not the kind of love you pull from watching romcoms — but the kind of love that feels so revolutionary it changes who you are and everything you’ve ever known about love. James credits all of that to his partner, Issa Pressman.

James and Issa

“When we got together, she just had this different kind of kindness and light and warmth and generosity. I’ve never met anyone so in touch with their soul just naturally. It was inspiring, and not in the music sense, just me as a person. I’ve learned so much from her,” he said about Issa.

“And I think that gave me just a brand new perspective on how to love myself and how to love other people. In a much greater way than just chiming in some lyrics, I think the whole perspective of Honey, I’m Home came from the love that she gave me.”

There was a big change in James’ writing, and it all boils down to his change in perspective.

“Just the way I look at love, and the way I look at life, and the way that I see what I’m supposed to be doing here, I think my whole perspective shifted. And I think that’s the biggest thing that changed with the music,” he told Rappler.

Honey, he’s home

With Honey I’m Home, then, you get a heavily layered record at its finest.

Take “Indiana” for instance. James and Issa have always dreamt of having a child of their own someday. The couple even already has a list of potential baby names, and one of them is Indiana. That’s how the song’s concept came to be in the first place: they already had so much love for a kid who wasn’t even born yet, and it was an indication of a love that transcends generations, time, and, eventually, death.

“I wanted to write it in a way where it says, ‘We love you so much, even though you’re not here. But also, we want you to know that far, far in the future when we’re gone, and you’re still here, that that love is still there,’” explained James. “And that made it extra hard, but I think I pulled it off. I imagine her still singing this song one day, even when I’m gone.”

James offers ‘Indiana’ as a love letter to his future child with Issa.

In writing “Unbecoming,” meanwhile, James scrutinized every fiber of his being to determine which parts of himself he didn’t like anymore. It was a difficult yet absolutely necessary process he had to go through to fully describe how he’s changed after experiencing Issa’s love.

“[It’s the kind of love] that is not so much about what you give me, and is not so much about what I can give you. But the kind that changes my world and makes me a better person,” he said.

James believes Issa helped him become a better person.

Yet the evolution isn’t just in the music itself, but in the village it took for all of this to happen. For the longest time, James was content with flying solo — doing all the work on his own, and even expressing reluctance toward the thought of having to rely on others to get things done.

When you look at the credits of Honey, I’m Home, you’ll be able to see that it was the product of consistent collaboration with other people. James attests that while it’s just his name on the record, it’s the hard work of those around him that made it all possible: his team at Careless, his producers Luke April and Brian Lotho, the featured artists on some of the tracks, and everyone else who contributed to the album in one way or another.

Above all, James is clearly no longer who he used to be.

James is right where he’s meant to be. Photo by @henzonlyhope

“I think happy is probably the best word to use, so much so that I felt confident enough in myself that I could go back into the industry that caused me so much stress and anxiety before,” he said, referring to his first teleserye comeback in nearly a decade.

“I’m definitely in a place where I feel like I can just keep shooting for the stars and then seeing where things go. Because I feel like even if I fall, I have a nice place to land no matter what.”

And so, for as long as there is love to give and receive, James and his music are here to stay. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIST: Community events, activities on 54th Martial Law commemoration
World.content:
From card games and pop culture trivia to film screenings and other activities, here are engaging ways to reflect and honor history this Martial Law anniversary

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos will mark the 54th anniversary of Martial Law on September 21, 2026, commemorating the declaration of Proclamation No. 1081 by then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos. It ushered in a dark period in Philippine history, marked by widespread human rights abuses and a crackdown on free speech.

While street protests remain a central fixture of remembrance, several groups are set to organize educational forums, film screenings, art exhibits, and interactive community gatherings across the country.

Here is a running list you can check to participate in this year’s Martial Law Anniversary:

Outside Metro Manila

1081 exhibit at UP Cebu

The ninth installment of the 1081 exhibit, honoring the victims of Ferdinand Marcos’ dictatorship, is open to visitors until Monday, September 21, at the UP Cebu Performing Arts Hall.

UP Baguio alternatibong klase

Students from UP Baguio will conduct alternative educational sessions in commemoration of the anniversary. Baguio-Benguet Laban sa Korapsyon will host talks, forums, and film viewings throughout the week, leading up to an assembly at the university on Monday, September 21, at 5:30 pm.

UP Los Baños film showing (Martial Law short films)

The UP Los Baños College of Arts and Sciences will screen seven short films about the Martial Law period at the CAS Auditorium on Monday, September 21, at 4 pm. Admission is free with online registration.

Panel and educational discussion – Anakbayan Toronto

On Monday, September 21, at 6 pm EDT (720 Spadina Ave, Canada), Anakbayan Toronto will host an educational discussion on historical resistance, anti-fascism, and organizing.

Metro Manila

Diktador game night

DIKTADOR! is an immersive role-playing card game about Martial Law history and Filipino resistance organized by Project Gunita. The creators are partnering with different organizations to hold game nights throughout the month:

Project Gunita: Saturday, September 19, 9 am, at the Constantino Foundation

Saturday, September 19, 9 am, at the Constantino Foundation DLSU University Student Government : Thursday to Friday, September 24 to 25, 4:15 pm at the Exhibit Area, Henry Sy Sr. Hall. Interested participants can register online.

Thursday to Friday, September 24 to 25, 4:15 pm at the Exhibit Area, Henry Sy Sr. Hall. Interested participants can register online. UP Diliman CSWCD: Friday, September 25, 4 pm, at Bulwagang Tandang Sora (Registration details on their page)

Sunday trivia hangout on political pop culture

The Women’s Legal and Human Rights Bureau Inc. is organizing a trivia night about Martial Law history and current events on Sunday, September 20, 12 pm, at Sunshineboy Cafe in Mahinhin 57, Quezon City. The event will also feature Project Gunita’s DIKTADOR! card game. Register for free (solo or as a team) online.

Igpaw Pasulong: Film showing, talkback session

GABRIELA Youth UP Manila and AlterMidya are hosting a screening of Igpaw Pasulong, which highlights stories of the Filipino masses during Martial Law. The event takes place at the UP Manila Theater on Wednesday, September 23, at 1 pm, followed by a discussion with women activists linking these narratives to present struggles. Registration fee is P30.

DLSU USG film screening of ‘Aswang’

The DLSU Committee on National Issues and Concerns (CoNIC), in partnership with Active Vista, is screening Aswang on Thursday, September 24, 2:30 pm, at the Teresa Yuchengco Auditorium. The 2019 documentary investigates extrajudicial killings during the war on drugs. Online registration is required.

‘Marcos, Martial Law, and the Complexities of Memory’ book talk

The UP Diliman Department of History will host a roundtable discussion on the book Marcos, Martial Law, and the Complexities of Memory in the Philippines on Tuesday, September 22 at Palma Hall. Editors and select authors will discuss how the memory of Martial Law continues to shape modern politics.

54th Martial Law anniversary candle lighting

Bantayog ng mga Bayani, Buhay Ang People Power, August Twenty-One Movement, and the Ninoy and Cory Aquino Foundation will host a candle-lighting ceremony for martyrs, heroes, and survivors on Monday, September 21, 5 pm, at the Bantayog ng mga Bayani in Quezon City.

EDSA Shrine mass rally

Multiple contingents will march on Sunday, September 20, to demand accountability from corrupt leaders and commemorate Martial Law:

Akbayan Youth: Marches from DLSU Greenhills at 9 am

Marches from DLSU Greenhills at 9 am People’s Assembly & Tindig: Gathers at Congress South Gate at 8 am

Gathers at Congress South Gate at 8 am August Twenty-One Movement: Assembles at Quezon Avenue at 7 am before marching to the Supreme Court

Assembles at Quezon Avenue at 7 am before marching to the Supreme Court Combined Mass Program: All groups meet at the EDSA Shrine at 10 am

Kilusang Bayan Kontra Kurakot Protest

The Kilusang Bayan Kontra Kurakot (KPKK) will hold an anti-corruption rally on Monday, September 21, 3 pm, at Liwasang Bonifacio. The mobilization marks the anniversary of Martial Law alongside the first anniversary of the Baha sa Luneta and Trillion Peso March, linking past human rights struggles to current anti-corruption advocacy.

Makabayan Mendiola protest

The Makabayan party will join forces with KPKK for a protest on Monday, September 21, at 5 pm in Mendiola, Manila, demanding government accountability and historical truth.

Do you know of other events, protests, or activities commemorating the 54th anniversary of the Martial Law declaration? Send the details to move.ph@rappler.com — Rappler.com

World.title: How Ubisoft Philippines helps bring game worlds to life
World.content:
In helping build a blockbuster game like ’Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced,’ Ubisoft brings the skills of talented Filipinos to the forefront

Ubisoft Philippines celebrated its 10th year in the country by inviting members of the media and industry advocates to their office in Taguig for a tour of the studio on September 10.

The tour focused on introducing the office to newcomers like mysefl as well as imparting the contributions the Philippine studio made to Ubisoft’s latest blockbuster release, Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced.

UBISOFT PHILIPPINES. The front of office at Ubisoft Philippines.

Through the tour and a subsequent interview with studio manager Sashi Menon and studio art director JP Tan, I found myself enamored with the earnest pride the Philippine team had in their work.

Redefining classic Creed with pride

Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced is a modernized take on the 13-year-old Assassins Creed Black Flag, so its overall structure existed long before the creation of the Philippine studio. But it’s what comes from the Philippine side that makes it magical.

It’s taking the nuts and bolts of the older game and working on updating game mechanics like harpooning, improving on existing art assets like the weapons and clothing, rebuilding and reimagining the game world’s towns and forts, and ensuring the game world’s audio brings life and vibrance to the proceedings.

HARPOONING MECHANICS. A Ubisoft programmer explains what they’ve done with harpooning in ‘Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced’

My attention was drawn to watching the visuals through recorded gameplay and watching other members of the media try out the game, but it was in the studio tour where I felt that sense of pride coming through.

The team members in charge of specific aspects of the game themselves were on point, delivering presentations on what their teams were in charge of.

While some were nervous, they were still eager to put their best foot forward in showing off what they had achieved.

AI in the workplace? ‘The work remains the same’

During my interview with Menon and Tan, I was curious about whether artificial intelligence (AI) plays a role now in helping to develop games, whether it’s in doing specific work or in adjusting workflow processes to help them do certain aspects at scale.

Tan said the game industry is in a kind of “figuring out stage” when it comes to using AI. He added that they were experimenting on use cases for AI but there hasn’t been anything yet that has grown into fruition.

WORLD PRESENCE. Ubisoft Philippines is one of a number of studios the company has internationally.

When it comes to art, for example, Tan said, “We highly prioritize the skill of our artists, so that’s the most important thing. Being an art director, I am always on the lookout of developing the fundamental skills of each artist and their expression.”

“On the other hand,” Tan added, “it’s hard to ignore the benefits or the potential of AI-assisted workflows. Meaning any of the work, sometimes the tedious work, or the manual work that takes away from the creativity of things, that’s what we are on the lookout for.”

Menon added that AI use can and does happen but primarily as a tool to defeat busywork that eats up time. This could include helping in speeding up research by scraping the internet for needed information, but “the work remains the same” in that the human touch is needed.

Menon also said unlike some companies that use generative AI to ostensibly do everything, “we don’t see value in that.”

Keeping their feet on the ground

Tan, in closing remarks, noted that AI is “a tool meant to be understood and harnessed.” The realities of game development — and of artificial intelligence in the workplace — require human understanding.

“The future is coming fast, and it’s scary, but also at the same time, we need to keep our feet on the ground and teach the right values to our teams,” Tan said.

“Game development is essentially a problem-solving endeavor. It is essentially solving multiple constraints happening at the same time, whether it be artistic constraints. technical constraints, and production constraints. If you ask me if AI can solve all of that, not yet,” he added.

A HUMAN TEAM. Ubisoft Philippines has a staff wall where they post photos from their work and play activities.

Ultimately, Ubisoft Philippines celebrating its 10th year of working in the country should be a cause for pride and celebration, as it brings triple-A games and the skills of talented Filipinos to the forefront of the games industry.

As Tan explained, “It always boils down to the person, the teamwork, their understanding of the game — what can be done for the game, what are the things that can be placed in the game and not in the game — that’s what makes it special.” – Rappler.com

World.title: IN DATA: How BARMM voted in its first-ever parliamentary elections
World.content:
The historic Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) election has concluded. How did the Bangsamoro people vote?

The results are mixed, with no single party getting a majority of the seats. But the parties that did successfully get seats are:

A look into where all the votes came from showed that local politics and key endorsements remained decisive in electing the BARMM Parliament. Here’s a breakdown of the numbers.

Votes per province

The top three regional parliamentary political parties (RPPPs) secured votes in different ways.

First placer BFP consistently got the most votes in four out of the BARMM’s six provinces: Basilan, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, and Tawi-Tawi. This could be due to the endorsements of local officials in these provinces.

The governors of Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, and Tawi-Tawi had endorsed the BFP. Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman had a hand in founding two other parties — the BGC and Bangsamoro Peoples Party — but his nephew and Vice Governor Jim Hataman-Salliman was a candidate of the BFP. Eleven Basilan mayors also endorsed the BFP.

Maguindanao del Norte is also the bailiwick of BARMM Interim Chief Minister and BFP president Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua. He previously served as acting governor of Maguindanao del Norte.

Second placer UBJP — which had initially been seen as the front-runner in the election — won in only one province: the Special Geographic Area (SGA), which is where Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and UBJP chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim and his family reside. The party was a strong second placer in four other regions.

The UBJP, the official party of the MILF, was the majority party in the region’s transition government for the past seven years. Support from the former rebel group’s members across the region was also expected.

Third placer BGC’s voter base was more concentrated, getting 53.83% of the votes from Lanao del Sur alone. This province is the region’s most vote-rich, making up 30.4% of the voting population.

This large showing in a single region is not surprising given that the BGC and one of its individual parties were established by the Adiong family, one of Lanao del Sur’s most entrenched and long-standing political clans.

For the sectoral races, the UBJP swept all six seats up for election. But a look at the provincial breakdowns showed that voting patterns in the provinces were still largely affected by political dynamics.

Going deeper into the municipal and city levels showed roughly the same pattern of key endorsements and strongholds, save for some breakthrough areas. But these areas were where candidates had their own hyperlocal pockets of power.

For example, in BGC-dominated Lanao del Sur, some UBJP bets still managed to win in their own strongholds: one unopposed bet and two former mayors — former Kapai town mayor Hamza Gauraki and former Poona Bayabao mayor Lampa Pandi.

In BFP and Macacua’s Maguindanao del Norte, former Maguindanao del Norte vice governor Abdulnasser Abas of the UBJP captured his own district. A scion of the Midtimbang clan is the lone UBJP winner in Maguindanao del Sur, where three other BFP bets won.

While BFP bet Butch Malang lost the race, he was still able to capture one of the four towns in Ebrahim’s bailiwick of the SGA. Malang was administrator of the Special Geographic Area Development Authority until recently.

Across its seven-year transition, the BARMM’s interim government — the Bangsamoro Transition Authority — had attempted to pass laws that would make the regional government move away from patronage politics toward more genuinely representative governance. Anti-political dynasty and anti-turncoatism provisions were put in place with the goal of making politics more about principles rather than prominence.

Still, the results of the region’s first parliamentary elections showed that clan and dynastic politics continue to have a tight hold on the Bangsamoro people.

Can the BARMM’s incoming elected parliament change that? – Rappler.com

World.title: This ‘hard to swallow’ Filipino film hopes to make Oscars history
World.content:
‘Filipiñana,’ the country’s official film entry to the Oscars, hopes the international audience sees something different — a ‘different side of the Philippines’ and a ‘different kind of Philippine cinema’

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines attempts to make history after selecting Filipiñana as the country’s official entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards.

A 100-minute film showing the Philippines’ class divide, Filipiñana tells the story of 17-year-old Isabela, who works as a “tee girl” in an exclusive golf club.

“It’s hard to accept a formalist film that isn’t a narrative,” said film producer Bianca Balbuena in Filipino.

Initially a short film, the full-length feature directed by Rafael Manuel and co-produced by Bradley Liew has been praised for its visual storytelling, but has also drawn critique for its slow pace.

“As director Rafael said, how he thought of this is not script-based, it’s more on verses, like music: verses, chorus. So it’s hard to accept. Even us (producers), when we first saw the cut, we said, ‘This is hard to swallow.”

But it’s this unique approach that Filipiñana hopes to bank on when it tries to earn a nomination at the Oscars. Since the inception of the Best International Feature Film category in 1956, no entry submitted by the Philippines has even made the official shortlist of 15 films.

Filipiñana’s strong reception at the international festivals, including the Sundance Film Festival where it bagged the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision, has kept everyone behind the film hopeful.

“I think the international audience saw a different side of the Philippines, and saw a different kind of what Philippine cinema can be and is. They were excited to see something different,” Balbuena said.

Locally, Filipiñana premiered as the closing film of the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival 2026

“Actually, Cinemalaya was our 22nd film festival,” Balbuena said. “Then now, we are in our 26th. It is going to Bangkok, going to Busan, Tokyo, Vienna, Hamburg, Singapore, and many more. It’s competing in Pingyao, China also.”

‘Filipiñana’ cast members Jorrybell Agoto (third from left) and Nour Hooshmand (left) with producers Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew receive from Film Academy of the Philippines director general Paolo Villaluna (right) their certificates as the Philippines’ official entry to the 2027 Oscars.

Jorrybell Agoto stars as Isabel, whose job as a tee girl includes setting up golf balls for elite patrons, including the country club’s president Dr. Palanca, played by Teroy Guzman.

Paolo Villaluna, the director general of the Film Academy of the Philippines (FAP), which announced Filipiñana’s Oscars selection last September 13, said the body will again support the country’s Oscars campaign.

“The film offers a visually distinct and controversial portrait of the Filipino experience,” said Villaluna. “The Film Academy will work closely with the Filipiñana team throughout the Oscars campaign, providing the support they need and make the most of this opportunity for Philippine cinema.”

Last year, the Philippines’ Oscars entry, Lav Diaz’s Magellan, made a strong push but still fell short of the Academy’s final cut.

But Filipiñana’s producers said they’ve been campaigning for the film internationally, even before it was selected as the country’s Oscars entry.

“Whether or not we get chosen, we already had a plan,” Balbuena shared. “It was [good timing] that we were at the North American release announcing [its selection]. So we can do an email blast to all the members to watch the North American theatrical run. We’ve also covered the biggest cities of the voters: US and UK. So we are ready since then.”

Aside from Filipiñana, FAP threw its support for the Oscars consideration of 58th (Best Documentary Feature Film) and Agapito (Best Live Action Short Film) in their respective categories.

A still from the animated film ’58th, which rotoscopes and dramatizes the 2009 Maguindanao maasacre. Film still courtesy of FFR

58th, directed by Carl Joseph Papa, is an animated docudrama film about the 2009 Maguindanao massacre, which claimed 58 innocent lives, but only 57 were officially recognized as the body of photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay has yet to be found.

“We want the film to be a reminder and an eye-opener: this happened in 2009, and it’s still happening all around the world,” Papa said. “I hope it’s an eye-opener and people will remember, so the tragic events won’t happen again.”

“This is officially the deadliest single day for journalists in the whole history that has ever been counted: 32 journalists killed in one go,” added film producer Nessa Valdellon. “We’re hoping that people who cover…who write stories will be able to appreciate it and realize, ‘God, this is the importance of [our] jobs.’”

Agapito, co-directed by Arvin Belarmino and Kyla Danelle Romero, tells the story of manual pinsetters in a vintage duckpin alley and explores the themes of love, family, and patience in a working-class setting.

“Agapito is about a real person, actually. He’s my brother who’s in the autism spectrum, special child,” said Belarmino. “It’s my first time to produce because mostly the films I make before are subcultured, sociopolitical. It’s my first time to show vulnerability to tell about the story of a loved one.”

A movie poster of ‘Agapito,’ a short film featuring pinsetters in a duckpin alley.

“Filipinos are still constantly telling their stories for the Filipinos. It’s just a matter of exposure to everybody,” said Jon Galvez, one of Agapito’s producers.

“My wish is: instead of trailers are shown outside cinemas, I hope it will be short films — to provide space for short filmmakers to show their films outside of festivals. Philippine cinema is worth it. Worth fighting for, worth watching.”

“Let’s just give it a chance,” Galvez added. “There are a lot of factors involved, that’s why it’s not supported all the time, but just give it a shot. The talent of Filipinos, the storytelling, it’s so different.”

The deadline for submission of films to the Academy Awards is on September 30, 2026, with the official shortlist of 15 films to be revealed on December 15, 2026.

In 2027, the five final nominees will be announced on January 21. The 99th Oscars ceremony is set on March 14, 2027 at the Dolby Theater in Los Angeles.

“I hope all eyes are on the Philippines now, all Hollywood eyes. I think we have a good chance with the three titles here,” Villaluna said.

“I hope the Filipinos support all our films. We are the masters of cinema, we are good storytellers.” – Rappler.com

Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

World.title: Asian Games Open in Nagoya as Kazakhstan Targets Bigger Medal Haul
World.content:
ASTANA – The 20th Asian Games opened in Japan on Sept. 19, bringing together thousands of the continent’s top athletes. Kazakhstan is represented by 558 athletes competing in 35 of the 43 sports on the program, reported the Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

The opening ceremony was held in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, and the Games run through Oct. 4.

More than 15,000 athletes are expected to compete for medals in 469 events across 43 sports, spanning both Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines. Several competitions will also count toward qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games, either by awarding direct quota places or points toward Olympic rankings.

Paris 2024 Olympic judo champion Yeldos Smetov and national table tennis team member Sarvinoz Mirkadirova carried the Kazakh flag at the opening ceremony. Smetov is a three-time Olympic medalist, having also won silver at the 2016 Rio Games and bronze at Tokyo 2020, while Mirkadirova is a multiple Kazakh champion and medalist on the WTT Feeder circuit.

The scale of Kazakhstan’s delegation reflects a broader push ahead of the Games to strengthen the national team system. The ministry said foreign specialists with international experience and modern training methods had been brought into the preparation process, with the longer-term goal of developing domestic coaching expertise as well as improving results at major international competitions.

The country won 80 medals, including 10 gold, 22 silver and 48 bronze, at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, finishing 11th in the medal standings. Ahead of the competition in Japan, the ministry has set a target of 99 medals. Meeting that goal will depend on sports in which Kazakhstan has traditionally been competitive in Asia, including boxing, wrestling, judo, fencing and shooting. But several of the country’s leading medal contenders arrive in Japan with another layer of pressure, according to the National Olympic Committee press office. Many will be facing opponents they already know from Olympic finals, world championships and previous Asian Games.

Familiar rivals

One of the examples comes in men’s team épée, where Kazakhstan and host Japan have developed one of the continent’s strongest fencing rivalries.

Japan beat Kazakhstan in the semifinals of the 2018 Asian Games, while Kazakhstan took silver and Japan gold at the following edition. A few years later in the semifinals of the 2025 world championships, Japan edged Kazakhstan 42-41 before going on to win the title.

A year later, Kazakhstan won its first men’s team épée world championship, defeating Ukraine 45-40 in the final. It also won the 2026 Asian championship, with Japan finishing second.

That means the two teams arrive at the Asian Games as winners of the past two world championships.

Boxing

Boxing brings another major regional test, particularly against Uzbekistan.

Kazakhstan finished first at the inaugural World Boxing Championships in Liverpool in 2025 with seven gold medals, while Uzbekistan won six. Kazakh and Uzbek male boxers won in 10 weight categories at the tournament, setting up the possibility of several high-profile rematches in Japan.

Among them is Aibek Oralbay, who defeated Uzbekistan’s Jakhongir Zokirov in the over-90-kilogram final in Liverpool.

Aida Abikeyeva could also renew her rivalry with Uzbekistan’s Navbakhor Khamidova after the pair finished first and second at major international events over the past year.

Torekhan Sabyrkhan could again face Japan’s Sewonrets Okazawa after defeating him in the 70-kilogram world championship final in Liverpool.

Another major Kazakh medal contender is Nazym Kyzaibay, one of the most decorated athletes on the team. The Paris 2024 Olympic bronze medalist has repeatedly reached the podium at major international tournaments and took silver at the 2025 world championships while competing in the 48-kilogram division.

In Nagoya, Kyzaibay moves up to 54 kilograms, where she faces a particularly strong field. Her potential rivals include reigning world champion Huang Hsiao-wen of Chinese Taipei, Paris Olympic silver medalist Pang Chol-mi of North Korea, South Korea’s Olympic bronze medalist Im Ae-ji and Japan’s Tokyo Olympic bronze medalist Tsukimi Namiki.

Namiki also has a history with Kyzaibay: the Japanese boxer defeated her in the semifinals of the 2022 Asian championships, giving a potential meeting in Nagoya the added dimension of a rematch.

Olympic champions

Kazakhstan also brings considerable experience into the judo competition.

Smetov, the reigning Olympic champion in the 60-kilogram division, could again face Chinese Taipei’s Yang Yung-wei. Yang won silver at the Tokyo Olympics and gold at the previous Asian Games, while Smetov defeated him in the Paris 2024 Olympic quarterfinals on his way to the title.

Smetov is himself a former Asian Games champion, having won gold in Incheon in 2014.

Abiba Abuzhakynova gives Kazakhstan another strong medal opportunity in judo. She won silver at the previous Asian Games and has since added bronze at the 2024 world championships and silver in 2025, giving her three senior world championship medals.

Some of Kazakhstan’s most intriguing contests could come against Japanese athletes competing before a home crowd.

In Greco-Roman wrestling, Demeu Zhadrayev could meet Japan’s Nao Kusaka in a rematch of the Paris Olympic final. Zhadrayev took an early lead back then before Kusaka came back to win 5-2 and claim Olympic gold. Both return in the 77-kilogram division in Japan.

In breaking, Amir Zakirov could renew his rivalry with Japan’s Shigekix, or Shigeyuki Nakarai. Zakirov beat the Japanese star at the Breaking for Gold World Series in Kitakyushu in 2023, while Shigekix later won Asian Games gold in Hangzhou and became world champion in 2025. Both also competed at the Paris Olympics.

Medal chances

Kazakhstan’s medal ambitions extend beyond its traditional strengths in boxing, wrestling and judo.

Skeet shooter Assem Orynbay enters the Games after beating China’s Jiang Yiting at the World Cup in Almaty in May, where Orynbay hit 33 targets in the final, equaling the world record.

In athletics, former world champion Norah Jeruto could line up against Bahrain’s Olympic champion Winfred Yavi in the women’s 3,000-meter steeplechase. Yavi won the world title in 2023 and Olympic gold in Paris, while Jeruto was world champion in 2022.

Rhythmic gymnast Akmaral Yerekesheva arrives after a breakthrough first senior season. She won three medals at the 2026 Asian championships and finished sixth in the all-around at the world championships, putting her among Kazakhstan’s emerging medal prospects in Nagoya.

The men’s water polo tournament carries another long-running rivalry.

Kazakhstan won six Asian Games titles between 1994 and 2018, including one-goal victories over Japan in the finals in both 2014 and 2018. Japan reversed the balance in Hangzhou, beating Kazakhstan 15-13 in the group stage before winning gold, while Kazakhstan finished with bronze.

The two sides are drawn together again and are scheduled to meet Sept. 26.

Olympic Games official website describes China, Japan and South Korea as “three traditional powerhouses at the Asian Games.”

“Those three National Olympic Committees have won the most gold medals between them at every single Asian Games since 1978, with 1974 the last time one of those three NOCs did not win at least the third-most gold medals at the Games,” reads the website.

World.title: Kulans Released Into Wild in Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – A group of kulans has been released into the wild in the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve as part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to restore the species’ population and return it to its historical range.

The animals were transferred from Altyn Emel National Park and released into their natural habitat, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Specialists will monitor the kulans’ adaptation, movements and condition following the release.

The kulan, a wild relative of the domestic donkey, is native to the steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia. In Kazakhstan, the species disappeared from most of its historical range in the first half of the 20th century, largely due to hunting and habitat loss.

Conservation efforts have gradually helped rebuild the population. In recent years, Kazakhstan has expanded reintroduction programs to several protected areas, including Ile-Balkhash and Altyn Dala.

In October 2024, 24 kulans were transported 2,139 kilometers from Altyn Emel National Park to the Altyn Dala Nature Reserve. The 50-hour journey was part of efforts to develop safer methods for relocating wild animals over long distances.

The Ile-Balkhash reserve has become one of the key sites for restoring native wildlife. The area is part of a wider ecosystem restoration project that includes the return of species alongside measures aimed at creating suitable conditions for the future return of the Turan tiger.

The reintroduction of kulans is intended to strengthen natural ecosystems as well as increase the number of animals in the wild. As large herbivores, kulans contribute to the functioning of steppe and desert habitats by influencing vegetation and forming part of the food chain.

The latest release marks another step in Kazakhstan’s broader biodiversity conservation strategy, which increasingly focuses on restoring species in their historical habitats and rebuilding entire ecosystems rather than protecting isolated animal populations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Cross-Border QR Payments as India’s UPI Offers Blueprint
World.content:
MUMBAI – Kazakhstan is moving toward expanding its domestic QR-payment infrastructure across borders, with India among 11 countries identified for potential cross-border QR-payment cooperation. The initiative comes as cashless payments continue to account for the overwhelming majority of transactions in Kazakhstan.

According to the National Bank of Kazakhstan, 84 million payment cards were in circulation as of Aug. 1, with debit cards accounting for 81.6% and credit cards for 15.5%. In July, transactions using cards issued by Kazakh banks reached 19.9 trillion tenge (US$44.4 billion), covering 1.3 billion transactions.

Non-cash transactions accounted for 17.6 trillion tenge (US$39.3 billion) and 1.3 billion transactions, increasing 8.4% in value and 7.5% in number compared with July 2025. Internet and mobile banking comprise 77.6% of the number and 89.6% of the value of non-cash payments and money transfers, while POS terminals accounted for 21.9% and 10%, respectively.

The figures provide a growing domestic base for Kazakhstan’s efforts to make QR payments interoperable across borders.

Kazakhstan launched its national Interbank Mobile-Payment System on July 19, allowing customers of participating banks to make real-time interbank transfers and payments using phone numbers and a single QR code. The system enables merchants to accept payments from customers of various participating banks without installing new equipment.

The next step is to make such payments work across borders.

India’s UPI model

India offers one example of how a nationally interoperable payment infrastructure can evolve into a cross-border service.

Speaking to foreign journalists in Mumbai on Sept. 16, Sonal Asnani, head of Asia Pacific at NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), outlined how India developed the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) from a domestic payment infrastructure into a system with international applications.

UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), is a payment infrastructure rather than a standalone application or card. It connects banks, fintech companies and customers through a common framework, allowing users to make payments through different applications while maintaining interoperability.

“It’s not an application, it’s not a card. It’s a payment layer,” Asnani said, explaining the basic architecture of UPI.

According to Asnani, one of the key factors behind UPI’s expansion has been the division of roles across the ecosystem. The Reserve Bank of India acts as the regulator, NPCI operates the national payment infrastructure and establishes standards, banks hold customers’ accounts and funds, while fintech companies develop customer-facing services.

This model has allowed users to make payments through various applications while relying on the same underlying infrastructure.

From domestic payments to international use

NPCI created NIPL in 2020 to take Indian payment technologies and expertise to international markets.

One of its main areas of activity is cross-border merchant payments. Under UPI Global Acceptance, Indian users can make QR-based payments at participating international merchants directly from UPI-enabled applications.

Asnani noted that users can scan a participating local QR code and review the transaction amount, exchange rate, and applicable fees before completing the payment.

She said NPCI International currently works with 11 countries on international merchant-payment acceptance.

The model allows an Indian traveler to use a familiar UPI-enabled application abroad rather than relying exclusively on cash or international payment cards.

“For example, when I travel to other countries, I can scan the local QR with my UPI app and still make a payment,” Asnani said.

For Kazakhstan, which is developing cross-border QR arrangements with India and other countries, interoperability could provide a similar mechanism for travelers and merchants.

The practical question, however, is how two national payment systems can be connected while preserving their respective regulatory and technical frameworks.

Asnani highlighted that such partnerships require due diligence and compliance procedures, while the presence of an established QR-payment ecosystem in the partner country can make integration more straightforward.

“Wherever there is a high level of QR adoption, and there is a QR system, it becomes natural for us to collaborate,” she said, describing the factors considered when establishing international partnerships.

Beyond QR payments

NPCI International’s activities extend beyond merchant payments. The organization also works on cross-border person-to-person remittances and provides technology to countries seeking to develop their own domestic payment infrastructure.

Asnani said some countries have adopted elements of India’s technology to develop sovereign instant-payment or card systems rather than building such infrastructure entirely from scratch.

That approach differs from simply connecting two existing payment systems. It involves sharing technological infrastructure and experience with countries that are developing or upgrading their own national payment systems.

Kazakhstan has a well-developed digital payments ecosystem. The next step is to connect its existing infrastructure with international payment networks while ensuring seamless interoperability and maintaining regulatory oversight.

The potential use cases extend beyond tourism. Cross-border QR payments could facilitate transactions for travelers, small businesses and merchants. At the same time, interoperability between payment systems could also support broader economic and financial links between Kazakhstan and its partner countries.

The country’s growing domestic use of digital payments provides a substantial base for such expansion. In January-July, QR-code payments within Kazakhstan accounted for 2.34 billion transactions worth 11.8 trillion tenge (US$26.3 billion), according to National Bank data.

As Kazakhstan moves from domestic QR interoperability toward international connectivity, India’s experience offers one possible path. This involves building common infrastructure, allowing banks and fintech companies to compete at the customer level, and using interoperable standards to make the payment experience seamless for users.

World.title: News Digest: Rybakina’s US Open Triumph, Kazakhstan-South Korea Ties and Oil Export Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights Elena Rybakina’s U.S. Open victory, strengthened Kazakhstan-South Korea cooperation, Astana Arena’s selection to host the 2028 UEFA Super Cup, and Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its oil export routes.

S. Korea, Kazakhstan sign MOU on preservation of historic sites linked to Korea’s independence movement

South Korea and Kazakhstan have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help better preserve historical sites in the Central Asian country that are linked to Korea’s independence movement against Japan’s 1910-45 colonial rule, Seoul’s veterans ministry said Wednesday, Yonhap reported on Sept. 16.

“Under the MOU, the two countries agreed to systematically preserve the historical records and cultural value of historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement while also strengthening academic exchanges. There are 25 historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement in the central Asian country, according to the ministry,” reads the article.

Seoul Cyber University chairman receives Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk

Lee Sang-kyun, chairman of Seoul Cyber University (SCU), received Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk, recognizing his contributions to expanding online education and promoting friendly cooperation between Korea and Kazakhstan, reported The Korea Times on Sept. 16.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who visited Korea this week for the first Korea-Central Asia Summit, personally presented the order to Lee on Monday. The Order of Dostyk is one of Kazakhstan’s highest state honors, awarded to figures at home and abroad for contributions to peace, friendship, international cooperation and social harmony.

U.S. Open final: Elena Rybakina smothers Aryna Sabalenka to dethrone reigning champion

For the second time this year, Elena Rybakina is a Grand Slam champion after defeating Aryna Sabalenka. The 27-year-old from Kazakhstan toppled Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday in the U.S. Open final, denying Sabalenka’s bid to win the tournament for a third straight year, The New York Times reported on Sept. 13.

“It is Rybakina’s first U.S. Open title, and her third Grand Slam title overall. It means she leaves the tournament as both the champion and the new world No. 1: Rybakina will replace Sabalenka at the top of women’s tennis on Monday,” reads the article.

Astana Arena in the capital of Kazakhstan selected to host 2028 UEFA Super Cup

The prestigious match, UEFA Super Cup, will take place at the Johan Cruyff Arena in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2027, before passing the baton to Astana Arena in Astana, Kazakhstan, in 2028. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country, Euronews reported on Sept. 15.

The decision was made and officially announced by the UEFA Executive Committee. Since 2013, the Super Cup venue has changed every year, moving to a new location each time. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country. For the uninitiated, the UEFA Super Cup is a single-match curtain-raiser where the Champions League and Europa League winners meet.

Kazakhstan is upgrading its oil export strategy: Here’s how

Astana is looking for more ways to move its oil. Russia, its principal export outlet, is rife with disruptions. Damage to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) Black Sea terminal in November 2025 suppressed exports into early 2026, while the recent July attacks on tankers threatened roughly 1.5 million barrels per day, writes Joseph Shumunov for EU Reporter on Sept. 15.

The vulnerability would not be so enormous if 80% of Kazakh oil exports did not move through the CPC terminal near Novorossiysk. But is Kazakhstan merely searching for emergency alternatives amid instability? Or is this a transformation it has been preparing for? The answer is consequential: Kazakhstan is attempting a wholesale upgrade of its oil-export strategy, one befitting a rising regional power. It is moving from rational efficiency toward strategic resilience, from accepting routes toward shaping them, and from concentrated dependence toward managed interdependence.

World.title: Italy, Central Asia Launch B5+Italy Platform to Expand Regional Business Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – Government and business representatives from Central Asia and Italy convened on Sept. 16 in Astana for the launch of the B5+Italy platform aimed at turning growing political engagement into investment, industrial cooperation and stronger trade links across the region.

The forum in Astana brought together government officials and businesses from Italy, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, with discussions focused on connectivity, sustainable growth and new opportunities for companies operating across Central Asia.

The meeting follows the first Central Asia-Italy summit at the leaders’ level, held in Astana in May 2025, when Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the presidents of the five Central Asian states agreed to deepen cooperation across trade, investment, transport, energy and other sectors.

The platform, proposed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, is designed to complement the political dialogue in C5+1 format by giving businesses a more direct role in shaping economic cooperation.

Italian Undersecretary of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Maria Tripodi said the new business format was intended to give that political dialogue an economic dimension.

“We consider that today’s meeting is important because it is the beginning of a new era. (…) We want to transform the political dialogue into investments, partnerships and new opportunities for our countries,” Tripodi told the forum participants.

“It is the companies, in fact, that are subject to transform the political relationship into a more solid one, investing time and effort,” she said.

A dynamic market

Addressing the gathering, Kazakh Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev said the forum gives an opportunity to Italian companies to approach Central Asia increasingly as a regional market rather than five isolated economies.

“Today, Central Asia is a market with a rapidly growing economy,” said the minister. “For Italian businesses, today’s forum represents an opportunity to work with the entire region and to expand production and market presence across several countries simultaneously.”

He said Central Asia should increasingly be viewed as an interconnected economic space where companies can establish production in one country while reaching consumers and supply chains across several neighboring markets.

For Kazakhstan, the regional format also offers an opportunity to use existing business infrastructure with Italy more broadly. Shakkaliyev highlighted the Kazakh-Italian Trade House that opened in Almaty earlier this year, saying it could serve not only bilateral commerce but wider links between Italian companies and Central Asia.

Growing interest from businesses

The push toward a regional format is also coming from companies and business associations that have traditionally worked through bilateral Kazakhstan-Italy ties. Marco Beretta, president of the Italian-Kazakh Trade Association, said the leaders’ summit in May 2025 convinced businesses that cooperation could be expanded beyond the two countries.

“In the last three years, we have been working very hard in order to promote collaboration between Italy and Kazakhstan,” Beretta told The Astana Times. “But after the visit of our prime minister last year in May, we understood that a much wider scope of work can be executed.”

He described Central Asia as an increasingly important economic link for Europe and said the expansion toward a five-country regional format represented a significant shift. Beretta said the association now wants to expand its Kazakh-Italian business forum into a broader Central Asian platform while keeping Kazakhstan as its base.

Diversifying trade structure

The forum comes at a time as Italy expands its economic engagement with Central Asia, with Kazakhstan accounting for a large share of that relationship. Italy was Kazakhstan’s third-largest trading partner last year, with bilateral trade reaching almost $17 billion in 2025, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration. Trade reached $9.79 billion in January-July this year, including $9 billion in Kazakh exports to Italy and $789.6 million in imports.

But Shakkaliyev said maintaining high trade volumes alone was not enough. He pointed to the big role of commodities in the current structure of bilateral commerce.

Kazakhstan is seeking to expand exports of higher-value goods and estimates that it has an additional $307.5 million in export potential on the Italian market, particularly in metallurgy, petrochemicals, food products, chemicals and machinery.

Shakkaliyev said Kazakhstan was interested in changing the structure of trade by increasing exports of processed and higher-value products. He pointed to opportunities in agriculture, chemicals, manufacturing and industrial cooperation, while Tripodi emphasized Italian expertise in engineering, machinery and advanced industrial technologies.

This ambition reflects a broader challenge for Central Asian economies of moving from exports of raw materials toward local processing, manufacturing and bigger participation in international value chains.

Connectivity as central theme

Transport and logistics featured prominently in the forum as Central Asian states seek to strengthen links between Asian and European markets. Kazakhstan, which has invested around $35 billion in this area in the past 15 years, has promoted its position along transcontinental trade routes, particularly the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea. The Middle Corridor, formally known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, links China and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

Shakkaliyev said the region’s transport infrastructure could provide Italian producers and investors with access not only to Central Asian markets but also to wider international supply chains.

Tripodi said Italy was ready to share technology and experience to support Kazakhstan’s economic diversification, pointing to logistics as one area for cooperation.

“Our connectivity depends on growth and on being connected in a safe, self-sufficient way in large international markets,” she said. “We want Italy to be at the same time the driver of this new road to Europe and also the protagonist of its realization. Our companies are ready to contribute.”

Diversifying economic ties

Beretta pointed to logistics, agriculture, technology and petrochemicals as areas where Italian companies could work across the region. He also tied diversification to the development of higher-value production in Kazakhstan rather than continued reliance on raw-material exports.

“We need to create added value,” Beretta said.

Beretta also said one project under discussion is the development of a logistics hub in Kazakhstan accompanied by local production, including sustainable aviation fuel. He said such projects could also be part of a wider push into decarbonization, renewable power generation, sustainable development and water treatment.

“Decarbonization, power generation in a green way, sustainable development and water treatment are very important for Central Asia,” he said, stressing that Italian companies could bring technologies and industrial experience in those areas.

According to Tripodi, Italian companies have built extensive presence in oil and gas, but they are also looking to expand into renewable energy, critical minerals and areas linked to energy transition.

Shakkaliyev also noted Italy’s experience with small and medium-sized industrial companies could be particularly relevant for Central Asia, where governments are seeking investment that creates production capacity and jobs.

In her remarks, Tripodi noted the region offered a large and relatively young market of around 80 million people, combined with energy resources, critical materials and a strategic position between Europe and Asia. The country sees potential for its companies in sectors where Central Asian governments are trying to move further up value chains, she said.

Tripodi said Italian companies could contribute through design, engineering and industrial technologies as Central Asian economies seek greater diversification.

World.title: Apple TV Launches in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — Apple TV has officially launched in Kazakhstan, giving users direct access to Apple Original films and series for the first time.

The streaming service is included in all iCloud+ plans alongside Apple Arcade, with no separate Apple TV subscription required.

The basic iCloud+ plan costs 499 tenge (US$1) per month and includes 50 gigabytes (GB) of cloud storage.

The service is available on Apple devices, compatible smart TVs, gaming consoles and other platforms.

World.title: Expert: Astana’s Financial Center Rating Rises 18 Points on Structural Progress
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana’s eight-place rise in the Global Financial Centers Index 40 (GFCI 40) should ultimately be measured by whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets and greater cross-border financial activity, Bakhtiyar Tleubekov, chairman of the Management Board of Astana International Financial Centre, told The Astana Times on Sept. 18.

In the 40th edition of the Global Financial Centers Index, Kazakhstan’s capital ranked 57th among 117 financial centers worldwide, climbing eight places from 65th. Astana’s rating increased by 18 points, from 684 to 702.

Astana retains regional leadership

The city retained its leading position in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, which it has held for more than three years. Astana was followed by Cyprus, which ranked 72nd globally, and Warsaw, which placed 78th.

Astana’s rise came against a 1.09% decline in the average rating of financial centers in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. It was also named among the ten financial centers survey participants expected to play a more significant role in the global financial system over the next two to three years, ranking ninth with 45 mentions.

In the separate FinTech ranking, Astana rose four places from 55th to 51st.

“Astana’s eight-place rise and continued regional leadership send an important signal of growing confidence in the AIFC and Kazakhstan among the international financial community. For us, a position in the ranking is not an end in itself, but an independent assessment of the work we are consistently pursuing: improving the legal and regulatory environment, developing capital markets and financial technologies, and expanding international ties,” said AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov.

From ranking to capital flows

“The real measure of success is whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets, more international financial institutions operating in Kazakhstan, and greater cross-border financial activity,” Tleubekov said.

According to him, over the next two to three years, the priority is to reinforce the conditions that international investors value most: political and macroeconomic stability, a predictable and transparent regulatory environment, consistent application of the law, and effective protection of investor rights.

Astana and Kazakhstan also need to continue strengthening their role as a regional gateway connecting international capital with opportunities across Central Asia and the wider Eurasian region.

“Kazakhstan’s geographic position and growing role in trans-Caspian transport and logistics create an opportunity to complement physical connectivity with financial connectivity,” he said.

Structural progress and international confidence

Tleubekov noted that the GFCI combines assessments from financial-sector professionals with quantitative indicators from more than 80 external sources covering the business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial-sector development and reputation.

“Therefore, an 18-point increase cannot be attributed solely to improved perception, nor can it be explained by any single indicator,” he said.

He attributed Astana’s performance to both external conditions and structural progress, including Kazakhstan’s relative political and economic stability, regulatory continuity and openness to international investment.

The AIFC has been consistently developing a legal and regulatory framework based on international standards, independent dispute-resolution institutions, capital-market infrastructure, fintech and digital-asset regulation, and mechanisms for international and regional investors.

“Ultimately, progress should be measured not only by rankings, but by new investment, international companies choosing the AIFC, and new opportunities for Kazakhstan’s businesses,” Bekturov said.

The GFCI is published twice a year by the Z/Yen Group in partnership with the China Development Institute and assesses financial centers across five areas: business environment, financial sector development, infrastructure, human capital and reputation.

Continuing the conversation

The Astana Times has been following the AIFC’s development and Kazakhstan’s evolving role in the international financial system through its coverage and interviews with AIFC leadership.

At the recent Astana Finance Days, Bekturov joined discussions on the future of finance and Kazakhstan’s role in the next digital frontier.

The AIFC also recently shared the results of its first 10 years with The Astana Times team, offering a closer look at the centre’s development, growing international presence and priorities for the next decade. Also watch our YouTube interview with AIFC leadership.
