World.title: 'Disappointed' disabled community fears early NDIS cut onslaught
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Canberra community members are concerned that the closure of a local NDIS program does not bode well for the disability community ahead of looming federal cuts to the scheme.

Carers ACT will close its hub disability day program and NDIS support coordination service at the start of October, citing operating costs and funding arrangements, with advocates worried it may not be the last.

The NDIS overhaul will result in many being kicked off or prevented from accessing the now-$50 billion scheme, and being moved to yet-to-be-built state- and territory-run supports.

The overhaul is expected to save an estimated $37.8 billion over the next four years.

The Carers ACT hub program aimed to help with independent living skills and daily activities including household chores, music and social outings.

Powerful testimonies heard at NDIS inquiry The key takeaways from the six-day Senate inquiry into a proposed NDIS shake-up.

Benjamin Zarew, a disability advocate and NDIS recipient himself, said he attended the ACT Carers day program to improve his mental wellbeing and spend time out of the house.

"I feel sad, but there's opportunity with other agencies [for me]," he said.

"I'm worried about the other people who may not be aware because of their disabilities … some people have to have a constant routine, and that change is going to feel that effect."

The federal government's NDIS bill passed after a deal between Labor and the Coalition, but not without heavy criticism from the Greens and ACT senator David Pocock.

Mr Zarew said he was very "disappointed in the politicians for basically allowing this bill to go through".

Looming NDIS cuts instil fear in Canberrans NDIS recipient Nicci Carlson, who is in constant pain and may soon lose her eyesight, says cuts to the scheme are making vulnerable people living with a disability scapegoats for Australians hit hard by cost-of-living pressures.

The now-passed bill includes a detail that has been heavily criticised by those living with a disability, their advocates and others in the disability sector.

The NDIS minister of the day has been given social and community participation budget cuts of up to 50 per cent. These cover things such as hiring support workers to take participants to the doctor or supermarket.

Mr Zarew faces that particular cut himself. His own plan is poised to be slashed as the changes come into effect.

Others have warned that their plans have already been cut, despite the changes not having come into full effect yet — they will be made official in October this year.

"It's going to limit what I can do; I'm a bit nervous about that," he said of the upcoming cuts.

"It's going to be challenging for everyone… I think it is going to be really harmful.

" They say they want disabled people in the community to be out, seen and heard, but we are going back to being ghosts essentially. "

Official concerns

In a statement posted to its website, Carers ACT said: "Like many organisations across the community sector, Carers ACT is responding to increasing operating costs, funding pressures and changes across the disability and aged care sectors".

"After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to close the Hub Disability Day Program and our NDIS Support Coordination services," the statement said.

"Changes to funding arrangements mean these services have increasingly required Carers ACT to subsidise their delivery, and this is no longer financially sustainable."

MLA Laura Nuttall says people are fearful over the looming NDIS cuts. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

ACT Greens MLA Laura Nuttall said the fear is reaching fever pitch in the community as the cuts loom, as "people don't know exactly what's coming".

"People are contacting our office all the time, saying, ' Hey, please fight this; we are really scared'," she said.

"And I don't blame them; their human rights are being put up for debate."

Ms Nuttall is concerned the local ACT government does not have a safety net for disability programs which will be affected by the cuts, as they begin to roll in.

"I think a lot of people in our community feel this is the sign of the times and that this is not the first or last program that we are going to see cut for people with a disability," she told the ABC.

" Where are these supports that are supposed to catch us? …I don't think the territory is prepared for it. "

Shannon Kolack, the CEO of Act Down Syndrome and Intellectual Disability, said the closure was devastating for the disabled community, as some had attended the hub five days a week for years, and she also wasn't sure how the ACT would shoulder more of the services.

She added that the closure of the Carers ACT NDIS support program was devastating as good support coordinators are hard to find.

"Day programs especially, or programs that rely on people's social and community participation [NDIS] funding may not be able to offer services anymore," she said.

Carers ACT has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Cairns man dedicates his life savings to helping local kids thrive
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After almost three decades working with at-risk young people through government departments, Rob Hodge found there were limits when working to change things.

He said it felt like there was a philosophy that young people came with risks, and those needed to be contained.

"It was really tough to be able to provide young people opportunities," he said.

In the Cairns community, he said it was hard convincing people to care.

So, Mr Hodge left his "fairly comfortable government job" and took his own risk, building a program with his own hands, money and family.

He founded Fresh Start Academy, which works with young people, including those considered "at-risk" by the youth justice department.

"My life savings has gone into this," he said.

During the program, the participants learn hands-on skills in mechanics. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Participants learn practical trade skills on the job, with the group offering a barbering course initially and now adding mechanics, and 24 young people attending each semester.

"If we get them early and if we provide a learning space for them that invigorates them, that's the real truth to sustainable diversion," Mr Hodge said.

The program has now received $300,000 in funding until January next year through the state government's Kickstarter program.

Half of Mr Hodge's students are kids aged 15-to-17-year-old who are "disengaged" with school or considered at risk of entering the justice system.

Purpose and pride

The latest Queensland Crime Report, released in June, found Far North Queensland had the highest number of serious repeat youth offenders.

They are young people who authorities say often influence other kids to offend.

However, Mr Hodge said his experience taught him while punishment had a place, purpose and pride created lasting change.

Mr Hodge says he needed to take a risk to help kids that come with risks. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

"We have young people who have been kicked from pillar to post from the time that they were born," he said.

" They've grown up knowing that they're the have-nots. "

In an earlier barbering program, Mr Hodge watched teens change how they viewed themselves after seeing smiles on customers' faces.

"If they don't have physical gifts that can change their position, then it's only temporary," he said.

Inside the workshop

Fresh Start Academy program coordinator, and Mr Hodge's son, Traye, said the program was a "win-win" for community members who donated their cars to get fixed.

"It's a full free service by our fully qualified mechanic here, and our young people are getting a chance to really learn hands-on," he said.

Traye Hodge says the workshop operates as a cheap mechanics service, with members of the public only paying for parts. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

The teenagers attend the program twice a week, obtaining a certificate in Automotive Vocational Preparation, while working directly with cars.

The program also uses the interactions to encourage school-aged students to engage with other forms of education.

Since the first semester, four young people have gone on to apprenticeships, and another four are continuing their studies at TAFE.

Some young people, including 16-year-old Robert Cutmore, join the program, not because they are "at risk" or involved with the justice system, but so they can try learning away from a classroom.

Robert said school "just wasn't really working", and said he struggled to sit still and absorb information from the board.

The program inspires the young participants to find a future in mechanics. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

"It's more of a one-on-one thing for me, hands-on work like here at Fresh Start," he said.

Since starting the program, Robert's mentors said he had become one of their best students.

He has now applied for apprenticeships and said he has found a future in mechanics.

Immeasurable benefits

Youth Advocacy Centre chief executive Katherine Hayes said programs like Mr Hodge's were "exactly what we should be supporting" to address juvenile crime.

She said grassroots, early intervention programs built skills like turning up, accountability and confidence, which were harder to measure but just as important.

"We're dealing with complex human beings here and it's not a conveyor belt of change," she said.

However, stigma remained a major barrier because young offenders were acutely aware of how they were perceived.

Ms Hayes says grassroots, early intervention programs are essential to supporting at-risk youth.

"I think it helps contribute to a sort of nihilism in their way of thinking that 'well, I've got nothing to lose'," Ms Hayes said.

She said most young people in the system were not violent offenders, and many had a chance of "coming out better" with support.

World.title: Wallaroos collapse against France as bus fire delays game
World.content:
Australia's Wallaroos have been left frustrated by a potentially massive Test win that got away as undisciplined France somehow escaped with a 29-26 win after being 19 points down and reduced at one point to just 11 players.

On an extraordinary day of Test rugby, exacerbated by off-field drama when the second half had to be delayed due to a bus on fire adjacent to the Stade Maurice David, home fans were left almost in disbelief at how their imploding and depleted side somehow still conjured a win.

The French were at one point in the first half down to 11 players after three yellow cards, including one upgraded to a 20-minute red, and a straight red.

A bus fire near the ground delayed the start of the second half. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

It enabled the Wallaroos to power into a 19-0 lead, but that was not enough to stop France fighting back with three second-half tries, even while suffering a sixth card after the break.

Australia, who also had Michaela Leonard sent to the bin in the second half to complete the card chaos, did not help itself as the French reeled off 17 unanswered points in the final 25 minutes to turn a 26-12 deficit into the most unlikely win.

Ultimately, the four Australian tries from Britanny Merlo, Tania Naden, Caitlyn Halse and Piper Duck were not enough for them to follow up last week's comprehensive defeat by England with a morale-boosting win.

The craziness began early, with the French being hit with four cards in 20 minutes, with Ambre Mwayembe, Lea Champon and Lea Murie all binned for high tackles — Mwayembe's being upgraded to a 20-minute red — before Chloe Correa got a straight red for eye-gouging in the maul.

Australia cashed in, with Merlo rolling over from the maul for her second international try after 17 minutes, Naden peeling off to score against a side left helpless when down to 11 and Halse then scoring the Wallaroos' slickest effort after a fine team move.

But when France started getting its numbers back, it became a very different game, as it reduced the deficit to 19-12 by half-time.

After Duck's early score five minutes into the delayed second half, Pauline Bourdon went over to narrow the gap.

When Leonard was binned for a high tackle, the hosts became increasingly encouraged, only to be checked again as Charlotte Escudero got penalised for 10 minutes for her own high challenge.

France then used its maul power to go over for a 68th-minute try through hooker Elisa Riffonneau before Teani Feleu crashed over in the corner for the clincher.

The Wallaroos play in Edinburgh next week against a Scotland side that lost 66-14 to 10-try New Zealand.

AAP

World.title: Photographers' vision for struggling town creates portrait of success
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When a growing number of stores were left empty in the town of Blackall, in western Queensland, graziers Sarah Pearson and Lisa Alexander put their heads together.

It was 2016 and years of drought had taken a financial and emotional toll on the community.

Lisa Alexander and Sarah Pearson's social media campaign became a movement for Blackall. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"[We] decided we need to showcase something big, showcase our area, our community, and we thought if we had community backing, it'd get momentum," Ms Pearson said.

The pair turned to their shared passion of photography, with their #BetterInBlackall social media campaign inspiring the community to take snapshots of the region that were then used to cover empty shop windows.

The Better in Blackall project added eye-catching signs to the town featuring the community's photos. (Supplied: Sarah Pearson)

Ms Pearson said the "flow-on effect" from that one idea over the last 10 years had been incredible, with the campaign triggering a revamp of the town's annual festival and becoming the basis of Blackall's welcome signs.

Quirkiness a valuable commodity for towns

First impressions were of great importance for towns, community consultant Peter Kenyon said.

Peter Kenyon (left) took the Small Town Reinvention Conference on the road in western Queensland. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"Things that we do with our town entrance statements, the state of our main street, what shops do with their window displays, all of those things matter," he said.

"We've got to constantly be looking at our communities with fresh eyes and asking, 'What can we do?'"

For the third National Small Town Reinvention Conference, Mr Kenyon took 80 delegates from around the country on a tour through outback Queensland, visiting eight towns in the central west.

He estimated 70 per cent of small towns were dying but Queensland's outback had bucked the trend.

"If I had to list, for example, the 20 best tourist attractions or events or activities that go on in small towns, at least a dozen of them would be out here in western Queensland."

Attracting people to visit and live in a town is a key issue for many communities. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Mr Kenyon said humour and quirkiness could have a real impact for towns that wanted to reinvent themselves.

"How do we make our community a place where we all want to keep raising our family, where our young people will go off, maybe to uni or travel the world, but want to one day come back and contribute?" he asked.

Councils strengthen local relationships

After moving from the city, Ben Forbes is passionate about strengthening his remote WA community. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Ben Forbes, CEO of Yilgarn Shire Council located between Kalgoorlie and Perth, said he attended in the hope of learning how his community could turn its trajectory around.

"You can talk to anybody that's been there forever and they can remember back in the heyday," he said.

"The wheat belt's in a bit of a slump at the moment."

Mr Forbes used to work in accounting in Perth, but found he was more inspired to use his skills to help a small community.

"I think people are just very genuine out in the country. There's no facade," he said.

"They care about their community."

The Big Yellowbelly project in Isisford was sculpted using local scrap materials. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Isisford's Big Yellowbelly sculpture stood out to him as an example of how a town could unite to tell its story.

"I think more than anything, it's building that shared identity," Mr Forbes said.

"Yilgarn has a lot of really good community members, a lot of little groups, because we're quite geographically spread out.

"So for me, primarily, it's about how can we bring that together into one sort of unified thing."

Community builds on heritage

The Blackall Masonic Lodge wound down in 2016 before its conversion into a cafe. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Blackall-Tambo Regional Council has continued its focus on improving the town's presentation with its Shopfront Renewal Program, which stimulated $315,000 of co-funded investment into landscaping, signage and painting.

Blackall-Tambo Councillor Boyd Johnstone said reinventing a town took the backing of locals.

"You need to have a grassroots push for such projects to be successful."

Boyd Johnstone says grassroots movements can help towns progress. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Cr Johnstone has experience in running with an idea to inject a spark into his community.

When Blackall Masonic Lodge disbanded in 2016, he preserved and restored the heritage-listed building into a cafe, gallery and antique store with his partner Chris Kadel.

"We love our community and sort of just gut instinct knew we would be supported and it was what the community needed," he said.

The former Blackall Masonic Lodge is now a cafe, gallery and antique store. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

He recalled it was over a coffee in the refurbished building with philanthropist Owen Stockwell and Louise Campbell from not-for-profit Red Ridge Interior that an idea was born to preserve the region's cultural items.

The idea has become the ongoing $21 million Blackall Cultural Precinct project funded by the federal government, Blackall-Tambo Council and Red Ridge Interior.

The $21 million Blackall Cultural Precinct is an ongoing project. (Supplied: Blackall-Tambo Regional Council)

"We now have two giant storage facilities, which have climate-controlled storage containers, fireproof safes. Yeah, it's pretty incredible," Cr Johnstone said.

The town has also harnessed its heritage with the restoration of the Blackall Historical Woolscour and the launch of the Outback Circus Carnival.

World.title: Victoria to introduce a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for rape
World.content:
Rapists, sex offenders and family violence perpetrators, including those who drive their partner to suicide, will face tougher penalties under sweeping new laws promised by re-elected Labor government in Victoria.

Under the commitment, the government will introduce a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for rape, and increase the maximum penalties for all serious sexual offences by five years.

Offenders who murder their current or former partner will also face a standard sentence of 30 years, up from 25 years.

"We must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks," the Premier Ben Carroll said.

Two high-profile family violence cases have inspired the Victorian Labor legislative reform pledge. (ABC News: Shane Willner-Browne)

Labor, if re-elected in November, has also pledged to introduce two new laws, in a bid to crack down on what it describes as family violence "loopholes".

An Australian-first offence will be introduced to criminalise family violence offenders abandoning victims in need of urgent medical help, following the deaths of Victorian women Narelle Simmons and Belinda Jones.

The government will also legislate a new form of manslaughter for abusers who drive their partners to suicide, with research finding women who have experienced domestic and family violence are three times more likely to have attempted to take their own life.

"These changes will hold perpetrators to account and set the standard for what Victorians will never tolerate," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny said.

The proposed changes would also extend to the courtroom, with Labor promising to amend legislation so that courts can consider an accused’s history of sexual abuse, including prior convictions for the same or similar offending, as evidence at trial.

The Evidence Act would also be altered to stop lawyers from using "humiliating" and "invasive" questioning techniques during cross-examination — a process frequently described by victim-survivors as retraumatising.

High-profile cases inspire law reform pledge

Narelle Simmons, 42, died in October 2021 after being punched twice in the face then elbowed in the head by her partner, who then left her without seeking medical assistance.

A coroner found Ms Simmons death could not be medically attributed to the assault despite her partner’s admission that it caused her to "hit the ground", due to other health complications.

Her partner was charged only with common assault and failing to report a reportable death.

In July 2023, Belinda Jones — who was six to seven months pregnant — died on her bedroom floor from a severe bacterial infection, after her partner left her there overnight then waited a further two hours to call an ambulance the following morning, despite finding her cold and unresponsive.

Victorian Labor has also pledged to stop lawyers from using "humiliating", "invasive" questioning techniques during cross-examination. (ABC News: Timu King)

Her partner, according to coronial documents, who had an extensive history of committing violent offences against Ms Jones, did not face any charges over her death.

In both cases, the Victorian Coroner recommended the government consider creating a new offence of abandoning a victim in medical need, and to amend the Family Violence Protection Act to include abandonment of a victim in medical need as an example of family violence.

In August, the Victorian government passed reforms making coercive control a standalone offence, and banned the use of "good character" references during sentencing.

A Coroners Court review of 1,172 suicides in Victoria between 2009 and 2016 found 24.5 per cent of the victims had experienced domestic and family violence.

World.title: The vital public transport service you've probably never heard of
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It has helped generations of Victorians and visitors through two global pandemics, migration waves, vastly changing times and a recent V/Line shutdown.

But it is likely you have never heard of Travellers Aid, a vital cog in Victoria's public transport system that helps more than 110,000 people a year.

These days, the not-for-profit organisation mostly helps people with mobility challenges get around the state's trains, buses and trams.

However, when it began in 1916, Travellers Aid was all about providing safe passage for women and children, during a time when many husbands had left to serve in World War I.

The service has adapted over the years to cater to society's changing needs. (Supplied: Travellers Aid)

"All the men went off to fight the war, and the women were starting to come into the big cities of Australia and do the work that the men traditionally would have done," CEO Elias Lebbos says.

"That happened all over the world, but it was happening here as well."

Volunteers began meeting weary travellers arriving by boat at Melbourne's Station Pier, or by train at major city stations.

Travellers Aid also helped to find suitable accommodation for women and children arriving in the city, along with job opportunities.

At one stage, Mr Lebbos says the service took the matchmaking a step further, helping to find husbands for some women.

Throughout the years, the organisation has also helped greet and accommodate a post-World War II wave of migrants, young Asian students arriving as part of the Colombo Plan in the 1950s and anxious train passengers during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.

A Telstra outage shut down the state's V/Line services in early July, causing widespread pandemonium. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

More recently, when a Telstra outage shut down the V/Line network in early July, Travellers Aid assisted passengers by providing information, helping them to reach replacement coaches or contact family members, among other things.

An impact that grows each year

As it celebrates its 110th birthday, Mr Lebbos says Travellers Aid is by no means a small operation.



Its 100 or so staff members and about 150 devoted volunteers assisted tens of thousands of people last financial year alone, with the free service funded by a broad range of government grants, corporate partnerships, commercial revenue and public donations.

Travellers Aid buggies often take the underground route at Southern Cross Station. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

There are buggy rides — some travelling underground via the old Spencer Street subway — along with wheelchair assistance, personal care, a travel companion service, and plenty of answers to questions involving directions and timetables.

At Southern Cross Station, a quiet lounge provides a spot to rest the legs and have a friendly chat. There are also showers that can be used for a small fee by anyone, from interstate footy fans arriving on overnight trains to people experiencing homelessness.

Travellers Aid, the only service operating at this scale in Australia, also operates out of the Flinders Street, Seymour and Ballarat railway stations.

The service has helped close to 3,400 people passing through the new Parkville station since it opened in December. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Late last year, it expanded to Geelong, the new Metro Tunnel station at Parkville and Melbourne Airport, where the service will expand when the airport's new pick-up and drop-off zones open next month.

Mr Lebbos says in the past 10 years or so, the team has also begun helping fans attend events including the Australian Open and the F1 Australian Grand Prix.

"We made a conscious decision some time ago that people's disability or impairment, or whatever the mobility challenge, doesn't just disappear once they cross the kerb of the station," he says.

A chauffeur is on hand to ferry passengers with mobility challenges to Southern Cross Station's various platforms. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A ride on the 'limousine'

Close friends Bev Keane from Warrnambool and Wendy Poulter from Ardeer in Melbourne's west are regulars at the service's Southern Cross site.

"I've got a disability breathing and can't really walk much. They come and get me [from the platform]," 83-year-old Ms Keane says.

"Bev's been staying with me back in Melbourne. I sit here and wait for her to be chauffeured in the 'limousine'," jokes Ms Poulter, who is 79 and has low vision.

Wendy Poulter (left) and Bev Keane (right) enjoy riding the "limousine". (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Ms Keane has a different nickname for Travellers Aid's popular buggy.

"I call it the billycart," she quips.

The pair used to work together and have been as close as sisters for about 35 years.

Having access to help at the station makes them feel secure in their V/Line travels to visit one another.

"I don't think I'd be confident to go without this," Ms Poulter says.

Travellers Aid has been helping people find their way for 110 years. (Supplied: Travellers Aid)

Helping patients during stressful periods

At the slick new Parkville station, staff clock up thousands of steps a day providing physical and emotional support for patients and visitors heading to nearby hospitals.

Site supervisor Joel Ubias says his team has helped close to 3,400 people at Parkville since last December, when a two-year pilot program got underway.

He and his staff often proactively approach people who look like they may need a hand.

"Some people are surprised and they really appreciate the way we ask," he says.

Joel Ubias is in demand as the service's site supervisor at Parkville station. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Train travellers might be going through anything from chemotherapy to a knee replacement, or be expectant mums nearing their due date.

Others will have just received bad news about a loved one or their own medical condition.

Surrey Hills resident Seng Tan has used Travellers Aid multiple times to get from Parkville station to the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre.

The 72-year-old says cancer treatment has weakened his spine.

"I'm on painkillers, but the painkiller doesn't stop the pain," he says.

Rather than struggle through the long walk to the centre using his walking frame, Travellers Aid spirits Mr Tan there and back in a wheelchair.

"Since I started using them, I can't stop using them," he says.

Joining at 22, Karen never left

Karen Lovell is Traveller's Aid's longest-serving staff member.

Her mum Maureen had been working at the organisation's cafe in 1990 when she asked if the then-22-year-old would like cover for another staff member for a few weeks.

Karen Lovell is Travellers Aid's longest-serving staff member, clocking up 36 years so far. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"I said, 'Yeah, I'll come and fill in', and I've been here ever since," she smiles.

The cafe near the Bourke Street Mall was a meeting point for country people visiting friends and served up staples like sandwiches and apple slices, along with countless pots of tea.

While the cafe has since closed, Ms Lovell — now the site supervisor at Southern Cross — says that ethos of helping people has remained at the heart of the growing organisation.

Karen Lovell (second from right) with workmates at the Travellers Aid cafe on Swanston Street in the 1990s. (Supplied: Travellers Aid)

She often assists people who are stranded, including those fleeing domestic violence or others who have been rushed to hospital from country areas.

"They've had to go to the hospital for an emergency, and they leave their wallet behind," Ms Lovell says.

Operations manager Maria Groner says Travellers Aid has helped a huge variety of people, including a single mother of three who had moved to Australia and couldn't afford public transport fares for her children to get to school (before public transport was free for kids).

Operations manager Maria Groner says staff and volunteers hear many stories, some of them sad. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

There's also the occasional prisoner who has been released with no wallet and no way to pay for public transport.

"You hear a lot of nice stories, and some very sad stories," Ms Groner notes.

'Good for the soul', volunteer says

Ken Clearihan, who has been with the organisation since 2019, is one of the many volunteers keeping the vast operation humming along.

He volunteers for five hours each Wednesday, driving the buggy and helping with office work and customer service.

Volunteering is "good for the soul", says Ken Clearihan. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr Clearihan says Travellers Aid has provided him with a "wonderful community" and many opportunities to support others.

"We improve their day. It's good for the soul; it's good for the heart," he says.

Ms Groner says many volunteers are retirees or international students.

"For them, it's an opportunity to gain some local experience and to have access to socialising and getting to know Australian culture, and getting to an event [like the Australian Open] they would not otherwise be able to afford," she says.

A slice of goodwill in a 'transactional' world

CEO Elias Lebbos believes in some ways, our world has become far too transactional, and goodwill far too rare.

"It seems to have disappeared, and hopefully it's coming back," he says.

CEO Elias Lebbos believes Travellers Aid has changed people's mindsets about inclusion. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr Lebbos hopes Travellers Aid is doing its bit to change mindsets, particularly given Australia's aging population.

He is proud of the way the service has encouraged other organisations or businesses to see inclusion not as an afterthought, but as something they should plan for.

Mr Lebbos says it is all about connecting the dots for people's journeys.

The not-for-profit organisation wants public transport and major events to be accessible for everyone. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

He hopes the service might one day be able to do something about the gaps in public travel assistance in other parts of the country.

"We're exploring opportunities interstate and places like Queensland are an obvious one — most of Australia's aging population moves up north," he says.

"But also, there's a big event happening in 2032 — the [Brisbane] Olympics. What role can we play in that?"

World.title: 'Absolute cracker looking' flower explodes in 'super bloom' across outback
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A perfect storm of weather conditions has seen South Australia's north erupt into a sea of colour with a super bloom of Sturt's desert peas.

"We're looking at three or four times the average [rain totals for the region]," Flinders and Outback Parks and Wildlife manager, Phillip Strachan, said.

He said the wildflowers had arrived early and were continuing to bloom en masse about the Flinders Ranges — the most rangers had seen in the area since 1974.

"It's like something out of Scotland. It's phenomenal," Mr Strachan said.

Park rangers say it is the most Sturt's desert peas they have seen in the area since 1974. (Supplied: DEW)

"I've never seen anything like it. They're everywhere.

"I don't think I've seen a more beautiful flower. It depends on what you're into, but I just reckon it's an absolute cracker looking flower."

Further east, the peas have also taken over paddocks and fields on the border of South Australia and New South Wales.

Sturt's desert peas, which typically present with elongated red petals and a large black boss in the centre, are beginning to bloom across the outback. (Supplied: Bella Gale)

Zanna Gale, who runs a sheep station 270 kilometres north of Broken Hill, said the flowers were particularly outstanding this year.

Ms Gale and her family have been documenting the array of flowers in shades of white, purple and pink, which they had previously never seen.

"We haven't seen them in the house paddock like this ever before," she said.

"It looks amazing — it's unbelievable."

Zanna Gale runs a sheep station north of Broken Hill. (Supplied: Zanna Gale)

The Adelaide Botanic Gardens' senior horticulture curator Matt Coulter said the variations were unusual, estimating the traditional red and black flower accounted for about 99 per cent of sightings.

"It doesn't happen a lot, but because it's such a big flowering thing happening this year, we're actually starting to see some quite different colours," he said.

"To see these variations is … really quite incredible, you might just see one or two flowers within a big patch of the red and black ones, but they really stand out."

Residents of some of the nation's most remote places have been treated to a rare assortment of pea blossoms. (Supplied: Bella Gale)

He said the Sturt's desert pea seeds could stay dormant for "many years" in arid land until the conditions were right to grow.

"To the north of our state, we've had the most rain we've had in probably about 52 years since 1974, so all that moisture actually helps with the germination," he said.

Mr Coulter recently returned from a trip to the Flinders Ranges to see the flowers in the wild.

Amid the outback super bloom have been rarely-seen colour variations, like these white and pink blooms among the typical red and black. (Supplied: Bella Gale)

"It's a real super bloom going on this year and to see whole hillsides of them flowering … for me it was a bucket list thing to see for sure," he said.

Tricky to grow

The Adelaide Botanic Gardens grows the flower from seed collected in Roxby Downs in 1997.

"It's a really important plant to us because it's our state flora emblem of South Australia and it has been ever since the 1960s when our director at the time put it forward to become a floral emblem," Mr Coulter said.

The Adelaide Botanic Garden grows the plant from seed collected in Roxby Downs in 1997. (Supplied: Adelaide Botanic Garden)

But for green thumbs wanting to try their hand at growing the species away from its desert home, Mr Coulter warns it can be a painstaking process.

"Every single one of the seeds that we propagate, we actually look at it under a microscope and take a little nick out of it so they all will germinate at the same time, and they can germinate within two or three days by doing this technique called scarification," he said.

Mr Coulter said the plant needed very good aeration in the soil to ensure moisture did not stay around its roots.

"The funny thing is they actually like moisture, but they just don't like it to be around the roots, so you need that moisture to be able to move away," he said.

Sturt's desert peas are a protected species, meaning it is illegal to pick them on public land. (Supplied: Bella Gale)

" But the biggest killer for them is any humidity because they come from a very arid, dry environment. "

Despite the challenge, Mr Coulter did concede that the pay-off was well worth it when the flower came to fruition.

"They almost look fake, they're just so perfect," he said.

World.title: Aboriginal man's fight for justice after alleged historical abuse at hospital
World.content:
Uncle Benjamin 'BJ' Cruse says he has lived with a lifetime of trauma stemming from a few days in hospital.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names and images of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of family.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

As a young boy, he was treated for dysentery, an intestinal infection which causes severe diarrhoea, with his siblings at Macleay District Hospital on the New South Wales Mid North Coast.

The Yuin and Monaroo elder remembers being placed on a verandah with his brother and sister at the health facility now known as Kempsey District Hospital, and the rooms being partitioned with "hessian bag material".

"That's where Aboriginal people were kept," he said.

The abuse is alleged to have happened at the then-known Macleay District Hospital. (Supplied: Macleay River Historical Society)

It was here Mr Cruse alleges he was physically and emotionally abused, including being slapped multiple times on the face by a nurse.

He said he was told to kneel on the bed with his back straight, as books were stacked on his head.

"When the nurse heard the books fall on the floor … she yanked me off the bed and slapped me on both sides of the face," he said.

The now 72-year-old also claimed being given apron strings to hold in each hand and forced to follow the nurse around the ward as she treated other patients.

"If she walked too fast, I'd pull both apron strings undone and she'd turn around and slap me on both sides of the face," he said.

The almost-week long ordeal left Mr Cruse with psychological issues, he said.

Ms Cruse-Rawiri says she can recall being in a dark room. (Supplied)

His sister, Aunty Rhonda Cruse-Rawiri, recalled being kept in a dark, separate room away from other patients.

"I could see out of that room where they had all the non-Aboriginal kids and it was really bright in there, all the toys and a big rocking horse," she said.

"I remember standing at the door waiting to go out and the nurse came … shooing us back in the room.

" And the [hospital] gown we had [on] had A-B-O across the back. "

Mr Cruse (left) pictured with his dad and mum. (Supplied)

Their father, Uncle Ossie Cruse, who is now in his early 90s, also remembered the gowns from when he picked his children up from the hospital.

"And I thought, 'Wow, we're out of here'," he told Australian Story in 2017.

"I just grabbed the kids, and we never even went to see the people. We just took them out and went home."

'An insult'

Now, Mr Cruse is calling for an apology and "proper and just" compensation for his alleged abuse, taking his demands to the state government, as well as the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.

But he said on multiple occasions the government referred him to existing schemes, including the NSW Stolen Generations Reparation Scheme, and the National Redress Scheme created following the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse schemes, both of which he is not eligible for.

"This is something that has gone under the radar, it's fallen through the cracks and just because it [the alleged abuse] doesn't meet that criteria," Mr Cruse said.

"I believe it shouldn't give the government the option to opt out of their responsibility."

Mr Cruse says he wants an apology and "proper and just" compensation for his alleged abuse. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

However, since engaging lawyers, Mr Cruse said the local health district had now offered him compensation.

Though for him, he said it was not enough to make it right.

"I would receive a payment of $30,000 in the hand and to me that is an insult," he said.

" The government is holding me at ransom … knowing I can't fight the matter in court and that's why I wanted to bring the matter to the nation. "

A Mid North Coast Local Health District spokesperson said in a statement it "does not comment on matters that are the subject of legal proceedings".

"The NSW government acknowledges and remembers the survivors of historical abuse and the past failures of governments and institutions to protect them," they said.

"The NSW government remains committed to ensuring survivors of historical abuse receive appropriate support and justice."

It also said all government agencies dealing with civil claims of child abuse followed guiding principles to make "litigation a less traumatic experience for victims".

'Deemed the right thing to do'

Mr Cruse said he and his siblings were taken to the Macleay District Hospital when he was about five years old, making it the late 1950s or early 1960s.

According to the Macleay River Historical Society, segregation ended at the hospital in July 1964.

Ms Best says some historical incidents need reconciling. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Former nurse, scholar and labour historian, Odette Best, said this was "a very thick and murky era" for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander staff and patients.

"It was deemed the right thing to do that Indigenous people were not allowed to be nursed in the same ward as non-Indigenous people," Dr Best, a Gorreng Gorreng, Boonthamurra and Yugambeh woman said.

"The contested care that has actually been inflicted upon Aboriginal people has been full of abuse and neglect … [and] has left very deep ongoing scars for many, many Indigenous people."

Dr Best acknowledged while many nurses "do absolutely amazing work and do care for our communities", there were historical aspects that needed to be reconciled.

"Nursing has really got this huge history of this contested care that has really never been spoken about, talked about or addressed as a profession … that we actually participated in some pretty horrendous acts against Indigenous people," she said.

Mr Newhouse says parts of old policies still exist in today's healthcare system. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

National Justice Project CEO George Newhouse said there were still remnants of past policies within the healthcare system.

"People can die as a result of a doctor, or a nurse, or a clinician having a closed mind," he said.

"So even today we see hangovers of the segregation in the past and the low standard of healthcare provided to First Nations people."

Fear of being taken

As a child, Mr Cruse and his family moved around as his father Uncle Ossie Cruse followed the fruit and vegetable picking seasons as a seasonal worker, which led them to stay near Kempsey.

Mr Cruse as a child [bottom right] with his family. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

"For those 11 years up until 1967, we lived in tents, on the riverbanks, or on the beaches … and dad fished off the beach with nets or worked in the timber industry as a sleeper cutter," Mr Cruse said.

"So, we were what they called itinerant workers, living on the fringe camps."

The family eventually moved to Sydney where Mr Cruse and Ms Cruse-Rawiri remembered the NSW Aborigines Welfare Board visited their home.

Up until the late 1960s, the welfare board previously named the Aborigines Protection Board, controlled the lives and affairs of Aboriginal people in NSW by enforcing policies of segregation, assimilation, child removal and wage withholding.

Ms Cruse-Rawiri says she grew up fearing the authorities would take her away. (ABC News: Sarah Moss)

"They went through the house, checked all our sheets, checked the cupboards, checked everything," Ms Cruse-Rawiri said.

"When my dad came home that afternoon he [went] into the room, and we had these little brown suitcases, and dad came back out to us and said whatever you can fit into those little bags you put it in cause we are leaving.

"My nan used to say if you see a car coming … you run as fast as you can and you hide.

"We were never stolen, but we grew up with the fear of being taken."

Ever since, Mr Cruse has been an advocate for his community and was involved in the land rights movement for decades.

It is Mr Cruse's mission now to advocate for others. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

His latest fight is his most personal: he is hoping to continue advocating for those who may have fallen through the cracks, like him.

"It's something that needs to be picked up and addressed because [there's been] much suffering for [our] people and their descendants … and it's still outstanding today," he said.

"I believe this will go a long way to healing."

World.title: Third woman killed in horror weekend across NSW after Bondi stabbing
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Third woman killed in horror weekend across NSW after Bondi stabbing Rachel Rasker and Jessica McSweeney Updated September 20, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 7:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three women in NSW have died just hours apart in separate incidents across the state, including an alleged domestic violence stabbing murder of a woman in her 90s in Bondi. On Saturday, at around 9.35pm, police were called to a domestic violence incident at Mole Creek in the state’s north, where they were told a 27-year-old man had entered a property and tried to steal a vehicle before assaulting the 74-year-old male home owner. The younger man was arrested and police then went on to search the neighbouring property where they found the body of a woman in her 70s. Part of the property was damaged by fire. A crime scene has been established and an investigation launched with help from the homicide squad.



Just hours earlier, another woman, in her 90s, was fatally stabbed in a Bondi apartment in the early evening, just metres from a busy pedestrian thoroughfare and the beach. A 47-year-old man was arrested after police were called to the unit in Chambers Avenue about 5.15pm following reports of a stabbing. A man has been arrested after a woman aged in her 90s died at a Bondi home. TNV Officers attached to Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command arrived and found the woman with significant injuries. She was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics, but died at the scene.



The man, who is believed to have been known to the woman, was arrested and taken to Surry Hills police station. On Sunday morning he was charged with domestic violence murder and refused bail. He’ll appear before a bail court on Sunday. Earlier on Saturday, at a home in Kooringal, a suburb of Wagga Wagga, a 23-year-old woman was also fatally stabbed inside a home. Police established a crime scene at in Chambers Avenue, Bondi. George Chan Emergency services responded about 11.45am on Saturday morning.



NSW Ambulance paramedics and police officers performed CPR on the woman, but she died at the home. An 18-year-old was arrested at the scene, but later released without charge. Police launched a search operation for a second man, who fled the residence before the arrival of emergency services. Later on Saturday night, about 8.30pm, the man was arrested at another home in Kooringal. The 31-year-old was taken to Wagga Wagga police station. All three people are believed to have been known to each other.



One woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25, according to recent data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. Of the 98 domestic homicide victims, 46 were killed by an intimate partner, 52 were killed by a family member, 20 were the child of the offender and 21 were the parent of the offender. Police have established a crime scene at the three locations and detectives have commenced inquiries. Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion Kristy Johnson September 20, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eyewear moguls Linda and Allen Hammond have put their contemporary home in Coopers Shoot in the Byron Shire on the market with a price guide of $13.5 million to $14.5 million. Linda is the founder, designer and chief executive officer of sunglasses business Otra Eyewear, and before that co-founded another sunglasses company, Quay Australia, with her husband Allen. They sold Quay Australia to a US private equity firm for an undisclosed sum in 2016. The co-founders of Quay Australia have put their architecturally designed home in the Byron Shire on the market. Quay Australia has collaborated with numerous A-listers including Kylie Jenner, Jennifer Lopez, Paris Hilton and Chrissy Teigen. It launched in 2004 at the Falls Festival in Melbourne, Victoria. Linda and Allen’s son Zak later joined the brand, and by 2009 it had entered the global market.



Linda Hammond, who sold Quay Australia with her husband Allen Hammond and is also the founder of Otra Eyewear, said they spend most of their year travelling. Linda said they have decided to sell the home as they have another property on the Gold Coast. “It’s a lock and leave as we spend most of our year travelling,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Philanthropist’s Byron Bay home with a zen room has $15m price hopes Records show the Hammonds purchased the existing dwelling on the site for $2,085,000 in 2016, which they then knocked down, enlisting Zaher Architects to design a stunning four-bedroom, two-bathroom build over two levels. Approved DA plans lodged with council in 2019 reveal works with an estimated cost of $2,677,860. The existing pool was retained, and three sculptural feature staircases were included in the design, along with timber-lined ceilings and Italian porcelain tiles.



Leisure zones include a gym, pool, Japanese-style bath, fire pit and balconies with hinterland and coastal views extending to Lennox Head. Emma and Tom Lane. Alicia Taylor The NSW North Coast’s house price record was broken in 2023 when the Coopers Shoot hinterland home of Tom and Emma Lane, of the Oroton fashion empire family, sold for $33.65 million. The buyer was a company in which tech entrepreneur Ben Bray, co-founder of Nakatomi, and architect Grace de Rome are listed as directors. The luxury farmhouse on 48 hectares with six bedrooms and eight bathrooms is complete with a mineral-based infinity pool and spa, an infrared sauna, gym, fire pit, macadamia grove and stable area. Will Phillips and Denzil Lloyd of Byron Bay Sotheby’s International Realty are accepting expressions of interest for the Hammonds’ residence.



Author lists Centennial Park home Author Libby Hathorn renovated her Centennial Park residence in Sydney over the years, and has now decided to sell. Award-winning author Libby Hathorn has listed her Centennial Park home in Sydney with a buyer’s guide of $11.5 million as she looks to downsize locally. Libby Hathorn Fiona-Lee Quimby Hathorn has written more than 80 books for children, young adults and adult readers, and her young adult novel Thunderwith was made into a movie called The Echo of Thunder, starring Judy Davis.



Hathorn’s accomplishments include The Lady Cutler Award in 2020 for distinguished services to Australian children’s literature and a Centenary Medal in 2003 for work in children’s literature. The circa 1924 property, purchased by Hathorn and her late husband John Hathorn, has been offered to the market for the first time in 45 years. There is a main residence, a one-bed cottage and loft studio, with a total of seven bedrooms and four bathrooms. Approved DA plans lodged with council over the years reveal $99,000 worth of alterations and additions and a replaced tile roof for $40,000. The main residence has high ornate ceilings, parquetry floors, timber architraves, bold feature walls and leadlight windows. There is a grand formal dining and living zone, a marble kitchen, sunroom and landscaped gardens. The buyer’s guide for the abode is $11.5 million.



Maclay Longhurst and Robert Le of Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty are selling the home and an auction has been scheduled for October. Former advertising bigwig to offload residence Retired ad executive Peter Hamilton and his wife Christine have put their grand Southern Highlands home on the market with a price guide of $12 million. Vendors Peter and Christine Hamilton have put their grand Fitzroy Falls home in the Southern Highlands on the market. Peter was an esteemed ad executive, with roles including worldwide executive vice president and regional director for Asia-Pacific at McCann Erickson, which is now called McCann.



Records show the couple purchased the address in Fitzroy Falls for $460,000 in 2001, and Peter’s time working abroad in New York’s Manhattan inspired the design for the five-bedroom, five-bathroom house which they built from scratch. Peter, a retired ad executive, and Christine, who was an avid horse rider, built the home from scratch. The price guide is $12 million. Across 100 acres of countryside, the rural estate features American Georgian architecture, a style known for its symmetry and classical entryways. There are wraparound verandahs, a pool, and a gym that could be made into an office. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court Christine was an avid horse rider and so ample equestrian areas were included, such as stabling, tack and feed facilities, and a sand arena.



The couple also own another property on the same street in Fitzroy Falls, a slightly smaller one on 75 acres with a three-bedroom, two-bathroom residence, which is on the market with a price guide of $3.2 million through the same listing agent. Their other properties outside the Southern Highlands are a property in Sydney’s Mosman and one in Queensland’s Noosa. The Southern Highlands residences are being sold by Elizabeth O’Brien of Atlas Southern Highlands.
