World.title: Albanese leaves door open for opt-out AI regime as he visits Apple Park
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Albanese leaves door open for opt-out AI regime as he visits Apple Park Rob Harris September 20, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cupertino, California: Anthony Albanese has left the door open to an opt-out copyright regime for artificial intelligence companies, despite warnings from Australian writers, artists and other creatives that such a system would undermine fundamental copyright protections. The prime minister raised the need for international rules governing AI during a visit to California, where he met Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the global tech giant’s executive team. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a press conference at Apple Park Visitor Center in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer Australia will join a collective middle-power effort at the United Nations this week amid an attempt to shape the global response to AI and a growing debate over whether the technology is developing faster than efforts to control its risks. The race is being played out largely between the United States and China, as Washington and Beijing compete for technological and strategic advantage. Asked whether there was a danger in handing too much power to tech companies, given warnings about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, Albanese said there were risks.



Related Article United Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat “I certainly accept that there are risks, and that’s why we need to mitigate. That’s why we need to act, and that is something that’s recognised by the companies themselves.” He said the international debate was already under way among leaders preparing to attend the UN General Assembly in New York. “What is being discussed this week, and has already been the subject of interaction between leaders who’ll be attending the UN this week, is what’s the international framework as well to take advantage of the benefits but also to mitigate the risks,” Albanese said. Spruiking Australia’s pioneering social media ban for under 16s, Albanese met with Apple executives behind closed doors for an hour at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Media were briefly allowed on site for a product demonstration, including the new foldable Duo phone, but were not allowed to film or take any photos of the meeting, buildings or any Apple employees.



After doomsday warnings over AI, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (US time) he was forming an “AI force,” despite many some within the industry recently sounded the alarm about the dangers of artificial intelligence continuing to grow unchecked. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump wrote. AI giants including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have flagged that Australia’s current copyright regime was a hurdle to their increased investment in the country. When asked, Albanese did not rule out the Australian government considering an opt-out system for copyright material used to train AI models.



Instead, he stressed the need for Australia to regulate AI and said legislation establishing Australian AI standards would be introduced before the end of the year. “Part of that will be protecting intellectual property,” Albanese said. “[The debate] shows the need to regulate and the need as well to acknowledge that sitting on the sideline is not an option because this is a global phenomenon that we are having.” Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The federal government is considering how to attract major AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, to establish or expand operations in Australia. The ABC last week reported that AI companies would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one plan put forward.



Under Australia’s existing copyright regime, the owner of copyright in a piece of writing, photograph or other creative work generally has the right to control how it is reproduced and commercially exploited. Creators and rights holders have warned that an opt-out model would reverse that principle by allowing AI companies to use copyright material unless individual creators took steps to prevent it. They argue the burden should instead fall on AI companies to seek permission before using protected works to train their models. Related Article Opinion

AI Albanese isn’t just betraying authors like me. He’s selling out Australia to AI colonists Richard Flanagan Writer Booker Prize-winning Australian author Richard Flanagan argued last week in this masthead that copyright was the foundation of Australia’s creative industries rather than an impediment to AI development. “No artist I know is happy to see destroyed a system that has developed over centuries to enable them to work,” Flanagan wrote. “Copyright law is not a block or a problem - it is the foundation of all the creative industries.”



Albanese said there were three components to dealing with AI: safeguards imposed by technology companies, national regulation and an international framework. “My government wants to make sure that we get the balance right, that we empower people, whilst recognising the many benefits that new technology can bring,” he said. “But we do need to make sure, with all of these new technologies, that people remain in control, and that is something that my government is determined to do.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Rivalry, what rivalry? Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel are ‘too old’ to fight any more
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Rivalry, what rivalry? Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel are ‘too old’ to fight any more Bridget McManus September 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irish chef Colin Fassnidge and his French counterpart Manu Feildel have made no secret of their rivalry, which, in the past, has spilled over into public spats. But after more than a decade together as judges on Seven’s enduring home cooking competition My Kitchen Rules, they are tighter than ever. For the second year in a row, they’re also travelling the length and breadth of Aotearoa New Zealand in the retro caravan they call Betty, sourcing fresh ingredients and cooking for one another on the campfire, for their companion series Off the Grid with Colin and Manu. Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel with Betty the caravan in Off the Grid. “Colin and I, we had our time when we had a lot of ego, and we were those types of guys that had to be strong in the kitchen,” says Feildel. “But things have changed now, and we’ve learned … I think men worldwide are changing. I think they are a little bit more open, a little bit more sharing with the problems. “We used to be taught to be hard and to be strong, but we’re just human beings … Colin and I had our grief in the past, but we’ve spent a lot of time together. We’ve got a lot in common. We just love being together. We love cooking and hunting.”



Fassnidge jumps in: “It’s also called getting old! We’ve got less friends, and the one we have, they’re real, strong friendships.” Related Article Australian TV ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues In Off the Grid, the pair meet food producers and restaurateurs, eat famed pies, dive for paua (abalone), cook southern blue cod in a ship’s galley, and hunt wild boar. “We had a bit of backlash last year when we were hunting deer,” says Fassnidge. “It’s not a sport. We hunted it for food. It’s also education. Lots of kids don’t even know where food comes from … Because we hunted a boar in this season, we were very aware that this could come back to bite us. So we made sure that the whole story was told – that these animals are pests and they have to be eradicated. And we actually cooked what we killed, so it wasn’t just done willy-nilly. It’s all done very respectfully.” They’re about to embark on another road trip across New Zealand for season three of Off the Grid, with a fourth planned around Australia. The typically five-week shoot is a welcome change from the precision and tension of the MKR set.



This 16th season is shaping up to be as dramatic as ever, with a cast of familiar tropes set to battle it out in each other’s dining rooms. Feildel hints of “shocks and bombshells” and is excited about the inclusion of Filipino cuisine, for the first time. “We have had Malaysian, Sri Lankan, Indonesian, Chinese, and a lot in between, but we’ve never had Filipino cuisine,” says Feildel. “Australia’s discovering something new again. It’s brilliant.” Manu Feildel and Colin Fassnidge look forward to the return of simpler food in this season of MKR. In another first, there is one contestant who is already known to Fassnidge. “I wasn’t too enthused about that,” Fassnidge says. “Because it can be misconstrued that you might go easier on them. I think they pretty much learned that I wouldn’t, and they got the same as everybody else.”



This season marks a noticeable return to simpler styles of cooking. Related Article Streaming Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV “It’s come back to being more basic,” says Feildel. “We’ve had a surge of people trying to do fine dining for a while, and fine dining works when it works, but when it doesn’t, it’s terrible. When you go classic and simple, food is nicer to eat, because there are less mistakes that you can make. And if you do it well, it’s delicious.” Real-world dinner parties, says Fassnidge, shouldn’t be a pressure test. “It’s called socialising. It’s just eating around the table with friends, or having a barbecue. It should be a weekly thing. That’s the way you show your friends that you like them, by cooking for them. And don’t make it a chore. Get your mates to come and help and peel the beans. Just all get together and cook together.” MKR and Off The Grid With Colin And Manu, double series return, 7.30pm on Monday, September 28; and 9pm, Tuesday, September 29, on Seven.

World.title: ‘Growth is good’: The towns avoiding the rural death spiral
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Towns are born, and towns die. Behind the Great Dividing Range, towns are on life support. In once-prosperous farming towns, six hours between Melbourne and Sydney, the pubs are shut, and weatherboard homes are boarded up. The rain has come, turning pastures into fields of green. But resentment runs deep: over illegal clearing prosecutions, net zero, fuel prices, stagnating local economies, and a city-country divide that is fuelling distrust about decisions being made in the capitals. Fewer jobs mean fewer people. Now there aren’t enough of them to staff critical services in regional areas across NSW and Victoria. Farmers Keith Rowe and Rod Hardie in West Wyalong. Janie Barrett “If you bring the people out, then services come as well, but they can’t come out because there are no bloody services,” says Keith Rowe, a farmer in West Wyalong, a six-hour drive from Sydney and Melbourne. “We really need more new people coming into our town. And we don’t care how that mix is made up.” No political party has been able to break the economic cycle of decline in parts of regional Australia. Fewer people means schools and shops close. Children leave. In 1960, the median age in West Wyalong was 26. Now it’s 43. In nearby Grenfell, it’s 52. The impact compounds as the years roll on, then steams home when those left behind realise all they once knew might one day be gone.



“I think about it a lot,” says Rowe. “It’s a real serious dilemma we’ve got.” Rowe’s friend, farmer Rod Hardie, issues this warning: “The current system, the current economy, the current way things are running – we won’t be here.” Once upon a time the Nationals were the natural representatives of the vast tracts of land spanning Nicholls and Mallee in Victoria and the Riverina and Parkes in NSW. One Nation’s victory in the Farrer by-election in May and its surging support in national polls mean that all four are now in play. In One Nation’s regional policy mix, immigration falls behind water buybacks and anti-net zero. Nevertheless, on a national scale, the party has harnessed the emotional impact of the perceived threat of immigration to its image of Australia, regardless of whether the large cuts it is proposing might do more harm than good to the economies it wants to represent. Betty Wu in her Chinese restaurant in West Wyalong. Janie Barrett Betty Wu has owned the last Chinese restaurant in West Wyalong for three decades. Now she is voting for One Nation. “I’m voting for the lady,” she says, referring to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who once claimed Australia was being “swamped by Asians” like Wu. “Something needs to change.”



Wu, who migrated to Australia from Guangdong in South China, once had multiple competitors along West Wyalong’s main drag. Nearby restaurant Lam and May has gone takeaway only. At lunchtime on a Thursday, Wu sits alone in a banquet room, hoping someone will walk in. “It’s hard,” she says. “There are no people. It’s so quiet.” Nearby, in the regional hub of Cowra, once a postwar centre for Eastern European migrants, the shift from farmhands to an increasingly mechanised workforce has reduced the working-age population, while its retirement-age population has surged. “I suppose we are the old WASPS, the white Anglo-Saxon Protestants and Catholics; that’s virtually what the town is these days, and that’s probably why we’re so conservative,” says mayor Paul Smith. More than 75 per cent of Cowra’s 12,000 residents have parents who were both born in Australia; those who weren’t were mostly born in England, Scotland or New Zealand. A quarter of the town is aged 65 or over. Meeting the needs of that population has become more challenging. “I go to mayors’ conferences, and they’ve all got the same problem,” says Smith. “We have a brand-new hospital, which is more attractive to young graduates. The thing is, to get a doctor here, you have to have work for their partner. Now, if they’re another doctor, there’s no trouble. But if they are an engineer … that can make it difficult.”



This is the paradox facing One Nation. Newly elected One Nation Farrer MP David Farley is grappling with an electorate bordering the Riverina that already lacks enough workers to pick fruit, let alone staff hospitals. Now his party wants to cut immigration by 750,000 temporary migrants, and put Australia into three years of population decline before stabilising at 130,000 a year, 100,000 fewer than the government’s target. It remains unclear if that 130,000 figure will exclude backpackers, nurses, Pacific Australia Labour Mobility workers and other skilled workers needed in the regions, as Farley suggested last month. His leader, Pauline Hanson, did not respond to requests for an interview. Cowra Mayor Paul Smith. Janie Barrett The story across the country is not uniform. Shepparton is two hours’ drive north of Melbourne. It sits within the federal electorate of Nicholls, bordering Farley’s seat of Farrer. Hanson has a foothold here too. Shepparton’s placid CBD is home to the office of Victoria’s only state One Nation MP, upper house member Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell. Polling suggests Tyrrell could be joined by up to 11 more One Nation MPs after November’s state election. Some union-commissioned research has suggested the party could win up to 30 seats. One Nation’s vote has jumped on the back of its anti-immigration message, Resolve Political Monitor polling shows, but a lot of that support is driven by anger that has nowhere else to go. It’s a lot easier to blame migrants than it is to blame the faceless forces of inflation and globalisation.



“It’s a story as old as time, where people feel insecure and when purse strings are tight,” says Professor Alan Gamlen, the director of the migration hub at the Australian National University. “The world is changing too fast for people to comprehend, and they need a simple explanation. And it’s always been the case that blaming the outsiders, the witches, the infidels or the plague of locusts has been a really successful political strategy.” Orchard farm owner Sunny Uppal. Eddie Jim Shepparton’s One Nation voting may be surging, but it has avoided the economic fate of West Wyalong and Cowra through waves of immigration that continue to this day. Sunny Uppal’s family moved to Shepparton from India, via New Zealand, in 2003. “We always wanted to do farming because it’s in the blood,” the 41-year-old says. For generations, Uppal’s family grew potatoes and wheat in Punjab. In Shepparton, they started with 30 acres of apple orchard and today have almost 200. “I love seeing something grow out of the dirt,” he says. “The trees start to flower, the seasons change. A year goes by pretty fast here.”

World.title: Faith does not mean getting what you want
World.content:
I was five years old when I drew a wrapped parcel from a school lucky dip that contained a little statue of Mary. She wore a white veil and a blue cloak over a white dress. She was standing on the head of a snake. Her hands were spread wide, as if in welcome. Other little girls that day drew out parcels containing hair elastics or clips and I was pleased to have received something so unique, so beautiful.

The suffering of Mary brings solace to people worldwide. iStock

Mary would become my guide through life, the gentle heavenly mother, easy to relate to through the example of my own mother, who was uplifting and creative, completely selfless and endlessly loving. Mary was my second mother, a model of strength and grace, someone to turn to in difficult times.

When my husband was diagnosed with stage four cancer three years ago, a friend asked me how that revelation affected our faith. Perhaps she expected that we would be angry or bitter and rail against the unfairness of this unexpected fork in the road of our very happy life. We found that our faith only deepened through adversity.

I now felt on a visceral level the suffering of Mary standing in the shadow of the cross in her powerlessness. I had a sense of progress in faith, of reaching a stage beyond thinking of Christ on the cross, and instead seeing Christ as restored to strength with heart blazing with compassion for humanity.

World.title: John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour after his health deteriorates
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCBD John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour after his health deteriorates Fiona Byrne September 20, 2026 — 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert being held in his honour on Sunday as he is receiving 24-hour-a-day nursing care at his home after his health declined over recent months. Farnham, 77, requires continuous oxygen support and now uses a wheelchair for mobility, his family revealed in a statement released late on Saturday. John Farnham’s health has taken a downturn his family confirmed on September 19, 2026. Farnham is pictured onstage in 2016. Getty Images Farnham, whose catalogue of hits includes the Australian anthem You’re The Voice, Age of Reason, Burn For You and Touch of Paradise, was diagnosed with a cancerous tumour inside his mouth in August 2022 and underwent major surgery to have it removed. In 2023, he was declared cancer free. Since his surgery he has retired from the public spotlight to manage his health.



The revelation about Farnham’s declining health comes as beloved singer is being honoured with a star-studded concert at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on Sunday night, to celebrate his extraordinary career. The Farnham family, John’s wife Jill and sons Rob and James, provided the sad update on the star’s health owing to fans hoping he would make an appearance at The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend concert. “Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending … to watch it all happen,” the family statement, which was posted to Instagram, read. John Farnham with his son Rob on Rob’s wedding day. Facebook “Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John’s health to help explain why.



“John’s health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility. It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it. “We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John’s changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John’s fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend. “If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person. “As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable.” John Farnham with wife Jill and sons Rob (front) and James in 2018.



The family said Farnham had been “deeply moved” that the concert was being staged in his honour and by the extraordinary work of the producers, the generosity of the artists performing and the dedication of the crew and production teams working on the project. The concert, which will feature artists including Keith Urban, Richard Marx, Tina Arena, Jimmy Barnes, Mahalia Barnes, Kate Ceberano, Diesel, Human Nature, Jack Jones, Jessica Mauboy, Jon Stevens, Mitch Tambo, Mark Vincent and Ross Wilson, as well as performances via satellite by Celine Dion and Hugh Jackman, will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia. Farnham’s life is also the subject of the stage musical Whispering Jack: The John Farnham Musical, which will premiere at the Sydney Theatre Company in November. Michael Paynter has been cast as Farnham. His most famous album, Whispering Jack, this year marks 40 years since its release in October 1986. His iconic song You’re The Voice was covered by The Jonas Brothers at the historic NFL game between the LA Rams and the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG earlier this month.

World.title: How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR Catherine Strohfeldt September 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tanya Bolt said when her eldest son, Seth, chose his senior subjects at the end of year 10, university was not something on his mind. Less than a year later, as the 16-year-old began showing an interest in university courses, Bolt said picking vocational subjects was the best decision he could have made. “Chatting with his English teacher, she said, ‘It breaks my heart because it actually gives a higher ATAR than had he gone for a [standard] ATAR pathway at school’,” Bolt said. The Bolt family, including 16-year-old Seth (right), dad Carson (top), siblings Dakota (middle) and Taj (left), and mum Tanya (centre left). Tanya Bolt The Gold Coast year 11 student opted to pursue a diploma in business as a vocational education and training (VET) subject, but remained eligible for an ATAR – universities’ key criterion for student selection into tertiary courses.



In Queensland, senior students studying vocational subjects can receive an ATAR provided they meet minimum maths and English requirements, complete their VET qualification before graduating, and study four general subjects at a year 12 level. Related Article University ‘ATARmaxxing’: The school trend experts say is quashing the creative sector When these requirements are met, the Queensland Tertiary Admissions Centre (QTAC) converts vocational subjects – graded on an A-to-E scale – into a score out of 100 that can be included in students’ ATAR calculations. Bolt said pursuing a standard ATAR pathway of six general subjects across year 11 and 12 would have been “a waste of time” for Seth. “Sitting in economics, sitting in psychology, sitting in woodwork – he just had no interest whatsoever,” she said.



Instead, Bolt said her son was keen to follow his father into property development, although he had also considered a sports coaching business or, more recently, studying town planning at university. However, in Seth’s case, Bolt said the 16-year-old would likely walk “straight in” to university with his diploma alone. QTAC chief executive Chris Veraa said many Queensland universities often considered external qualifications above a certificate IV level – the step below a diploma – on their own. “Traditionally, universities have assessed VET qualifications by assigning them a selection rank or ATAR equivalent to determine an applicant’s competitiveness for entry,” he said.





Veraa said universities were increasingly offering guaranteed and direct admissions pathways based on VET qualifications, with direct entries growing by 21.2 per cent since 2024. “This reflects a broader shift in how VET is being used within tertiary pathways, with applicants increasingly considering VET as either an input to, or an alternative pathway into, higher education,” he said. World.title: Third woman killed in horror weekend across NSW after Bondi stabbing
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Third woman killed in horror weekend across NSW after Bondi stabbing Rachel Rasker and Jessica McSweeney Updated September 20, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 7:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three women in NSW have died just hours apart in separate incidents across the state, including an alleged domestic violence stabbing murder of a woman in her 90s in Bondi. On Saturday, at around 9.35pm, police were called to a domestic violence incident at Mole Creek in the state’s north, where they were told a 27-year-old man had entered a property and tried to steal a vehicle before assaulting the 74-year-old male home owner. The younger man was arrested and police then went on to search the neighbouring property where they found the body of a woman in her 70s. Part of the property was damaged by fire. A crime scene has been established and an investigation launched with help from the homicide squad.



Just hours earlier, another woman, in her 90s, was fatally stabbed in a Bondi apartment in the early evening, just metres from a busy pedestrian thoroughfare and the beach. A 47-year-old man was arrested after police were called to the unit in Chambers Avenue about 5.15pm following reports of a stabbing. A man has been arrested after a woman aged in her 90s died at a Bondi home. TNV Officers attached to Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command arrived and found the woman with significant injuries. She was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics, but died at the scene.



The man, who is believed to have been known to the woman, was arrested and taken to Surry Hills police station. On Sunday morning he was charged with domestic violence murder and refused bail. He’ll appear before a bail court on Sunday. Earlier on Saturday, at a home in Kooringal, a suburb of Wagga Wagga, a 23-year-old woman was also fatally stabbed inside a home. Police established a crime scene at in Chambers Avenue, Bondi. George Chan Emergency services responded about 11.45am on Saturday morning.



NSW Ambulance paramedics and police officers performed CPR on the woman, but she died at the home. An 18-year-old was arrested at the scene, but later released without charge. Police launched a search operation for a second man, who fled the residence before the arrival of emergency services. Later on Saturday night, about 8.30pm, the man was arrested at another home in Kooringal. The 31-year-old was taken to Wagga Wagga police station. All three people are believed to have been known to each other.



One woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25, according to recent data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. Of the 98 domestic homicide victims, 46 were killed by an intimate partner, 52 were killed by a family member, 20 were the child of the offender and 21 were the parent of the offender. Police have established a crime scene at the three locations and detectives have commenced inquiries. Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion Kristy Johnson September 20, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eyewear moguls Linda and Allen Hammond have put their contemporary home in Coopers Shoot in the Byron Shire on the market with a price guide of $13.5 million to $14.5 million. Linda is the founder, designer and chief executive officer of sunglasses business Otra Eyewear, and before that co-founded another sunglasses company, Quay Australia, with her husband Allen. They sold Quay Australia to a US private equity firm for an undisclosed sum in 2016. The co-founders of Quay Australia have put their architecturally designed home in the Byron Shire on the market. Quay Australia has collaborated with numerous A-listers including Kylie Jenner, Jennifer Lopez, Paris Hilton and Chrissy Teigen. It launched in 2004 at the Falls Festival in Melbourne, Victoria. Linda and Allen’s son Zak later joined the brand, and by 2009 it had entered the global market.



Linda Hammond, who sold Quay Australia with her husband Allen Hammond and is also the founder of Otra Eyewear, said they spend most of their year travelling. Linda said they have decided to sell the home as they have another property on the Gold Coast. “It’s a lock and leave as we spend most of our year travelling,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Philanthropist’s Byron Bay home with a zen room has $15m price hopes Records show the Hammonds purchased the existing dwelling on the site for $2,085,000 in 2016, which they then knocked down, enlisting Zaher Architects to design a stunning four-bedroom, two-bathroom build over two levels. Approved DA plans lodged with council in 2019 reveal works with an estimated cost of $2,677,860. The existing pool was retained, and three sculptural feature staircases were included in the design, along with timber-lined ceilings and Italian porcelain tiles.



Leisure zones include a gym, pool, Japanese-style bath, fire pit and balconies with hinterland and coastal views extending to Lennox Head. Emma and Tom Lane. Alicia Taylor The NSW North Coast’s house price record was broken in 2023 when the Coopers Shoot hinterland home of Tom and Emma Lane, of the Oroton fashion empire family, sold for $33.65 million. The buyer was a company in which tech entrepreneur Ben Bray, co-founder of Nakatomi, and architect Grace de Rome are listed as directors. The luxury farmhouse on 48 hectares with six bedrooms and eight bathrooms is complete with a mineral-based infinity pool and spa, an infrared sauna, gym, fire pit, macadamia grove and stable area. Will Phillips and Denzil Lloyd of Byron Bay Sotheby’s International Realty are accepting expressions of interest for the Hammonds’ residence.



Author lists Centennial Park home Author Libby Hathorn renovated her Centennial Park residence in Sydney over the years, and has now decided to sell. Award-winning author Libby Hathorn has listed her Centennial Park home in Sydney with a buyer’s guide of $11.5 million as she looks to downsize locally. Libby Hathorn Fiona-Lee Quimby Hathorn has written more than 80 books for children, young adults and adult readers, and her young adult novel Thunderwith was made into a movie called The Echo of Thunder, starring Judy Davis.



Hathorn’s accomplishments include The Lady Cutler Award in 2020 for distinguished services to Australian children’s literature and a Centenary Medal in 2003 for work in children’s literature. The circa 1924 property, purchased by Hathorn and her late husband John Hathorn, has been offered to the market for the first time in 45 years. There is a main residence, a one-bed cottage and loft studio, with a total of seven bedrooms and four bathrooms. Approved DA plans lodged with council over the years reveal $99,000 worth of alterations and additions and a replaced tile roof for $40,000. The main residence has high ornate ceilings, parquetry floors, timber architraves, bold feature walls and leadlight windows. There is a grand formal dining and living zone, a marble kitchen, sunroom and landscaped gardens. The buyer’s guide for the abode is $11.5 million.



Maclay Longhurst and Robert Le of Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty are selling the home and an auction has been scheduled for October. Former advertising bigwig to offload residence Retired ad executive Peter Hamilton and his wife Christine have put their grand Southern Highlands home on the market with a price guide of $12 million. Vendors Peter and Christine Hamilton have put their grand Fitzroy Falls home in the Southern Highlands on the market. Peter was an esteemed ad executive, with roles including worldwide executive vice president and regional director for Asia-Pacific at McCann Erickson, which is now called McCann.



Records show the couple purchased the address in Fitzroy Falls for $460,000 in 2001, and Peter’s time working abroad in New York’s Manhattan inspired the design for the five-bedroom, five-bathroom house which they built from scratch. Peter, a retired ad executive, and Christine, who was an avid horse rider, built the home from scratch. The price guide is $12 million. Across 100 acres of countryside, the rural estate features American Georgian architecture, a style known for its symmetry and classical entryways. There are wraparound verandahs, a pool, and a gym that could be made into an office. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court Christine was an avid horse rider and so ample equestrian areas were included, such as stabling, tack and feed facilities, and a sand arena.



The couple also own another property on the same street in Fitzroy Falls, a slightly smaller one on 75 acres with a three-bedroom, two-bathroom residence, which is on the market with a price guide of $3.2 million through the same listing agent. Their other properties outside the Southern Highlands are a property in Sydney’s Mosman and one in Queensland’s Noosa. The Southern Highlands residences are being sold by Elizabeth O’Brien of Atlas Southern Highlands.

World.title: Albanese leaves door open for opt-out AI regime as he visits Apple Park
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Albanese leaves door open for opt-out AI regime as he visits Apple Park Rob Harris September 20, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cupertino, California: Anthony Albanese has left the door open to an opt-out copyright regime for artificial intelligence companies, despite warnings from Australian writers, artists and other creatives that such a system would undermine fundamental copyright protections. The prime minister raised the need for international rules governing AI during a visit to California, where he met Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the global tech giant’s executive team. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a press conference at Apple Park Visitor Center in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer Australia will join a collective middle-power effort at the United Nations this week amid an attempt to shape the global response to AI and a growing debate over whether the technology is developing faster than efforts to control its risks. The race is being played out largely between the United States and China, as Washington and Beijing compete for technological and strategic advantage. Asked whether there was a danger in handing too much power to tech companies, given warnings about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, Albanese said there were risks.



Related Article United Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat “I certainly accept that there are risks, and that’s why we need to mitigate. That’s why we need to act, and that is something that’s recognised by the companies themselves.” He said the international debate was already under way among leaders preparing to attend the UN General Assembly in New York. “What is being discussed this week, and has already been the subject of interaction between leaders who’ll be attending the UN this week, is what’s the international framework as well to take advantage of the benefits but also to mitigate the risks,” Albanese said. Spruiking Australia’s pioneering social media ban for under 16s, Albanese met with Apple executives behind closed doors for an hour at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Media were briefly allowed on site for a product demonstration, including the new foldable Duo phone, but were not allowed to film or take any photos of the meeting, buildings or any Apple employees.



After doomsday warnings over AI, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (US time) he was forming an “AI force,” despite many some within the industry recently sounded the alarm about the dangers of artificial intelligence continuing to grow unchecked. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump wrote. AI giants including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have flagged that Australia’s current copyright regime was a hurdle to their increased investment in the country. When asked, Albanese did not rule out the Australian government considering an opt-out system for copyright material used to train AI models.



Instead, he stressed the need for Australia to regulate AI and said legislation establishing Australian AI standards would be introduced before the end of the year. “Part of that will be protecting intellectual property,” Albanese said. “[The debate] shows the need to regulate and the need as well to acknowledge that sitting on the sideline is not an option because this is a global phenomenon that we are having.” Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The federal government is considering how to attract major AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, to establish or expand operations in Australia. The ABC last week reported that AI companies would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one plan put forward.



Under Australia’s existing copyright regime, the owner of copyright in a piece of writing, photograph or other creative work generally has the right to control how it is reproduced and commercially exploited. Creators and rights holders have warned that an opt-out model would reverse that principle by allowing AI companies to use copyright material unless individual creators took steps to prevent it. They argue the burden should instead fall on AI companies to seek permission before using protected works to train their models. Related Article Opinion

AI Albanese isn’t just betraying authors like me. He’s selling out Australia to AI colonists Richard Flanagan Writer Booker Prize-winning Australian author Richard Flanagan argued last week in this masthead that copyright was the foundation of Australia’s creative industries rather than an impediment to AI development. “No artist I know is happy to see destroyed a system that has developed over centuries to enable them to work,” Flanagan wrote. “Copyright law is not a block or a problem - it is the foundation of all the creative industries.”



Albanese said there were three components to dealing with AI: safeguards imposed by technology companies, national regulation and an international framework. “My government wants to make sure that we get the balance right, that we empower people, whilst recognising the many benefits that new technology can bring,” he said. “But we do need to make sure, with all of these new technologies, that people remain in control, and that is something that my government is determined to do.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Rivalry, what rivalry? Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel are ‘too old’ to fight any more
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Rivalry, what rivalry? Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel are ‘too old’ to fight any more Bridget McManus September 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irish chef Colin Fassnidge and his French counterpart Manu Feildel have made no secret of their rivalry, which, in the past, has spilled over into public spats. But after more than a decade together as judges on Seven’s enduring home cooking competition My Kitchen Rules, they are tighter than ever. For the second year in a row, they’re also travelling the length and breadth of Aotearoa New Zealand in the retro caravan they call Betty, sourcing fresh ingredients and cooking for one another on the campfire, for their companion series Off the Grid with Colin and Manu. Colin Fassnidge and Manu Feildel with Betty the caravan in Off the Grid. “Colin and I, we had our time when we had a lot of ego, and we were those types of guys that had to be strong in the kitchen,” says Feildel. “But things have changed now, and we’ve learned … I think men worldwide are changing. I think they are a little bit more open, a little bit more sharing with the problems. “We used to be taught to be hard and to be strong, but we’re just human beings … Colin and I had our grief in the past, but we’ve spent a lot of time together. We’ve got a lot in common. We just love being together. We love cooking and hunting.”



Fassnidge jumps in: “It’s also called getting old! We’ve got less friends, and the one we have, they’re real, strong friendships.” Related Article Australian TV ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues In Off the Grid, the pair meet food producers and restaurateurs, eat famed pies, dive for paua (abalone), cook southern blue cod in a ship’s galley, and hunt wild boar. “We had a bit of backlash last year when we were hunting deer,” says Fassnidge. “It’s not a sport. We hunted it for food. It’s also education. Lots of kids don’t even know where food comes from … Because we hunted a boar in this season, we were very aware that this could come back to bite us. So we made sure that the whole story was told – that these animals are pests and they have to be eradicated. And we actually cooked what we killed, so it wasn’t just done willy-nilly. It’s all done very respectfully.” They’re about to embark on another road trip across New Zealand for season three of Off the Grid, with a fourth planned around Australia. The typically five-week shoot is a welcome change from the precision and tension of the MKR set.



This 16th season is shaping up to be as dramatic as ever, with a cast of familiar tropes set to battle it out in each other’s dining rooms. Feildel hints of “shocks and bombshells” and is excited about the inclusion of Filipino cuisine, for the first time. “We have had Malaysian, Sri Lankan, Indonesian, Chinese, and a lot in between, but we’ve never had Filipino cuisine,” says Feildel. “Australia’s discovering something new again. It’s brilliant.” Manu Feildel and Colin Fassnidge look forward to the return of simpler food in this season of MKR. In another first, there is one contestant who is already known to Fassnidge. “I wasn’t too enthused about that,” Fassnidge says. “Because it can be misconstrued that you might go easier on them. I think they pretty much learned that I wouldn’t, and they got the same as everybody else.”



This season marks a noticeable return to simpler styles of cooking. Related Article Streaming Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV “It’s come back to being more basic,” says Feildel. “We’ve had a surge of people trying to do fine dining for a while, and fine dining works when it works, but when it doesn’t, it’s terrible. When you go classic and simple, food is nicer to eat, because there are less mistakes that you can make. And if you do it well, it’s delicious.” Real-world dinner parties, says Fassnidge, shouldn’t be a pressure test. “It’s called socialising. It’s just eating around the table with friends, or having a barbecue. It should be a weekly thing. That’s the way you show your friends that you like them, by cooking for them. And don’t make it a chore. Get your mates to come and help and peel the beans. Just all get together and cook together.” MKR and Off The Grid With Colin And Manu, double series return, 7.30pm on Monday, September 28; and 9pm, Tuesday, September 29, on Seven.

World.title: ‘Growth is good’: The towns avoiding the rural death spiral
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Towns are born, and towns die. Behind the Great Dividing Range, towns are on life support. In once-prosperous farming towns, six hours between Melbourne and Sydney, the pubs are shut, and weatherboard homes are boarded up. The rain has come, turning pastures into fields of green. But resentment runs deep: over illegal clearing prosecutions, net zero, fuel prices, stagnating local economies, and a city-country divide that is fuelling distrust about decisions being made in the capitals. Fewer jobs mean fewer people. Now there aren’t enough of them to staff critical services in regional areas across NSW and Victoria. Farmers Keith Rowe and Rod Hardie in West Wyalong. Janie Barrett “If you bring the people out, then services come as well, but they can’t come out because there are no bloody services,” says Keith Rowe, a farmer in West Wyalong, a six-hour drive from Sydney and Melbourne. “We really need more new people coming into our town. And we don’t care how that mix is made up.” No political party has been able to break the economic cycle of decline in parts of regional Australia. Fewer people means schools and shops close. Children leave. In 1960, the median age in West Wyalong was 26. Now it’s 43. In nearby Grenfell, it’s 52. The impact compounds as the years roll on, then steams home when those left behind realise all they once knew might one day be gone.



“I think about it a lot,” says Rowe. “It’s a real serious dilemma we’ve got.” Rowe’s friend, farmer Rod Hardie, issues this warning: “The current system, the current economy, the current way things are running – we won’t be here.” Once upon a time the Nationals were the natural representatives of the vast tracts of land spanning Nicholls and Mallee in Victoria and the Riverina and Parkes in NSW. One Nation’s victory in the Farrer by-election in May and its surging support in national polls mean that all four are now in play. In One Nation’s regional policy mix, immigration falls behind water buybacks and anti-net zero. Nevertheless, on a national scale, the party has harnessed the emotional impact of the perceived threat of immigration to its image of Australia, regardless of whether the large cuts it is proposing might do more harm than good to the economies it wants to represent. Betty Wu in her Chinese restaurant in West Wyalong. Janie Barrett Betty Wu has owned the last Chinese restaurant in West Wyalong for three decades. Now she is voting for One Nation. “I’m voting for the lady,” she says, referring to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who once claimed Australia was being “swamped by Asians” like Wu. “Something needs to change.”



Wu, who migrated to Australia from Guangdong in South China, once had multiple competitors along West Wyalong’s main drag. Nearby restaurant Lam and May has gone takeaway only. At lunchtime on a Thursday, Wu sits alone in a banquet room, hoping someone will walk in. “It’s hard,” she says. “There are no people. It’s so quiet.” Nearby, in the regional hub of Cowra, once a postwar centre for Eastern European migrants, the shift from farmhands to an increasingly mechanised workforce has reduced the working-age population, while its retirement-age population has surged. “I suppose we are the old WASPS, the white Anglo-Saxon Protestants and Catholics; that’s virtually what the town is these days, and that’s probably why we’re so conservative,” says mayor Paul Smith. More than 75 per cent of Cowra’s 12,000 residents have parents who were both born in Australia; those who weren’t were mostly born in England, Scotland or New Zealand. A quarter of the town is aged 65 or over. Meeting the needs of that population has become more challenging. “I go to mayors’ conferences, and they’ve all got the same problem,” says Smith. “We have a brand-new hospital, which is more attractive to young graduates. The thing is, to get a doctor here, you have to have work for their partner. Now, if they’re another doctor, there’s no trouble. But if they are an engineer … that can make it difficult.”



This is the paradox facing One Nation. Newly elected One Nation Farrer MP David Farley is grappling with an electorate bordering the Riverina that already lacks enough workers to pick fruit, let alone staff hospitals. Now his party wants to cut immigration by 750,000 temporary migrants, and put Australia into three years of population decline before stabilising at 130,000 a year, 100,000 fewer than the government’s target. It remains unclear if that 130,000 figure will exclude backpackers, nurses, Pacific Australia Labour Mobility workers and other skilled workers needed in the regions, as Farley suggested last month. His leader, Pauline Hanson, did not respond to requests for an interview. Cowra Mayor Paul Smith. Janie Barrett The story across the country is not uniform. Shepparton is two hours’ drive north of Melbourne. It sits within the federal electorate of Nicholls, bordering Farley’s seat of Farrer. Hanson has a foothold here too. Shepparton’s placid CBD is home to the office of Victoria’s only state One Nation MP, upper house member Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell. Polling suggests Tyrrell could be joined by up to 11 more One Nation MPs after November’s state election. Some union-commissioned research has suggested the party could win up to 30 seats. One Nation’s vote has jumped on the back of its anti-immigration message, Resolve Political Monitor polling shows, but a lot of that support is driven by anger that has nowhere else to go. It’s a lot easier to blame migrants than it is to blame the faceless forces of inflation and globalisation.



“It’s a story as old as time, where people feel insecure and when purse strings are tight,” says Professor Alan Gamlen, the director of the migration hub at the Australian National University. “The world is changing too fast for people to comprehend, and they need a simple explanation. And it’s always been the case that blaming the outsiders, the witches, the infidels or the plague of locusts has been a really successful political strategy.” Orchard farm owner Sunny Uppal. Eddie Jim Shepparton’s One Nation voting may be surging, but it has avoided the economic fate of West Wyalong and Cowra through waves of immigration that continue to this day. Sunny Uppal’s family moved to Shepparton from India, via New Zealand, in 2003. “We always wanted to do farming because it’s in the blood,” the 41-year-old says. For generations, Uppal’s family grew potatoes and wheat in Punjab. In Shepparton, they started with 30 acres of apple orchard and today have almost 200. “I love seeing something grow out of the dirt,” he says. “The trees start to flower, the seasons change. A year goes by pretty fast here.”

World.title: Faith does not mean getting what you want
World.content:
I was five years old when I drew a wrapped parcel from a school lucky dip that contained a little statue of Mary. She wore a white veil and a blue cloak over a white dress. She was standing on the head of a snake. Her hands were spread wide, as if in welcome. Other little girls that day drew out parcels containing hair elastics or clips and I was pleased to have received something so unique, so beautiful.

The suffering of Mary brings solace to people worldwide. iStock

Mary would become my guide through life, the gentle heavenly mother, easy to relate to through the example of my own mother, who was uplifting and creative, completely selfless and endlessly loving. Mary was my second mother, a model of strength and grace, someone to turn to in difficult times.

When my husband was diagnosed with stage four cancer three years ago, a friend asked me how that revelation affected our faith. Perhaps she expected that we would be angry or bitter and rail against the unfairness of this unexpected fork in the road of our very happy life. We found that our faith only deepened through adversity.

I now felt on a visceral level the suffering of Mary standing in the shadow of the cross in her powerlessness. I had a sense of progress in faith, of reaching a stage beyond thinking of Christ on the cross, and instead seeing Christ as restored to strength with heart blazing with compassion for humanity.

World.title: John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour after his health deteriorates
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCBD John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour after his health deteriorates Fiona Byrne September 20, 2026 — 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert being held in his honour on Sunday as he is receiving 24-hour-a-day nursing care at his home after his health declined over recent months. Farnham, 77, requires continuous oxygen support and now uses a wheelchair for mobility, his family revealed in a statement released late on Saturday. John Farnham’s health has taken a downturn his family confirmed on September 19, 2026. Farnham is pictured onstage in 2016. Getty Images Farnham, whose catalogue of hits includes the Australian anthem You’re The Voice, Age of Reason, Burn For You and Touch of Paradise, was diagnosed with a cancerous tumour inside his mouth in August 2022 and underwent major surgery to have it removed. In 2023, he was declared cancer free. Since his surgery he has retired from the public spotlight to manage his health.



The revelation about Farnham’s declining health comes as beloved singer is being honoured with a star-studded concert at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on Sunday night, to celebrate his extraordinary career. The Farnham family, John’s wife Jill and sons Rob and James, provided the sad update on the star’s health owing to fans hoping he would make an appearance at The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend concert. “Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending … to watch it all happen,” the family statement, which was posted to Instagram, read. John Farnham with his son Rob on Rob’s wedding day. Facebook “Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John’s health to help explain why.



“John’s health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility. It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it. “We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John’s changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John’s fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend. “If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person. “As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable.” John Farnham with wife Jill and sons Rob (front) and James in 2018.



The family said Farnham had been “deeply moved” that the concert was being staged in his honour and by the extraordinary work of the producers, the generosity of the artists performing and the dedication of the crew and production teams working on the project. The concert, which will feature artists including Keith Urban, Richard Marx, Tina Arena, Jimmy Barnes, Mahalia Barnes, Kate Ceberano, Diesel, Human Nature, Jack Jones, Jessica Mauboy, Jon Stevens, Mitch Tambo, Mark Vincent and Ross Wilson, as well as performances via satellite by Celine Dion and Hugh Jackman, will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia. Farnham’s life is also the subject of the stage musical Whispering Jack: The John Farnham Musical, which will premiere at the Sydney Theatre Company in November. Michael Paynter has been cast as Farnham. His most famous album, Whispering Jack, this year marks 40 years since its release in October 1986. His iconic song You’re The Voice was covered by The Jonas Brothers at the historic NFL game between the LA Rams and the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG earlier this month.

World.title: How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR Catherine Strohfeldt September 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tanya Bolt said when her eldest son, Seth, chose his senior subjects at the end of year 10, university was not something on his mind. Less than a year later, as the 16-year-old began showing an interest in university courses, Bolt said picking vocational subjects was the best decision he could have made. “Chatting with his English teacher, she said, ‘It breaks my heart because it actually gives a higher ATAR than had he gone for a [standard] ATAR pathway at school’,” Bolt said. The Bolt family, including 16-year-old Seth (right), dad Carson (top), siblings Dakota (middle) and Taj (left), and mum Tanya (centre left). Tanya Bolt The Gold Coast year 11 student opted to pursue a diploma in business as a vocational education and training (VET) subject, but remained eligible for an ATAR – universities’ key criterion for student selection into tertiary courses.



In Queensland, senior students studying vocational subjects can receive an ATAR provided they meet minimum maths and English requirements, complete their VET qualification before graduating, and study four general subjects at a year 12 level. Related Article University ‘ATARmaxxing’: The school trend experts say is quashing the creative sector When these requirements are met, the Queensland Tertiary Admissions Centre (QTAC) converts vocational subjects – graded on an A-to-E scale – into a score out of 100 that can be included in students’ ATAR calculations. Bolt said pursuing a standard ATAR pathway of six general subjects across year 11 and 12 would have been “a waste of time” for Seth. “Sitting in economics, sitting in psychology, sitting in woodwork – he just had no interest whatsoever,” she said.



Instead, Bolt said her son was keen to follow his father into property development, although he had also considered a sports coaching business or, more recently, studying town planning at university. However, in Seth’s case, Bolt said the 16-year-old would likely walk “straight in” to university with his diploma alone. QTAC chief executive Chris Veraa said many Queensland universities often considered external qualifications above a certificate IV level – the step below a diploma – on their own. “Traditionally, universities have assessed VET qualifications by assigning them a selection rank or ATAR equivalent to determine an applicant’s competitiveness for entry,” he said.





Veraa said universities were increasingly offering guaranteed and direct admissions pathways based on VET qualifications, with direct entries growing by 21.2 per cent since 2024. “This reflects a broader shift in how VET is being used within tertiary pathways, with applicants increasingly considering VET as either an input to, or an alternative pathway into, higher education,” he said. World.title: National vows to limit screen time in schools, early childhood centres
World.content:
National vows to introduce measures to end individual-device use in early childhood education centres (ECE) and limit screen use in primary schools.

The policy

End screen and individual-device use in ECE, tightly limit screen and individual-device use in Years 1 to 3, and introduce age-appropriate limits for older primary students

Introduce a School Start Check at ECE before children transition to primary school

Introduce clearer developmental milestones throughout ECE and report this progress to parents

Identify areas where children may need additional support and address that through the Early Intervention Service

Require the writing component of twice-yearly primary school assessments to be completed on paper

National's Education spokesperson Erica Stanford said these changes would form part of National's Set Up for Success policy, focused on school readiness, better information for parents and earlier support where needed.

"Young children are spending increasingly longer on screens, at the same time as the evidence tells us we should be cautious about excessive use.

"For younger children, we want to place greater emphasis on books, handwriting, conversation, hands-on activities and direct interaction with teachers and other children," Stanford said.

She said technology still had a place in education, but said it should enhance learning, not become the default way children learn.

The second major component of Nationals promise is a 'School Start Check' at ECE before children transition to primary school.

"Teachers are reporting an increasing number of new entrants are starting school lacking basic skills such as toilet training and eating and dressing independently.

"Children are arriving at school having never held a pencil or scissors, without the oral skills they need, and many cannot identify letters in their own name," Stanford said.

World.title: Tiaki Wai warning wastewater discharged in Lower Hutt stream
World.content:
Tiaki Wai is warning that wastewater is being discharged into Lower Hutt's Waiwhetū Stream.

The organisation, which replaced Wellington Water in July, said high rainfall caused the plant in the suburb of Seaview to overflow.

It said the wastewater has been fully treated, but may cause the water to appear cloudy or murky, and have some odour.

World.title: Suffrage Day marked with promise to boost women's health, safety and financial security
World.content:
New Zealand is marking 133 years since women won the right to vote, with the Government using Suffrage Day to highlight its focus on women's economic security, health and safety.

Minister for Women Nicola Grigg said the day was a chance to honour the women who changed New Zealand's history and paved the way for future generations.

She said the suffragists had campaigned for more than the right to vote, including greater opportunity, dignity and fairness.

"The best way to honour the suffragists' legacy is to keep building a New Zealand where women and girls can fully participate, where they can lead and they can have their voices heard," she said.

New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give women the right to vote in 1893.

The Government said its focus now included improving women's health, safety and financial security.

It said the gender pay gap was 5.3 percent this year, close to its record low.

The Government was also focused on getting more women into higher-paid jobs, which it said would help close gender pay and retirement savings gaps.

The Government also said it had strengthened protections for women experiencing stalking and harassment and launched resources for stalking victims and women facing online abuse.

Former Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner Dame Judy McGregor said a narrowing gender pay gap did not necessarily mean women had economic security.

She said the 5.3 percent gender pay gap did not tell the whole story, particularly for Māori, Pacific and migrant women.

"It's great to see that the gender pay gap is coming down," she said.

"But that reflects several things. One, it doesn't account for the very much greater disparity for Māori and Pacific and migrant women."

McGregor said focusing on getting more women into higher-paid jobs overlooked those in lower-paid work.

World.content: “I had a few different political parties approach me and after talking to a lot of the people in my life who I love, and those who often can proffer some pretty critical advice, decided that I would regret it if I didn’t just try and throw myself at the wall as much as possible to pursue this deep sense of the need for fairness and justice and everybody to be able to participate in society.

World.title: Number of meth pipes, bongs seized by Customs soars
World.content:
The number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs confiscated at the border is soaring, with Customs officers seizing almost 40,000 in the first seven months of this year - more than in all of 2025.

An RNZ investigation found glass pipes for smoking meth are widely available at vape stores, $2 shops and dairies around the country

A law in place since 2014 makes it illegal to import or sell meth pipes, cannabis bongs or hash pipes

New Customs figures show importers are trying to bring a soaring number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs into the country, despite a law banning the sale or importation of drug utensils.

Over the first seven months of this year, Customs seized just under 40,000 pipes and bongs at the border - more than the 37,000 seized during all of last year and a massive 25 times more than 2024.

Earlier this year, RNZ visited vape stores, $2 shops and dairies in two Far North towns, and found roughly two-thirds openly sold glass pipes for smoking the class A drug methamphetamine, also known as meth or P.

Most shops had no age restrictions in place and some displayed the pipes on store counters, next to children's novelty items.

Anecdotal evidence suggests similar availability around the country, despite a law in force since 2014, making it illegal to import or sell meth pipes, hash pipes or cannabis bongs.

Customs northern inspections manager Jared Nicholson said prohibited drug utensils could arrive through any border pathway, including air cargo, mail, sea cargo and passenger luggage.

Meth pipes can be bought at vape stores, $2 shops and dairies around the country. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He said Customs used intelligence and risk assessment to identify goods and people of concern. Frontline officers then carried out targeted inspections and searches based on those assessments.

Critics of the ban on importing drug paraphernalia said it wouldn't solve New Zealand's drug problems, but Nicholson said minimising drug harm required action on several fronts.

"By seizing prohibited drug utensils at the border, Customs helps prevent them from being used to administer drugs or sold for criminal profit," he said. "Customs takes the illegal importation of drug utensils seriously."

If the offending was serious or commercial in scale, the people responsible could be investigated and prosecuted.

In May, Customs intercepted a shipping container at the Port of Auckland containing roughly 1600 three-litre canisters of nitrous oxide, 21,400 meth pipes and 219kg of illicit tobacco sent from China.

As a result, three men, aged 35, 39 and 44, were charged with importing and possessing prohibited goods and defrauding Customs revenue.

In another case, an Auckland couple was sentenced that same month for the large-scale importation of thousands of illegal weapons, bongs and meth pipes.

The 50-year-old man was sentenced to eight months' home detention and their company was fined $45,000.

Nicholson said the number of items seized each year could fluctuate, depending on how many commercial-scale consignments were intercepted.

While Customs has enforced the import ban for several years, an RNZ investigation this year found widespread confusion among police, politicians, councils and retailers about whether it was legal to sell meth pipes.

RNZ enquiries bounced around government departments and ministers, before a briefing paper prepared for Health Minister Simeon Brown finally confirmed selling drug utensils was against the law.

First issued in 2014 and updated in 2020, the Misuse of Drugs (Prohibited Utensils) Notice makes it illegal to import or sell cannabis bongs, hash pipes or meth pipes.

The notice spells out the physical characteristics of each type of pipe, so retailers cannot escape prosecution by claiming the pipes are intended for another purpose - such as decorative ornaments, ingesting herbs or tiny flower vases.

Glass pipes like this one seized at the border are illegal to import or sell. Supplied / Customs

The maximum penalty is three months' jail or a fine of $1000 for an individual, or $5000 for a business.

Possession of a meth pipe is a different matter. That is illegal under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, but police must prove the person caught with the pipe intended to use it for smoking meth.

Customs could not break down how many of the almost 40,000 utensils seized this year were meth pipes and how many were for smoking cannabis. Some utensils could be adapted for use with either drug, making it difficult to arrive at separate figures.

Customs data shows the number of seizure operations is falling, which suggests consignment size is increasing sharply.

The complete figures are as follows:

Number of drug utensils seized: 2023 - 5599, 2024 - 1515, 2025 - 37,068, 2026 (January to July) - 39,196

World.title: Wellington firefighters douse flames in Thorndon firetruck
World.content:
A Wellington firetruck has been taken off the road, after its engine caught fire, prompting a response from a fellow crew.

Firefighters responded in the Northland area, where they found a fire inside the Thorndon aerial-ladder truck about 6.10pm Saturday.

The flames are extinguished.

The New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union said the truck was only one of two high-reach heavy aerial-ladder trucks in the capital.

No-one was hurt in the blaze and the fire was extinguished.
